facets.q: What is the practical difference between an ASNT Level II and a code inspector certification?
facets.a: A Level II is qualified to set up, perform, interpret and report one NDT method against a written procedure. A code inspector is qualified to accept or reject the equipment against a published code and sign the disposition: interval, repair acceptance, return to service. Test scope versus equipment scope. The Level II report is an input to the code inspector's decision.

facets.q: Who issues each certificate?
facets.a: Under SNT-TC-1A your employer certifies you as a Level II through its written practice, covering training, experience, examinations and vision. ASNT's own Level II programme supplies central general and specific examinations while the employer still runs the practical and job-specific ones. API certifies code inspectors centrally under an ANSI-accredited scheme, and that certificate travels with the person.

facets.q: Can an API 510 inspector perform the ultrasonic testing themselves?
facets.a: Only if they separately hold a UT certification. The API certificate examines pressure vessel code knowledge and grants no method qualification. An inspector who wants to take their own thickness readings needs a UT Level II under a written practice or an equivalent central certificate, held and renewed on its own cycle alongside the three-year API term.

facets.q: Should internal QA inspectors hold both a pressure vessel and a piping certification?
facets.a: Both, if they sign dispositions on both equipment classes: the code and your owner-user programme point at the certificate, and cross-training without it produces someone competent who cannot sign. One certification plus documented cross-training is sufficient where the second class has a named, available signatory. Build the coverage matrix before setting the rule.

facets.q: How do the renewal cycles compare?
facets.a: API 510, 570 and 653 run a three-year term requiring 24 CPD hours, continued inspection experience and an online open-book quiz every six years, with a 90-day pre-expiry application window and a 90-day grace period. AWS CWI renews at three and six years and requires nine-year recertification by examination or 80 professional development hours. Method certificates run their own clocks.

facets.q: Which certification should a technician pursue first?
facets.a: The method certification, in almost every case. It is the entry credential, it pays immediately, and the field time it generates is what API eligibility counts: one year of inspection activity with an engineering degree, three years with a high school diploma, five or more with no formal education, all within the last ten years.

sections.heading: The difference in one signature line
paragraphs: Put both credentials against a single question: whose name goes on the disposition? An ASNT NDT Level II signs an examination report — this weld, this technique, these indications, accept or reject against the criterion in the procedure. That is a technical statement about a test. An API 510 inspector signs something categorically different: this vessel continues in service, on this interval, with this repair accepted. That is a statement about the equipment, and it carries the code, the owner-user programme and the insurer behind it.

The confusion arises because both people say 'accept' and 'reject'. The Level II accepts an indication against a procedure written and approved by a Level III. The code inspector accepts the equipment against a published code and a documented integrity case. One judgment is bounded by a procedure; the other is bounded by a code and by professional judgment about degradation the procedure never anticipated. Identical vocabulary, entirely different exposure when the decision is examined afterwards.

Every downstream difference follows from that split: who issues the certificate, what the examination tests, how long it stays valid, what happens when it lapses, and whose professional liability responds if a disposition proves wrong. Career paths diverge there too — method depth leads toward Level III and procedure ownership, while code authority leads toward fixed-equipment inspection, integrity engineering and programme ownership. The [ASNT certification path](/asnt-certification) and the API ICP path are parallel ladders, not two rungs of one.

sections.heading: Who issues the certificate is the tell
paragraphs: An ASNT NDT Level II under the SNT-TC-1A route is certified by the employer, not by ASNT. SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice that tells an employer how to build its own certification programme through a written practice covering training hours, experience, examinations and vision testing. The certificate travels with the employer, not the person. Change employers and the new one re-certifies you under its written practice, normally on the strength of your documented training history and logged experience.

ASNT also runs a central examination programme carrying the ASNT NDT Level II name, with published prerequisites per method. Ultrasonic and radiographic testing each require 12 days of training, 120 days of experience in the method and 229 days of total NDT experience, against 2 days of training and 30 days in method for penetrant testing. That programme renews every five years, and the employer still administers the visual acuity, practical and job-specific examinations under its own written practice. Central examination does not remove employer responsibility.

API ICP works the other way round. API certifies the individual centrally, the certificate is portable between employers, the programme is ANSI-accredited to ISO/IEC 17024, and the term is a fixed three years regardless of who you work for. The difference between an employer-based scheme and a central one is the whole subject of [SNT-TC-1A versus CP-189](/blog/asnt-snt-tc-1a-vs-cp-189-comparison), and the same axis explains why a code inspector's certificate follows the person while a Level II's often does not.

sections.heading: What an ASNT Level II can and cannot sign
paragraphs: A Level II selects the technique, calibrates the equipment, performs the examination, interprets and evaluates the results against the code, standard or specification named in the procedure, and writes the report. In practice they also brief Level I technicians and verify their work. In a plant, a UT Level II is the person whose thickness data feeds every corrosion rate the integrity programme uses, which makes their competence load-bearing for decisions they themselves do not make.

A Level II cannot approve the procedure they work to, cannot certify another technician, and cannot set an inspection interval or accept a repair on the equipment itself. The first two belong to a Level III; the third belongs to a code inspector. Nothing in SNT-TC-1A grants a Level II any authority over the equipment, because the certificate scope runs to the examination method and stops there. Training hour requirements differ sharply by method for exactly this reason — the technique is what is being certified.

That boundary is why method choice matters so much on a CV. Twelve training days and 120 in-method days for UT or RT against two or three days for PT and MT reflects the difficulty of the interpretation, and it maps straight through to pay. The full breakdown sits in [NDT training hour requirements by method](/blog/ndt-training-hours-requirements-by-method), and the pay consequence of that difficulty gradient shows up clearly in the [NDT Level II salary](/ndt-level-2-salary) data for the US market.

sections.heading: What a code inspector can and cannot do
paragraphs: An API 510 holder judges a pressure vessel against the code: whether inspection findings support continued service, what the next internal or on-stream interval should be, whether a repair or alteration meets the code, whether a rerating is justified. API 510 defines the authorized pressure vessel inspector as an employee of an authorized inspection agency, qualified and certified under the code, which means the authority is organisational as well as personal. The certificate alone does not confer it outside that structure.

What the certificate does not do is qualify anyone to perform an NDT method. An API 510 holder with no UT certification cannot take the thickness readings their own decision depends on. This surprises people who assume the higher-authority credential contains the lower one. It does not, at any point. The two are examined separately, recorded separately, and expire on different cycles — a fixed three years for API ICP, an employer-set or five-year cycle for the method certificate.

The same non-containment applies to welding. An API 570 inspector judging a piping repair relies on weld acceptance work an AWS CWI performs against a welding code, and on metallurgy knowledge that API 577 covers as a supplemental certification. Where those three credentials overlap and where they emphatically do not is set out in the comparison of [AWS CWI, API 577 and ASNT Level II](/compare/aws-cwi-vs-api-577-vs-asnt-level-ii), which is the fastest way to see the boundaries side by side.

sections.heading: The stack senior fixed-equipment inspectors actually hold
paragraphs: The common stack in a US refinery or terminal is a code certification against the equipment class, at least one NDT method certification at Level II, and a welding inspection credential. A tank specialist carries API 653 plus UT Level II plus CWI. A piping specialist carries API 570 plus UT and often RT interpretation, plus CWI. Each addition buys a different signature rather than a better version of the same one, which is why the stack grows sideways instead of upward.

Above that, API 571 for corrosion and materials and API 580 for risk-based inspection turn an inspector into someone who can design the programme rather than execute it, while an ASNT Level III turns them into the person who owns the procedures and certifies the technicians. Those are two different careers heading in different directions, and the [NDT Level III salary](/ndt-level-3-salary) data separates the procedure-ownership track cleanly from Level II execution work.

Stacking carries a maintenance cost that policies routinely underestimate. Each credential runs its own clock: API ICP renews every three years with 24 CPD hours and a web quiz every sixth year, AWS CWI renews at three and six years with a nine-year recertification requiring an examination or 80 professional development hours, and method certificates renew independently. A three-credential inspector has three unrelated expiry dates, which is why holding them in a [certification tracking register](/erp/ndt-personnel-certification-tracking) beats a spreadsheet.

sections.heading: Should QA inspectors hold both a vessel and a piping certification?
paragraphs: Cross-training and certification are not the same thing, and the question usually conflates them. If your internal QA inspectors sign dispositions on both pressure vessels and piping circuits, they need both API 510 and API 570, because the certificate is what the code and your owner-user programme point at. Cross-training without the certificate produces a person who is genuinely competent and cannot sign, which is the worst of both worlds — you have paid for the capability and still cannot use it.

If they sign on one class and support the other — reviewing data, coordinating scope, escalating findings — then one certification plus documented cross-training is sufficient, provided the programme names who signs for the second class and that person is reachable on the timescales your intervals demand. Build the coverage matrix first: equipment classes down one axis, shifts and turnaround phases across the other, certified signatories in the cells. The certification requirement falls out of the empty cells rather than out of a headcount rule.

The overlap argument for holding both is real and worth acting on. API 510 and API 570 share substantial ground in damage mechanisms, NDE selection, welding and repair rules, and both examinations are 170 questions over 7.5 hours with the same closed-book and open-book split. A candidate who has just passed one is at their strongest for the second, and taking them in consecutive exam windows costs considerably less preparation time than spacing them years apart.

sections.heading: The time and cost decomposition, in published third-party figures
paragraphs: API publishes its ICP fees openly, which makes half the budget easy to fix. Initial certification for API 510, 570 or 653 is $875 for API members and $1,125 for non-members; recertification is $745 and $855. API 1169 and 1184 are $435 and $580 initially, $310 and $435 to recertify. Those figures cover the examination and the certification, and nothing else — not preparation, not travel, not the standards the open-book half is sat against.

AWS publishes its own list. The CWI nine-year recertification course is $2,130 for members and $2,395 for non-members, and the Prometric endorsement examinations for MT and PT sit at $1,295 for members and $1,560 for non-members each. ASNT's Level II prerequisites are counted in training days and experience days rather than dollars, and that is where the real cost sits: 12 training days plus 120 in-method days for UT is most of a year of deliberately assigned work.

That asymmetry is the planning insight most employers miss. The code certification is a money-and-scheduling problem measured in weeks. The method certification is a time-and-supervision problem measured in months of logged experience against a written practice. Employers who treat both as 'send them on a course' get the first and miss the second entirely, and the missing piece is documented on-the-job hours — the mechanics of which are in our guide to [OJT hours log requirements](/blog/ndt-ojt-hours-log-requirements).

sections.heading: Writing the distinction into job descriptions and the written practice
paragraphs: Job descriptions cause most of this confusion in the market. A posting asking for an 'API 510 certified NDT inspector' collapses two roles into one line and attracts applicants who hold one credential and assume it implies the other. Split the requirement into two statements: the code certification required for the dispositions the role signs, and the method certifications required for the examinations the role performs, each marked required or preferred. Recruiters screen better, candidates self-select accurately, and the audit file matches the posting.

Your written practice does the same job internally. It defines your qualification levels, training and experience requirements, examinations and recertification intervals for NDT personnel, and it is the document an auditor reads to test whether your Level II certifications mean anything at all. Code certifications sit outside it and are evidenced by the API certificate itself. Keeping the two documents distinct is what stops an auditor finding a Level II signature on a code decision, which is a finding nobody argues their way out of.

The third document is the coverage matrix, and it is the one most programmes lack. Certificates in a folder prove individuals are qualified; a matrix proves the programme is covered, and auditors ask the second question. Building or rewriting all three is what [written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development) covers, and where a company has no internal Level III to hold the technical pen, an [outsourced ASNT Level III](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) can sign and maintain them.

sections.heading: Which one to get first
paragraphs: Get the method certification first, in almost every career. It is the entry credential, it generates the field experience API eligibility counts, and it pays from the first day. API ICP eligibility is written in years of experience: one year of inspection activity for a candidate with an engineering degree or three-plus years of technical military service, two years with a two-year technical degree, three years with a high school diploma, five or more with no formal education — all acquired within the last ten years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency.

The exception is the engineering graduate entering integrity work directly. With a degree and one year of qualifying inspection activity, API 510 or 653 is reachable early, and a method certification added afterwards makes that person credible in the field rather than only on paper. That order is unusual and it works only where the employer can supply supervised inspection experience quickly, which most contract shops cannot and most owner-operators can.

For welders moving across, the sequence is method certification, then CWI, then code certification once the experience clock has run — the route mapped in the [welder to NDT inspector career path](/blog/welder-to-ndt-inspector-us-career-path-2026). Whichever order you take, the credentials never substitute for one another. Atlantis delivers ASNT method training and employer programme support rather than API ICP training; see [NDT training in the USA](/training-usa) for the method side of that path.

faq.q: Does an API 510 certificate include NDT method qualification?
faq.a: No. API 510 examines code knowledge about pressure vessels. Performing UT, RT, MT, PT or ET requires a separate method certification issued by your employer under a written practice or obtained through a central scheme. The two credentials are examined separately, held separately and expire on different cycles, and holding one gives no standing under the other.

faq.q: Can an ASNT Level II set an inspection interval?
faq.a: No. A Level II interprets examinations against a procedure. Setting an inspection interval is a code decision about the equipment, assigned by API 510, 570 or 653 to the certified inspector working within an authorized inspection agency. The Level II report is an input to that decision and frequently the most important one, but it is not the decision itself.

faq.q: Is an ASNT NDT Level II certificate portable between employers?
faq.a: Under SNT-TC-1A the certificate is issued by the employer, so a new employer re-certifies you under its own written practice using your documented training, experience and examination history. Central examination results transfer; the certification decision does not. API ICP certificates are issued centrally and are portable between employers for their full three-year term.

faq.q: Do we need both API 510 and API 570 for the same inspector?
faq.a: Only if that inspector signs dispositions on both pressure vessels and piping circuits. If they sign for one class and support the other, one certification plus documented cross-training works, provided your programme names an available signatory for the second class. Where both examinations are needed, consecutive exam windows cost less preparation time than years apart.

faq.q: Which pays more, an ASNT Level III or an API code certification?
faq.a: They pay for different things and are commonly held together. Level III pay reflects procedure ownership and authority to certify other technicians; code certification pay reflects authority to disposition equipment. Compare the published bands in the [NDT Level III salary](/ndt-level-3-salary) and [NDT inspector salary](/ndt-inspector-salary) breakdowns rather than treating either credential as ranking above the other.

title: API Ended Remote ProProctor for 510, 570, 653 and 1169
description: Remote ProProctor ended for API 510, 570, 653, 1169 and 1184 in September 2024. What is still remote, and how to plan windows, seats, travel and recerts.
h1: API ICP Exam Delivery After September 2024: What a Field Team Must Plan For
answer: API discontinued remote ProProctor delivery for API 510, 570, 653, 1169 and 1184 starting with the September 2024 exam window. Those five exams are test-centre only at Prometric today. ProProctor still runs for API 571, 577, 580, 936, 982, SIRE, SIEE and SIFE. Plan travel and seat booking for the five core credentials.
expansion: Three facts are confirmed on API's own pages. Remote proctored delivery through Prometric's ProProctor application was withdrawn for API 510, 570, 653, 1169 and 1184 effective from the September 2024 exam window, and API's current scheduling page states that those five programmes are not available for remote testing. ProProctor delivery continues for the supplemental and source-inspector programmes: API 571, 577, 580, 936, 982, SIRE, SIEE and SIFE. API's stated reasons were examination security and validity, the controlled and consistent environment a test centre provides, and a stated industry preference for face-to-face proctoring. Everything else a field team plans around — three-week windows, application deadlines roughly nine weeks ahead, first-come seating at Prometric centres, and no retest inside the same window — was already true before the change and is unaffected by it.

facets.q: Are remote-proctored API ICP exams still available for our field personnel?
facets.a: Not for the core five. API 510, 570, 653, 1169 and 1184 are test-centre only at Prometric, following the withdrawal of ProProctor from the September 2024 exam window. Remote sittings remain available for API 571, 577, 580, 936, 982, SIRE, SIEE and SIFE. Confirm on the specific programme page before booking, because API's remote-eligible list changes with programme revalidations.

facets.q: What exactly changed after September 2024?
facets.a: Delivery mode, and nothing else. ProProctor remote proctoring was withdrawn for API 510, 570, 653, 1169 and 1184 beginning with the September 2024 exam window. Eligibility rules, body of knowledge, question counts, scoring and the three-year certification term were untouched. A preparation plan written before the change remains valid; only the travel and scheduling section needs rewriting.

facets.q: Why did API discontinue remote proctoring for those exams?
facets.a: API cited the need for a reliable, stable internet connection through a long sitting, technical interruptions and distractions affecting the experience, risks to examination integrity and security, and a stated industry preference for face-to-face proctoring from employers, regulators and customers. A test centre delivers a controlled environment that is consistent between candidates, which matters for an ANSI-accredited scheme.

facets.q: How far ahead do we need to apply?
facets.a: Roughly nine weeks. API's published 2026 calendar sets a 31 October 2025 deadline for the 2 to 23 January API 510 window and a 9 January 2026 deadline for the 13 March to 3 April API 653 window, a consistent nine-week lead. Candidates may only test inside the approved window and cannot move to another once scheduled with Prometric.

facets.q: What happens if a candidate fails?
facets.a: No retest is permitted inside the same exam window. The candidate reschedules for the next window through the standard application process, which pushes the attempt out by roughly a quarter and repeats the travel. Budget a contingency window for every group of candidates rather than assuming a first-time pass, because the schedule impact of a failure is months.

facets.q: Does the six-year recertification quiz require a test centre?
facets.a: No. The web quiz is an online, open-book quiz taken as part of recertification, 25 questions with a four-hour limit on API 653, not a proctored sitting. Holders in a quiz year need no window, no seat and no travel. Only initial certification, a second equipment class, or a lapse past the 90-day grace period sends someone back to a Prometric centre.

sections.heading: What is confirmed, and what this page will not claim
paragraphs: Confirmed, from API's own pages: remote proctored delivery through Prometric's ProProctor application was discontinued for API 510, 570, 653, 1169 and 1184, with the September 2024 exam window as the starting point. API's current ICP examination scheduling page states that those five programmes are not available for remote testing, and lists API 571, 577, 580, 936, 982, SIRE, SIEE and SIFE as the programmes a candidate can still take remotely. That is the entire scope of the change.

What is not confirmed, and what this page does not claim: that any of the five will return to remote delivery, that the remote-eligible list is permanent, or that any national or regional exception exists to it. API revalidates each examination programme on a five-to-seven-year cycle, and programme details move with those revalidations. Check the specific programme page on api.org before you book travel, commit a compliance date, or write a certification target into a contract.

One further point is confirmed and frequently missed: the change was to delivery only. Eligibility rules, examination content, question counts, scoring and the three-year certification term were untouched by it. If your team's preparation plan was written before September 2024, the study side of that plan is still correct and only the logistics chapter needs rewriting — a much smaller job than the volume of rumour traffic around this change would suggest to anyone reading forums.

sections.heading: Why API made the change
paragraphs: API gave four reasons publicly through the training providers that relayed the announcement: the need for a reliable and stable internet connection throughout a long remote sitting, technical interruptions and distractions affecting the examination experience, risks to the integrity and security of remotely proctored examinations, and a stated preference within industry for face-to-face proctoring. Employers, regulators and customers were named among those preferring in-person assessment as a more reliable measure of competency.

The security argument carries the most weight for the core five, because those are the credentials that carry signing authority over equipment. API 510, 570 and 653 are ANSI-accredited to ISO/IEC 17024, and accreditation applies sustained pressure on examination security and on demonstrable consistency of conditions between candidates. A test centre delivers a controlled environment identical for everyone sitting it. A remote sitting in a hotel room on a pipeline spread does not, however well the software behaves.

There is a practical read for asset owners here as well. If your corporate certification policy relies on API ICP as the credential carrying disposition authority, the delivery decision strengthens the credential you are relying on rather than weakening it, and that argument belongs in the policy document itself. How it fits into a global mandate is set out in [mandating API 510, 570 and 653 across a portfolio](/blog/should-we-mandate-api-510-570-653-portfolio-policy).

sections.heading: The window system, not the proctoring, is the real constraint
paragraphs: Remote delivery never removed the window. API ICP core examinations run in fixed three-week testing windows, and a candidate may only schedule inside the window approved on their application. Application deadlines land roughly nine weeks before a window opens. API's published 2026 calendar shows a 31 October 2025 deadline for the 2 to 23 January 2026 API 510 window, 5 December 2025 for the 6 to 27 February API 570 window, 9 January 2026 for the 13 March to 3 April API 653 window, and 6 February 2026 for the 10 April to 1 May API 1169 and 1184 window.

Once scheduled with Prometric, a candidate may reschedule inside the same window but cannot move to a different one. Miss the window entirely and the application has to be resubmitted for a new one. Fail, and no retest is permitted inside the same window — the candidate reschedules for the next one through the standard process. Those three rules govern your calendar far more tightly than the proctoring mode ever did, and they were all in place before September 2024.

The practical effect for a supervisor is a nine-week commitment horizon on every candidate. The decision to certify someone must be made roughly two months before the study period even matters, and the cost of a failed attempt is measured in months rather than weeks. Roster against the published window calendar first and fit training courses around it, never the reverse. Where expiry dates and window dates live in the same system, conflicts surface early — that is the job of a [personnel certification tracking register](/erp/ndt-personnel-certification-tracking).

sections.heading: Seats, centres and travel
paragraphs: API delivers computer-based examinations through Prometric at more than 500 locations worldwide, and seating is first come, first served. API states plainly that it does not guarantee a candidate a seat at a specific location or on a specific day inside a testing window. With remote delivery gone for the core five, that single sentence is now the binding constraint on a distributed field team rather than the footnote it used to be when ProProctor was an escape hatch.

The operational rule follows directly: book the seat on the day the application is approved, not the week before the window opens. Approval-to-booking latency is the one genuinely controllable variable in this process. Everything else — window dates, application deadlines, retest rules — is fixed by API. A crew supervisor who batches approvals and books late finds the nearest centre full and ends up choosing between a much longer drive and a later window.

Geography decides the cost. A candidate in Houston, Baton Rouge or Edmonton has centres within an hour. A candidate on a remote pipeline spread, an offshore rotation or an overseas assignment is looking at a travel day either side of a 7.5-hour sitting, and rotation schedules rarely align with three-week windows by accident. Cost that travel and the lost rotation slot into the certification decision before you commit, because it usually exceeds the examination fee itself.

sections.heading: Instant scoring moved the other end of the timeline
paragraphs: The delivery change takes the attention, but a second 2024 change moved results in the opposite direction and is worth as much to a planner. Starting with the April 2024 examination window, API ICP began providing instant scoring following most computer-based examinations. Candidates receive score reports by email from Prometric within 24 hours of testing, viewable online with the Prometric exam confirmation number, which collapsed what used to be a multi-week wait.

Final results upload to the ICP portal within three business days, and certifications issue for applications with no outstanding deficiencies. Hard-copy certificates post 2 to 4 weeks after final scores are released, once deficiencies are cleared. API rolled instant scoring out programme by programme: API 571, 577, 580, 936 and 1169 in April 2024, API 510 in May, API 570 in June, API 653 alongside TES, SIRE, SIEE, SIFE, AQ1 and AQ2 in July, and API 1184 and 982 in December.

One documented exception is worth planning around. API revalidates each programme on a five-to-seven-year cycle, and at the end of that process a new standard setting fixes the passing score. For that single administration instant scoring is suspended and results take approximately ten weeks after the last day of the testing window. API notifies candidates before an affected window opens. If a candidate's certificate expiry sits close to that date, the ten-week lag is the risk to manage, not the examination.

sections.heading: Recertification timing, which the change did not touch
paragraphs: API 510, 570 and 653 certifications run a three-year term. Recertification requires 24 continuing professional development hours per three-year cycle, continued inspection experience, and an online open-book web quiz every six years. Applications open 90 days before expiry and a 90-day grace period follows. Up to 12 CPD hours carry over into the next period, and no activity shorter than 50 contact minutes counts toward the total at all.

API tightened the CPD evidence requirements in the September 2025 revision of its programme document, and teams collecting evidence loosely will fail against it. Certificates, transcripts or letters from training providers must state the course title, delivery method, dates, instructor or provider, and the number of contact hours or CEUs earned. Documentation without verifiable contact time or an equivalent recognised measurement is not accepted, and a registration confirmation with proof of payment alone is not evidence of attendance.

For a team the consequence is that CPD has to be captured as it happens, with the right fields on the certificate, rather than assembled in the ninety days before expiry from whatever paperwork survives. Method training your technicians attend produces qualifying evidence when the provider documents it correctly, and that documentation discipline is built into how we run [corporate NDT training](/corporate-ndt-training) programmes for inspection departments.

sections.heading: The recertification quiz is online, and that matters more than people expect
paragraphs: The six-year web quiz sits outside the ProProctor withdrawal entirely. It is an online open-book quiz taken as part of the recertification process rather than a proctored sitting at a test centre — 25 questions with a four-hour limit on the API 653 programme. A certificate holder in a quiz year does not travel, does not need an approved window, and does not need a Prometric seat. Confusing the quiz with the initial examination is the most common planning error in this area.

That gives a team two very different cost profiles depending on where each holder sits in the cycle. Years one to three of a first term, and every third-year renewal, are paperwork and CPD evidence. Every sixth year adds an online quiz that costs a morning. Only initial certification, and a lapse pushing someone past the grace period into a fresh application, requires the full travel-and-window process with everything that carries.

Build the roster around that distinction. Count how many people face an initial certification against how many are simply recertifying, and the travel line usually shrinks sharply. The candidates who genuinely need a window and a seat are new hires, existing inspectors adding a second equipment class, and anyone who let a certificate run past the grace period. Everyone else recertifies from their desk, provided the CPD evidence was collected correctly along the way.

sections.heading: Fees you can budget from published figures
paragraphs: API publishes its ICP fee schedule openly, which makes the controllable part of the budget straightforward to fix. Initial certification for API 510, 570 and 653 is $875 for API members and $1,125 for non-members. Recertification is $745 and $855 respectively. API 1169 and 1184 are $435 and $580 for initial certification, and $310 and $435 to recertify. Those figures cover examination and certification only, and they are the smallest line in most plans.

The uncontrolled part is everything the withdrawal of remote delivery added: travel to a Prometric centre, one or two nights of accommodation for candidates outside a metropolitan area, and a lost field day either side of a 7.5-hour sitting. For a crew on rotation the real cost is the rotation slot, and it routinely exceeds the fee by a wide margin. Preparation courses from third-party providers sit on top of both, priced independently by each provider.

Set the budget per candidate rather than per certificate, and include a contingency for one failed attempt, because the retest rule pushes any failure into the next window and the next travel cycle. That single line — a second window budgeted for every group of candidates — is what separates certification plans that land on schedule from the ones that quietly slip a year and surface during an audit.

sections.heading: A planning checklist for a field team
paragraphs: Six steps, in order. Pull the current window calendar and application deadlines for each programme from api.org. Work backwards nine weeks and set the application submission date in your own calendar. Confirm the delivery mode on the specific programme page, because the remote-eligible list moves with revalidations. Identify each candidate's nearest Prometric centre and the travel it requires. Book the seat on the day approval lands. Budget one contingency window for every group of candidates you put forward.

Two additions for a distributed organisation. Hold certificate expiry dates, CPD hours and window dates in one register rather than across site spreadsheets, so a certificate expiring in March and a window closing in January surface as a conflict back in October when there is still time to act. And decide in advance who signs dispositions while a candidate is between certificates, because the code decision does not wait for the examination calendar to catch up.

Where a plant has no certified internal authority to cover that gap, an outsourced route works. [API 510 pressure vessel inspector services](/consulting/api-510-pressure-vessel-inspector-services) and [API 653 tank inspector services](/consulting/api-653-tank-inspector-services) cover the signature while your own people are in the certification pipeline, and an [API 510 programme audit](/consulting/api-510-program-audit) identifies the coverage gaps before an auditor does. Atlantis does not deliver API ICP training or examinations; our training work is ASNT method certification and employer programme support.

faq.q: Which API programmes can still be taken remotely?
faq.a: API's current ICP scheduling page lists 571, 577, 580, 936, 982, SIRE, SIEE and SIFE as available through ProProctor. API 510, 570, 653, 1169 and 1184 are test centre only. Verify on the individual programme page before booking travel, because the list moves as API revalidates programmes on its five-to-seven-year cycle.

faq.q: How quickly do results arrive now?
faq.a: Score reports arrive by email from Prometric within 24 hours of testing under the instant scoring programme that began with the April 2024 window, viewable online with the Prometric exam confirmation number. Final results upload to the ICP portal within three business days, and hard-copy certificates post 2 to 4 weeks after final scores release, once any deficiencies are cleared.

faq.q: Is there any exam where instant scoring does not apply?
faq.a: Yes. API revalidates each programme on a five-to-seven-year cycle, and the administration at the end of that cycle waits for a new standard setting to fix the passing score. Results for that window take approximately ten weeks after the last testing day. API notifies affected candidates before the window opens, so the delay is knowable in advance.

faq.q: Can a candidate reschedule to a different exam window?
faq.a: No, once the exam is scheduled with Prometric. Rescheduling inside the same window is permitted, subject to seat availability. A candidate who does not test inside the approved window must submit a new application for a new window, which adds another nine-week application lead time on top of the missed sitting.

faq.q: Does this change affect the API recertification cycle?
faq.a: No. The three-year term, the 24 CPD hours per cycle, the continued inspection experience requirement, the six-year online open-book quiz, and the 90-day pre-expiry application window with its 90-day grace period are all unchanged. Only the initial certification examinations moved to test-centre-only delivery.

faq.q: Should we still plan API certification for personnel on offshore or remote rotations?
faq.a: Yes, with the travel cost priced in from the start rather than discovered later. Match each candidate to their nearest Prometric centre, check that centre's availability against the three-week window, and align the sitting with a crew-change date. A candidate whose rotation cannot reach a centre inside the window needs a different window, not a different plan.

title: RT vs UT Weld Inspection: Pick by Defect Orientation, Not Cost
description: RT catches volumetric flaws, UT catches planar ones. Decide by defect orientation, thickness, access and code route — with ASME and AWS D1.1 clauses cited.
h1: Choosing Between Radiography and Ultrasonics on a Weld
answer: Choose UT when the expected defect is planar — lack of fusion, lack of penetration, cracks — or when you cannot clear the area. Choose RT when the defect is volumetric — porosity, slag — or when the client wants an image anyone can re-read years later. Thickness settles ties: AWS D1.1 caps UT of groove welds at 8 in. (200 mm).
expansion: The five queries that land on this page are all one question: which method finds the flaw that will actually be there. Ultrasonics interrogates the weld with a sound beam that reflects hardest off a surface facing it, so a vertical lack-of-fusion face in a bevel returns a strong signal. Radiography measures density loss along the beam path, so the same lack-of-fusion face — thin, tight, edge-on to the film — returns almost nothing, while a gas pore lights up. That single asymmetry drives most of the code language that follows. Everything else is a constraint stacked on top of it. AWS D1.1 8.19.1 limits conventional UT of groove welds to 5/16 in. through 8 in. inclusive. ASME lets UT replace required RT only above 1/2 in. and only with encoded, computer-based acquisition. Radiography forces an exclusion boundary; ultrasonics does not. Cost follows those three facts, not the other way round.
source: ASME BPVC Code Case 2235-13 (approval date July 9, 2014); ASME BPVC Section V Article 4 and Article 1 Mandatory Appendix I; Section VIII Div 1 UW-51(a)(4) and Section VIII Div 2 para. 7.5.5, as summarised by Hartford Steam Boiler; AWS D1.1/D1.1M:2025 Structural Welding Code — Steel, Clause 8 Parts E and F, Tables 8.2 and 8.3, Annex G, Annex H (Normative) and Annex N; 10 CFR 20.1003, 20.1301 and 34.43.

Code Case 2235-13 carries an approval date of July 9, 2014 and addresses Section I and Section XII; Section VIII Division 1 routes through UW-51(a)(4) instead.

facets.q: Which method finds lack of fusion more reliably?
facets.a: Ultrasonics. Lack of sidewall fusion is a flat face lying parallel to the bevel, which presents a mirror to an angled sound beam and returns high amplitude. The same flaw is a few thousandths of an inch of missing metal along the radiographic beam path, so it produces almost no density change on film. Angle-beam UT or PAUT is the correct call whenever the procedure history shows fusion defects.

facets.q: Which method finds porosity and slag more reliably?
facets.a: Radiography. Rounded voids and slag pockets have genuine volume, remove density along the beam path, and appear as unambiguous dark indications that a second reader confirms without re-scanning anything. Ultrasonics detects them, but scattered small reflectors are slower to characterise and easier to dismiss as noise. Where the dominant repair mode on a job is porosity, RT stays the efficient choice.

facets.q: Does UT need access to both sides of the weld?
facets.a: No. Ultrasonics scans from one surface, which is why it survives on vessels with internals, on nozzles, on pipe with limited clearance and on structures where the back face is buried. Radiography needs the source on one side and film or a digital detector on the other. On a closed vessel or a backed joint, that requirement alone eliminates RT before any technical comparison starts.

facets.q: How large is a radiographic exclusion zone in practice?
facets.a: It is set by survey, not by a fixed number. 10 CFR 20.1003 defines a radiation area as more than 0.005 rem in 1 hour at 30 cm and a high radiation area as more than 0.1 rem in 1 hour at 30 cm. 10 CFR 20.1301 caps the dose in an unrestricted area at 0.002 rem in any one hour. The radiographer sets and watches the boundary against those readings.

facets.q: Which method leaves the better permanent record?
facets.a: Both, once the ultrasonic examination is encoded. Radiographic film or a digital image is re-readable by anyone. Manual UT leaves a report of one person's opinion. Encoded PAUT and TOFD close that gap: ASME Code Case 2235-13(e) requires the data set to be recorded in unprocessed form with no gating, filtering or thresholding, so a third party reopens the raw response later.

facets.q: Is UT cheaper than RT on a weld inspection job?
facets.a: On the shot itself, RT is often cheaper per weld on thin wall. On the project, UT wins whenever radiography stops other trades. Encoded PAUT costs more per weld in equipment and qualified time, then returns it by removing night shifts, exclusion boundaries and the standby crews that sit idle while a source is exposed. Price the schedule, not the line item.

sections.heading: Start With the Defect You Expect, Not the Kit in the Van
paragraphs: Every argument about RT versus UT collapses once you name the flaw. A root pass with a cold lap, a bevel face that never fused, a hydrogen crack running down a heat-affected zone — those are planar. They have almost no volume to remove density from a radiographic image, and they sit at angles that put a flat reflecting face square into an angled sound beam. Porosity, slag inclusions and shrinkage cavities are the opposite: real volume, low aspect ratio, no preferred orientation. Decide which family the process is likely to produce and the method chooses itself.

Process history tells you which family to expect. Submerged arc on heavy plate with a tight bevel generates lack of sidewall fusion. Manual SMAW out of position with damp consumables generates porosity and slag. Pipe welded with a hot-pass problem generates lack of penetration at the root. A fabricator running the same procedure for two years already knows their failure mode from the repair log. Pull that log before writing the NDE plan rather than after the first rejection, and the method selection stops being a preference argument.

This is the step most NDE specifications skip, and it is the one that decides whether a programme pays for itself. Writing the method choice into the procedure with the reasoning attached is exactly what a [written practice and NDT procedure development engagement](/consulting/written-practice-development) produces. Where a plant has inherited a spec that calls radiography on everything out of habit, an [NDT programme audit and gap assessment](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) tends to find the same avoidable cost sitting in the same place: RT ordered against a failure mode RT does not see well.

sections.heading: Orientation Is the Whole Argument
paragraphs: Radiography is a transmission method. It records how much energy survives the path through the part, so it responds to the thickness of material removed along that path. A spherical pore 1 mm across removes 1 mm of steel from the path and shows up. A lack-of-fusion plane 0.05 mm wide removes 0.05 mm from the path when it lies edge-on to the beam and disappears into film grain. Rotate that same plane so its width lies along the beam and it becomes visible — which is why radiographers chase source angles on suspected planar flaws.

Ultrasonics is a reflection method. It responds to acoustic impedance mismatch across a surface and to how much of the beam that surface throws back toward the receiver. A flat face perpendicular to the beam returns nearly everything. A face tilted away returns a fraction. A spherical pore scatters in every direction and returns a modest signal from any angle. So the two methods have opposite blind spots, and the blind spots are geometric rather than a matter of equipment quality.

The practical consequence is that neither method is a superset of the other, and specifications that treat one as a straight substitute produce escapes. Where the same joint carries both risks — a heavy-wall nozzle with fusion risk on the bevel and porosity risk in the cap — the defensible answer is UT for the volume and a surface method for the cap, not a single volumetric shot chosen on price. Getting that combination approved is routine work for an [outsourced ASNT Level III](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services).

sections.heading: Thickness and Geometry Set Hard Boundaries
paragraphs: AWS D1.1 draws the line explicitly. Clause 8.19.1 applies conventional ultrasonic testing to groove welds and heat-affected zones from 5/16 in. (8 mm) through 8 in. (200 mm) inclusive, and excludes tube-to-tube T-, Y- and K-connections from that procedure. Below 5/16 in. the near-field and the geometry of the entry surface stop conventional angle-beam work from resolving anything useful, and radiography takes the joint. Above 8 in. the code sends you to a qualified alternative rather than the standard clause.

ASME sets a different floor for a different purpose. Code Case 2235-13 permits ultrasonic examination in lieu of radiography on welds in material 1/2 in. (13 mm) or greater in thickness. Below that thickness there is no in-lieu-of route under that Case at all, so a thin-wall vessel weld that the drawing calls for RT stays an RT weld. The same Case fixes the examination volume: the weld plus the lesser of 1 in. (25 mm) or t on each side for material 8 in. (200 mm) or under.

Geometry then removes options that thickness left open. Nozzle-to-shell welds, set-through configurations, dissimilar-metal joints with a clad interface and small-bore socket welds all degrade ultrasonic coverage in ways a scan plan has to demonstrate rather than assert. Radiography degrades differently, through geometric unsharpness and source-to-film distance, which is why some awkward joints end up with both methods applied to different parts of the same weld. Neither problem is solved by buying a better instrument.

sections.heading: Radiation Safety Is a Schedule Cost, Not a Footnote
paragraphs: The regulatory numbers are specific. 10 CFR 20.1003 defines a radiation area as one where an individual could receive more than 0.005 rem in 1 hour at 30 cm, and a high radiation area as more than 0.1 rem in 1 hour at 30 cm. 10 CFR 20.1301 limits the dose in any unrestricted area from licensed operations to 0.002 rem in any one hour and 0.1 rem in a year to a member of the public. The radiographer surveys, ropes and posts the boundary against those figures before the source leaves the camera.

Personnel requirements are equally concrete. Under 10 CFR 34.43(a) no individual acts as a radiographer until they have received training in the listed subjects, completed a minimum of two months of on-the-job training, and been certified through a radiographer certification program by a recognised certifying entity — the NRC accepts ASNT's IRRSP for isotope radiography. Refresher safety training runs at intervals not exceeding 12 months, and a supervisor observes each radiographer during actual operations at six-month intervals.

None of this applies to ultrasonics. There is no exclusion boundary, no source transport, no radiation work permit, no adjacent trades stood down, and no night-shift premium bought simply to empty the area. On a live plant that difference is frequently larger than the whole inspection budget. Contractors tracking who holds which radiation credential against which job usually end up handling it inside [NDT personnel certification tracking](/erp/ndt-personnel-certification-tracking) rather than a spreadsheet that expires quietly.

sections.heading: The Record: Film, Digital Images and Encoded Data
paragraphs: The strongest genuine argument for radiography is the artefact it leaves. A radiograph is a record a second party reopens in five years without the original technician, the original instrument or the original calibration block. Digital radiography and computed radiography keep that property and add archiving and image processing. In a dispute — a failed hydrotest, an insurance claim, a fitness-for-service argument — an image everyone can look at settles questions that a written interpretation reopens.

Manual ultrasonics has the opposite property. What survives is a report describing indications one person saw on a screen that no longer exists. That asymmetry is real, and it is why clients who have been burned once insist on radiography long after the technical case has moved on. It is also the asymmetry that encoded ultrasonics erases. Code Case 2235-13(e) requires the complete data set to be recorded in unprocessed form, with no gating, filtering or thresholding of the response from the examination volume.

So the honest comparison is three-way, not two-way: radiography, manual UT, and encoded PAUT or TOFD. Manual UT loses the records argument outright. Encoded ultrasonics matches it and adds through-wall depth information that a radiograph never carried. Where a corrosion or fitness-for-service case will later be built on the data, that depth record is worth more than the image — which is why [fitness-for-service assessment under API 579](/consulting/fitness-for-service-api-579) starts from encoded ultrasonic data rather than film.

sections.heading: What ASME Permits When You Swap UT for RT
paragraphs: Section VIII Division 1 authorises the swap in UW-51(a)(4), which requires the examination to meet Section VIII Division 2 paragraph 7.5.5 and points to Section V Article 4 Mandatory Appendix VIII for fracture-mechanics-based acceptance, used together with Mandatory Appendix IX. Section I permits the substitution through Code Case 2235, Code Case 2816, or PW-52.1 — the two Code Cases carrying fracture-mechanics acceptance criteria while PW-52.1 routes to Section V Article 4 Mandatory Appendix VII and workmanship-based criteria. Those are different acceptance philosophies reaching different verdicts on the same indication.

The technique restriction is the part that surprises people. Across Sections I, VIII Division 1 and VIII Division 2, the permitted examinations are limited to TOFD and phased array with computer-based data acquisition and analysis, using equipment mechanically mounted and guided on the examination surface by automatic or semi-automatic means. Manual straight-beam UT, manual angle-beam UT and manual phased array are not permitted as substitute techniques when UT replaces required RT.

Code Case 2235-13 spells out the rest of the burden. Paragraph (b) requires a documented scan plan showing transducer placement, movement and coverage together with beam angles, beam directions relative to weld centreline and the volume examined. Paragraph (c) requires a written procedure conforming to Section V Article 4, demonstrated on qualification blocks containing at least three flaws — one at the OD surface, one at the ID surface and one subsurface. Paragraph (f) restricts data analysis and interpretation to Level II or III personnel certified under their employer's written practice.

sections.heading: What AWS D1.1 Permits on Structural Steel
paragraphs: AWS D1.1 keeps radiography and ultrasonics in separate parts of the same clause. Clause 8 Part E covers Radiographic Testing and Clause 8 Part F covers Ultrasonic Testing of Groove Welds, with 8.15 governing extent of testing. Acceptance sits in Table 8.2 for statically loaded nontubular connections and cyclically loaded connections in compression, and Table 8.3 for cyclically loaded nontubular connections in tension — the familiar amplitude-and-length method, with the tension table markedly tighter.

The 2020 edition added a third route, retained in D1.1/D1.1M:2025, the 25th edition: Annex H (Normative) — Phased Array Ultrasonic Testing (PAUT). Annex H carries Table H.1 for PAUT essential variables, Table H.2 for PAUT acceptance criteria and Table H.3 for discontinuity classification, and it works from encoded linear scanning rather than hand rastering. Annex G governs qualification and calibration of UT units with approved reference blocks, and Annex N remains informative guidance on UT of welds by alternative techniques.

For a structural fabricator the practical reading is that PAUT is no longer an engineering-approved deviation under 8.8 but a named normative annex the code owns. That changes the conversation with an engineer of record from a request for concession to a citation. Fabricators putting crews through that transition normally run it as [on-site corporate NDT training](/corporate-ndt-training) tied to their own mockups rather than a generic classroom course.

sections.heading: Where the Cost Actually Lands
paragraphs: On a per-weld basis, radiography on thin wall is usually the cheaper shot. A crew, a camera, a set of films, an exposure calculation and a reading. That number is the one that appears on quotes and the one that keeps RT on specifications that should have moved years ago, because it is the only cost anyone measures.

The costs that swamp it are schedule costs. Clearing a boundary means adjacent trades stop. Working the shot at night means a shift premium on the radiography crew and on everyone who has to stay. Source transport, security, dosimetry and area surveys carry administrative overhead that no per-weld figure captures. On a turnaround where the critical path runs through a weld, the difference between examining it with the unit live and examining it with a floor evacuated is measured in production, not in inspection.

Ultrasonics inverts the profile. Higher equipment and qualified-time cost per weld, near-zero interference cost. It also front-loads spending: procedure qualification, demonstration blocks, encoders and scanners, and technicians trained on the specific instrument. That front-loading is precisely what makes the decision an owner decision rather than an inspection-contractor decision. Owners weighing it against inspection interval and risk generally take it into [risk-based inspection programme design](/consulting/rbi-program-design) rather than settling it weld by weld.

sections.heading: Where PAUT and TOFD Have Already Displaced RT
paragraphs: Heavy-wall pressure equipment moved first, because that is where the fracture-mechanics acceptance criteria pay. Radiographic acceptance rejects on indication length against a workmanship standard. The Code Case route accepts flaws against Tables 1, 2 and 3 by thickness band, using measured height and through-wall position — significantly more tolerant of a flaw that a fracture-mechanics analysis shows is harmless. Fewer unnecessary repairs on a thick weld is a large number, and repairs on thick welds carry their own risk of introducing worse defects.

Pipeline girth welds moved next, for the same reason plus mechanised zonal discrimination that reports which weld zone each indication sits in. Storage tank shell welds and structural steel followed as encoded PAUT acquired its own code home. In every one of those cases, the displacement happened when a code gave the technique a citation, not when the technology first worked — the equipment predated the acceptance by roughly a decade.

What has not displaced is thin-wall work, small-bore piping, and any joint where the client specification names radiography without an alternative clause. The full decision path — what ASME permits, what a client accepts, and what the qualification burden actually costs — is worked through in the companion piece on [when phased array replaces radiography](/blog/paut-vs-rt-when-phased-array-replaces-radiography). Vessel and tank owners applying it in service usually pair it with [API 510 pressure vessel inspector services](/consulting/api-510-pressure-vessel-inspector-services).

sections.heading: Writing the Choice Into a Procedure That Survives Review
paragraphs: A method selection that lives in an inspector's head fails the first audit. Put it in the procedure: the construction code, the clause authorising the method, the expected defect family, the thickness range, the acceptance table and the personnel level allowed to interpret. Code Case 2235-13 models the format well — every requirement is a numbered paragraph with a demonstrable output, from the scan plan in (b) to the unprocessed data record in (e) to the Level II-or-III interpretation restriction in (f).

Personnel qualification is where these procedures most often fall over. The Code Case requires personnel to be qualified and certified in accordance with their employer's written practice, with ASNT SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 used as a guideline, and requires that the people who acquire and analyse data be trained on the specific equipment and take part in the procedure demonstration. A technician certified for conventional UT is not automatically qualified to interpret encoded phased array data, and an auditor will ask for the demonstration record.

If your organisation has no Level III to own that document, the gap is structural rather than administrative. Bringing in an [interim NDT Level III](/consulting/interim-ndt-level-3) closes it, and method-specific [ASNT training delivered in the United States](/training-usa) builds the bench underneath. Either way, decide the method against the defect, cite the clause, and stop letting habit choose between radiography and ultrasonics.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing legally replace radiography under ASME?
faq.a: Yes, through named routes. Section VIII Division 1 authorises it in UW-51(a)(4), which requires compliance with Section VIII Division 2 paragraph 7.5.5 and Section V Article 4 Mandatory Appendix VIII with Appendix IX. Section I permits it via Code Case 2235, Code Case 2816 or PW-52.1. Code Case 2235-13 applies to welds 1/2 in. (13 mm) and thicker and requires a device employing automatic computer-based data acquisition.

faq.q: Why is RT still specified when UT finds cracks better?
faq.a: Three reasons hold it in place: a permanent image any third party re-reads without the technician, lower per-weld cost on thin wall, and client specifications written before encoded ultrasonics had a code home. The first is genuine and is only answered by encoded PAUT or TOFD, which record the complete unprocessed data set. The second ignores schedule cost. The third is inertia that a citation fixes.

faq.q: What thickness range does AWS D1.1 allow for ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Clause 8.19.1 applies conventional ultrasonic testing to groove welds and heat-affected zones between 5/16 in. (8 mm) and 8 in. (200 mm) inclusive, and excludes tube-to-tube T-, Y- and K-connections from that procedure. Acceptance comes from Table 8.2 for statically loaded nontubular connections and cyclically loaded connections in compression, and Table 8.3 for cyclically loaded nontubular connections in tension.

faq.q: Does radiography require shutting down the work area?
faq.a: It requires a controlled boundary. 10 CFR 20.1003 sets a high radiation area at more than 0.1 rem in 1 hour at 30 cm, and 10 CFR 20.1301 limits unrestricted areas to 0.002 rem in any one hour. The radiographer surveys, posts and physically controls the boundary and maintains continuous direct visual surveillance against unauthorised entry. In practice adjacent trades stop or the shot moves to night shift.

faq.q: Is TOFD a substitute for RT or an addition to UT?
faq.a: Both, depending on the code route. ASME treats TOFD as one of only two acceptable technique families — with phased array — when UT replaces required RT, provided acquisition is computer-based and the equipment is mechanically mounted and guided. Section V Article 4 Mandatory Appendix III carries its technique rules. On many heavy-wall procedures TOFD is paired with encoded PAUT so that each covers the other's near-surface and lateral-wave blind zones.

faq.q: Who is allowed to interpret the results of each method?
faq.a: Under Code Case 2235-13(f), personnel performing and evaluating ultrasonic examinations must be qualified and certified in accordance with their employer's written practice, with ASNT SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 used as a guideline, and only Level II or III personnel analyse data or interpret results. For industrial radiography, 10 CFR 34.43(a) requires certification through a recognised radiographer certification program plus at least two months of on-the-job training.

title: PAUT in Lieu of RT: What ASME and AWS Actually Permit
description: ASME Code Case 2235-13 permits UT in lieu of RT above 1/2 in., but bars manual PAUT. Where phased array replaces radiography, and where it still cannot.
h1: When Phased Array Is Allowed to Replace Radiography
answer: PAUT replaces radiography when the construction code says so and the client's specification allows it. ASME Code Case 2235-13 permits UT in lieu of RT on welds 1/2 in. (13 mm) and thicker, but only with automatic computer-based data acquisition — manual PAUT is excluded. AWS D1.1 gives structural steel its own route through normative Annex H.
expansion: The displacement of radiography by phased array did not happen when the instruments got good. It happened when codes issued citations. ASME published Code Case 2235 in 1996 with fracture-mechanics acceptance criteria, followed by separate Code Cases for manual phased array E-scan, linear E-scan and linear S-scan examinations between 2006 and 2008, and folded those techniques into Section V Article 4 Mandatory Appendices in 2010. AWS D1.1 added normative Annex H for PAUT in its 2020 edition, retained in the 2025 edition. Before those dates, a fabricator proposing phased array was requesting a concession. After them, they cite a clause. The remaining barrier is neither the physics nor the code — it is the qualification burden. Every route demands encoded acquisition, a documented scan plan, a demonstrated procedure on flawed blocks, and analysts who took part in that demonstration.
source: ASME BPVC Code Case 2235-13, approval date July 9, 2014, paragraphs (a) through (i) and Tables 1, 2 and 3; ASME BPVC Section V Article 4 Mandatory Appendices III, IV, V, VII, VIII and IX; Section V Article 1 Mandatory Appendix I definitions of SAUT and AUT; Section VIII Division 1 UW-51(a)(4), Section VIII Division 2 paragraphs 7.5.4 and 7.5.5, Section I PW-52.1, as summarised by Hartford Steam Boiler; AWS D1.1/D1.1M:2025 Annex H (Normative); ASNT published scheme and course pages.
