table.note: Regime scopes are drawn from the current published texts of the NAVSEA technical publication and the two IACS Unified Requirements. UR W35 covers new construction; UR Z17 covers service suppliers whose results a surveyor relies on in survey decisions. W35 section 1.1(iii) states that NDT service suppliers under W35 sit outside the scope of Z17.

facets.q: Does NAVSEA accept an ASNT Level III certificate on its own?
facets.a: No. T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 defines a Level III NDT Examiner as the person the activity delegates authority to, and section 1.6.2.1 requires a specific examination for each method covering the employer's own products, procedures and the administration of the written practice. The employing activity, independent of the Examiner being tested, must prepare, approve and administer that examination. An ASNT card starts the process rather than finishing it.

facets.q: Can a Jacksonville firm carry over certifications from a technician hired away from BAE?
facets.a: No. Section 1.6.9 of the NAVSEA technical publication prohibits transfer of NDT certifications between activities except as authorised by NAVSEA. Section 1.7.4 applies the same bar to procedures. Every hire from another Jacksonville yard is a fresh qualification event under the receiving firm's own written practice, examined and certified by that firm's own Level III Examiner.

facets.q: Why does Jacksonville LNG work trigger IACS UR W35 rather than Z17?
facets.a: W35 covers NDT on new construction of classed ships and offshore structures, and its scope names the fabrication of independent fuel or cargo tanks, including the type A, B and C tanks described in the IMO IGC and IGF Codes. Jacksonville's LNG-fuelled fleet and bunkering infrastructure put that scope in play locally. Z17 instead governs service suppliers producing results a surveyor relies on during survey.

facets.q: How often must Mayport-facing NDT personnel be recertified?
facets.a: Operators and inspectors at intervals not greater than three years, and Level III Examiners at intervals not greater than five. Section 1.6.4 is explicit that recertification on evidence of continuing satisfactory technical performance, or on the basis of ASNT certifications granted without examination, is not permitted. The SNT-TC-1A shortcut most commercial programmes lean on is closed for Navy work.

facets.q: Can an outsourced Level III act as our Level 3 for a classification society?
facets.a: Under IACS UR W35 section 2.4 a supplier that does not employ a full-time Level 3 in every method practised may employ an external Level 3 certified by an accredited certification body in the methods not covered. A supplier may also appoint a full-time supervisor certified to Level 2 and contract external Level 3 services for procedure development, approval and review.

facets.q: What does a Jacksonville yard have to show to bid Navy repair work at all?
facets.a: A Master Ship Repair Agreement, issued and controlled centrally by NAVSEA headquarters. The criteria include facilities capable of overhauling an FFG or larger, performance of 55 percent or more of the job with the firm's own workforce and facilities, and access to a Navy-certified dry dock in the immediate geographic area. An on-site survey precedes issue.

sections.heading: The Jacksonville market an inspection firm is actually selling into
paragraphs: BAE Systems Jacksonville Ship Repair is the anchor. Its published facility data lists a 25,000-ton shiplift, marine railways rated at 4,000 and 1,000 tons, 1,630 feet of pier, cranes to 150 tons, and 41 feet of river depth with no overhead obstructions. It runs around the clock, holds ISO 9001:2015, and carries Lloyd's Register certification on the shiplift and land-level facility system design. More than a dozen US Navy ships depend on it for sustainment.

Naval Station Mayport supplies the workload. It has homeported Arleigh Burke destroyers including USS Donald Cook, USS Mason and USS Winston S. Churchill, alongside Freedom-variant littoral combat ships such as USS Billings and USS Cooperstown, with USS Cleveland joining as the last of that class. A single docking selected restricted availability on USS The Sullivans was awarded to BAE at $108.6 million and runs into March 2027. That is one hull, one availability, and years of subcontracted inspection scope.

The commercial half is JAXPORT. Blount Island covers 754 acres with 7,094 linear feet of deepwater berth and eleven container cranes. Talleyrand carries containerised and breakbulk cargo, autos and liquid bulk, with Crowley among its tenants. Dames Point adds 5,002 linear feet of berth. Together they move close to 800,000 TEU a year, and Blount Island alone handles more than eighty percent of it.

Behind those names sits the tier that actually buys inspection: the machine shops, valve and pump rebuilders, structural fabricators and coatings contractors along Heckscher Drive and Talleyrand Avenue holding subcontracts into BAE and into JAXPORT tenants. They are the firms told, weeks into a bid, that the customer needs to see a written practice, a qualified procedure and a named Level III before purchase orders release. That notice period is the whole problem, and it is why the qualification work has to exist before the opportunity does.

sections.heading: Mayport work turns SNT-TC-1A from a recommended practice into a floor
paragraphs: NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 Revision 1 is the document that governs nondestructive testing on Navy surface ship work. Section 1.6 requires personnel to be certified in accordance with the activity's own written practice, developed as required by ASNT SNT-TC-1A. It then removes the discretion most commercial programmes rely on: SNT-TC-1A as modified by the publication is invoked as mandatory minimum requirements for training hours, experience and examinations, and is not to be treated as recommendations or guidelines.

That single sentence is where most Jacksonville subcontractors get caught. A written practice drafted for commercial refinery or structural work usually reproduces SNT-TC-1A's flexibility verbatim, including recertification on the basis of continuing satisfactory technical performance. Section 1.6.4 prohibits exactly that, and also prohibits recertification on the basis of ASNT certifications granted without examination. The document your quality manager submits to the Government inspector has to have those clauses removed and replaced.

The practical consequence is that a Jacksonville firm bidding Mayport scope needs a second written practice, not an amended one. Even the relief clauses are bounded. Section 1.6.1.1 permits reduced training, experience and examination for personnel who perform one operation of a multi-operation method or inspections of limited scope, but never fewer than fifteen questions on the general examination and ten on the specific, and every limitation has to appear in both the written practice and the certification record. We build that second document alongside your existing commercial programme through /consulting/written-practice-development, so one organisation holds two schemes without either contaminating the other.

sections.heading: The Level III Examiner is a named, signing role
paragraphs: Section 1.5.5 defines the Level III NDT Examiner as the individual to whom the activity delegates responsibility and authority to examine and certify NDT personnel, and to whom the activity assigns responsibility for approving NDT procedures and workmanship standards. The Examiner is stated to be equivalent to the Level III in ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Administration and grading of examinations can be delegated to a representative of the Examiner and recorded, but the delegation itself has to be documented.

Section 1.6.2 allows Examiner testing to be administered by the employing activity, by ASNT, or by another outside agency. Section 1.6.2.1 then requires a specific examination for each method covering the specifications, equipment, techniques and procedures applicable to the employer's products, plus administration of the employer's written practice, and requires the employing activity, independent of the Examiner being tested, to prepare, approve and administer it.

This is the exact function a small Jacksonville firm cannot self-supply. The independence requirement means the person being examined cannot write, approve or administer his own examination, and section 1.6.3 leaves the employing activity responsible for the adequacy of the whole NDT programme regardless of who holds the certificate. Section 1.6.5 offers one narrow bridge, allowing personnel certified under programmes meeting MIL-STD-2132 or NAVSEA 250-1500-1 to work to this document where the procedure, a specific examination and the SNT-TC-1A education and training requirements are all satisfied. Our /consulting/ndt-level-3-exam-oversight work supplies that independent hand, prepares and approves the specific examination, and documents the delegation inside the written practice so the authority is traceable on audit day.

sections.heading: Class work on the JAXPORT trades runs on an entirely different rulebook
paragraphs: When an ABS, DNV or Lloyd's Register surveyor relies on your thickness readings to make a decision affecting classification, IACS UR Z17 section 4.2 requires that your firm be approved and verified by that society. The scope in section 4.1.2 covers thickness measurements on ships and mobile offshore units, with two carve-outs: non-ESP ships under 500 gross tonnage, and all fishing vessels. Reading those exclusions correctly decides whether a Jacksonville firm needs approval at all.

Annex 1 section 1 sets the technical bar. The responsible supervisor is qualified to a recognised national or international NDT standard such as ISO 9712 Level II, and operators are certified at Level I with enough knowledge of ship structure to select a representative position for each reading. On coated surfaces the annex requires pulsed-echo or multiple-echo instruments; single-echo instruments are confined to uncoated surfaces that have been cleaned and ground.

Approval is not a paperwork exercise. Section 5.3 requires an audit after document review, and section 5.4 makes certification conditional on a practical demonstration of the service plus satisfactory reporting. Renewal for thickness-measurement firms is at intervals not exceeding three years. Section 8.2 lets a society cancel approval where a service was improperly carried out or results were improperly reported.

sections.heading: LNG is the Jacksonville differentiator, and it lands inside UR W35
paragraphs: No other US port has committed to LNG the way Jacksonville has. TOTE Maritime operates Isla Bella and Perla Del Caribe, the first LNG-powered containerships built, and introduced Clean Jacksonville as North America's first LNG bunker barge. Crowley homeports the ConRo vessels El Coqui and Taino at Talleyrand and has since added Quetzal. JAX LNG liquefies at Dames Point and Eagle LNG runs a West Jacksonville plant plus a Talleyrand holding facility serving Crowley.

IACS UR W35 Rev.1 applies to NDT on new construction of classed ships and offshore structures, and its scope explicitly names the fabrication of independent fuel or cargo tanks, including the type A, B and C tanks described in the IMO IGC and IGF Codes, along with the welding of components integrated into the structure. Fabrication shops feeding Jacksonville's LNG buildout sit inside that scope, whether they think of themselves as shipyards or not.

W35 section 2.7 requires written procedures for every method applied, written, verified or approved by the supplier's Level 3, internal or external, defining defect evaluation against the society's acceptance criteria, with all procedures acceptable to the society. Section 2.2 adds a structural constraint that catches shipyard in-house departments: where the supplier operates as a Type C inspection body under ISO/IEC 17020, production staff are not permitted to inspect their own work. Cryogenic and nickel-steel weld procedures for LNG tank fabrication are where both clauses bite hardest, and we draft and qualify them through /consulting/ndt-technical-procedure-development.

sections.heading: Aviation next door pulls a third, incompatible scheme into the same building
paragraphs: Fleet Readiness Center Southeast at NAS Jacksonville is a naval aviation depot in the same metro, and its supplier base sits within a short drive of the same yards that feed Mayport. A Jacksonville NDT firm that takes airframe or component work alongside ship repair is now running a maritime scheme and an aerospace scheme in one shop, under one quality manual, with one pool of technicians.

Those schemes are not interchangeable. Aerospace prime and depot supply chains qualify NDT personnel under NAS 410 and audit under AC7114, which assigns a Responsible Level 3 with duties that do not map cleanly onto the NAVSEA Examiner role or the IACS supervisor role. Cross-certifying a technician across all three without a documented basis is the finding that ends the audit.

The separation has to be designed before the work is accepted, not after a nonconformance. In practice that means one quality manual with two clearly bounded annexes, a technician authorisation matrix naming the scheme each certification was issued under, and training hours logged against the correct scheme rather than pooled. We map those boundaries against NAS 410 and AC7114 and cover the aerospace side through /consulting/aviation-ndt-consulting, so a Jacksonville firm holds maritime and aviation approvals concurrently with a defensible line between them and can show an auditor exactly where that line runs.

sections.heading: The three findings Jacksonville firms actually collect
paragraphs: First, procedure qualification evidence. Section 1.7.2 requires each procedure to have been qualified by proving that known discontinuities, natural or artificial, can be reliably detected and evaluated, with the discontinuities representative of expected flaw types and sized near the threshold of acceptance and rejection. The demonstration data has to be produced to the Government inspector on request. Firms routinely hold the procedure and not the demonstration record.

Second, annual oversight. Section 1.6.10 requires oversight of personnel performing NDT to be evaluated and documented by the Examiner or a designated representative, with the methodology defined in the written practice. Section 1.6.10.1 requires at least one witnessed in-process inspection, reinspection, or technical performance evaluation documented every twelve months, and section 1.6.10.2 requires a technical performance evaluation before the end of the second year of the certification cycle for personnel performing acceptance inspections.

Third, vision records. Section 1.6.7 requires annual vision testing, with near-distance acuity sufficient to read J1 letters on a standard Jaeger chart at not less than twelve and not more than sixteen inches, met by one or both eyes, plus colour differentiation where the work requires it at initial certification. Section 1.6.8 requires the records for the current and preceding certification period. Missing prior-period records is a live finding.

Fourth, records that survive a change of personnel. Section 1.6.8 requires the training and experience obtained before initial certification to be kept as long as the person stays certified, the results of all current examinations correlated to a retained master copy of each examination, and a certification statement signed by the activity's Examiner. Section 1.8.3 requires written signatures on inspection records unless NAVSEA has approved an alternative system. Digital sign-off workflows adopted without that approval turn a well-run programme into a documented nonconformance.

sections.heading: What an outsourced Level III engagement looks like in Jacksonville
paragraphs: The sequence is the same whether the trigger is a subcontract at BAE, a class approval application, or a fabrication contract feeding the LNG trades. We read the contract clauses and the invoked documents first, then write or rewrite the written practice to the specific regime, then draft and qualify the method procedures, then administer the examinations and issue the certification statements. Nothing is signed that has not been demonstrated.

For firms holding both Navy and commercial scope, the engagement produces two controlled document sets and one clear rule about which technician is authorised on which job. That is what survives a SUPERVISOR audit under NAVSEA Standard Item 009-04, where process control procedures are submitted for acceptance a minimum of fourteen working days before use and the quality system is audited throughout the contract.

The full scope of the role is set out in /consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services. Firms comparing their position against the densest Navy repair market in the country should read /consulting/maritime-ndt-consulting-norfolk, where the certification-transfer prohibition bites hardest and every experienced hire arrives with nothing the receiving firm can use. Talk to us about a demo of the document set, or request a quote for a Jacksonville engagement through /contact.

faq.q: We already hold ISO 9001. Is that enough for a Jacksonville Navy subcontract?
faq.a: No. ISO 9001 is a quality management system standard and does not qualify NDT personnel. NAVSEA Standard Item 009-04 requires a documented quality management system submitted for acceptance and audited by the SUPERVISOR throughout the contract, while T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 separately requires a written practice, qualified procedures and a Level III Examiner. Both are needed.

faq.q: Does Atlantis provide API 510, 570 or 653 training?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not sell API 510, 570 or 653 training. Our Jacksonville work covers ASNT Level III consulting, written practice development, NDT procedure development and qualification, examination oversight, and audit readiness. Where a Jacksonville client needs fixed-equipment programme review on the terminal side, that is handled as consulting rather than as a training course.

faq.q: Our Level III just left for another Jacksonville yard. How exposed are we?
faq.a: Immediately exposed on both regimes. Under an employer-based scheme the certification is tied to employment, and IACS UR W35 states the employer's certification is deemed revoked when employment ends. On the Navy side the Examiner is the only person who can approve procedures and certify personnel. Recovery runs through interim contracted coverage, an independently examined successor, and a documented handover with no gap in the approval chain.

faq.q: Can one written practice cover Mayport work and classification society work?
faq.a: No. NAVSEA removes SNT-TC-1A's recertification flexibility and prohibits certification transfer between activities. IACS UR W35 requires the written practice to align with ISO 9712:2021 apart from the impartiality clauses and to be reviewed and accepted by the society. Those are different documents with different acceptance authorities. Running one against both produces findings on at least one side.

faq.q: How do we train technicians toward these certifications locally?
faq.a: Training is delivered on your Jacksonville site and mapped to the written practice that governs the work, so the hours logged count toward the correct scheme rather than a generic one. Where a technician will hold both Mayport and class scope, the two training records stay separate from the first hour. Scope and delivery are quoted on request against your method mix and headcount.

title: Tampa NDT Approval Runs Through Class Rules and Tank Codes, Not MSRA
description: Port Tampa Bay demand is barges, dredges, terminals and cruise turnarounds. What an outsourced ASNT Level III does to get a Tampa firm approved and audit-clear.
h1: Outsourced ASNT Level III Support for Tampa Bay Ship Repair and Terminal Inspection Firms
answer: Tampa is not a warship market. Demand comes from Gulf Marine Repair, International Ship Repair, Coast Guard and MARAD hulls, dredges, phosphate and petroleum terminals, and a cruise fleet with no schedule slack. Approval runs through IACS UR Z17 thickness-measurement certification and shoreside fixed-equipment codes. An outsourced ASNT Level III supplies the supervisor qualification, procedures and examinations.
expansion: Port Tampa Bay is Florida's largest and most diversified seaport, moving 32 million tons of cargo in fiscal 2025 and handling 45 percent of the state's gasoline and jet fuel, with an economic impact the port puts above $15.1 billion. The repair cluster around it is mid-tier and Jones Act oriented: Gulf Marine Repair works 50 waterfront acres with 3,200 linear feet of bulkhead and four drydocks, taking Coast Guard, MARAD, Army Corps and NOAA vessels alongside tugs, barges and dredges. International Ship Repair operates five drydocks from a 600-ton unit to a combined 39,600-ton capability. Add Mosaic's phosphate terminal, the petroleum berths, and a cruise operation that carried a record 1.66 million passengers in 2025 across three terminals already at capacity. None of that is governed by a Master Ship Repair Agreement. It is governed by class rules, Coast Guard inspection and fixed-equipment codes.
source: Verified against IACS UR Z17 Rev.21 (2025), sections 4 to 8 and Annex 1 sections 1 to 3; IACS UR W35 Rev.1 (October 2023); Port Tampa Bay and Florida Ports Council published cargo, fuel and cruise figures for fiscal 2025 and calendar 2025; Gulf Marine Repair's published facility and service description and the 2026 US Maritime Administration Small Shipyard Grant award of $1,007,678; International Ship Repair's published drydock and berth schedule; NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 Rev 1 for the government-contract comparison.

facets.q: Does a Tampa barge and tug repair firm need class approval at all?
facets.a: Not automatically. IACS UR Z17 section 4.1.2 excludes non-ESP ships under 500 gross tonnage and all fishing vessels from the thickness-measurement approval requirement. A large part of the Tampa Bay brownwater and harbour fleet falls inside those exclusions. The trigger is whether a surveyor relies on your readings for a classification decision, which section 4.2 makes the deciding test.

facets.q: What does the Z17 audit actually consist of?
facets.a: Document review first, covering the company outline, subcontractor list, operator training and qualification records, equipment description, training programmes, record formats and quality manual. Section 5.3 then requires an on-site audit to confirm the firm is organised as documented. Section 5.4 makes certification conditional on a practical demonstration of the service plus satisfactory reporting, not on paperwork alone.

facets.q: How does Tampa's cruise schedule change the inspection programme?
facets.a: Port Tampa Bay carried a record 1.66 million cruise passengers in 2025 across three Channelside terminals running at or near capacity. A vessel with a published sailing has no float in its window. Procedures, calibration records and technician authorisations have to be closed out before the gangway comes off, which moves the Level III's work forward of the job rather than into it.

facets.q: Can the same technician cover class thickness work and terminal tank work?
facets.a: Yes, with two documented qualification bases. Z17 Annex 1 requires operators to hold recognised certification and enough ship-structure knowledge to select representative reading positions. Tank floor and shell work is qualified under the owner's or contractor's written practice against the applicable API programme. One person, two authorisation records, and a written practice that says plainly which scope each covers.

facets.q: What gets a Tampa firm's class approval cancelled?
facets.a: Z17 section 8.2 lists four grounds: where a service was improperly carried out or results improperly reported; where a surveyor finds deficiencies in the approved operating system and corrective action is not taken; where the quality system relevant to the certificate is altered without written notification to the society; and where a requested intermediate audit has not been carried out.

facets.q: Gulf Marine Repair won a MARAD grant for a training centre. Why does that matter?
facets.a: The 2026 Small Shipyard Grant award of $1,007,678 funds berth improvements in the south slip, wheel loaders, and equipment for the company's training centre. That last line is the local signal: Tampa yards are spending federal capital on qualification capacity because trained, certified people are the binding constraint on the work they can accept, not steel or dock time.

sections.heading: The Tampa Bay demand picture, named
paragraphs: Port Tampa Bay is the state's largest and most diversified seaport by tonnage and land mass, moving 32 million tons of cargo in fiscal 2025. It handles 45 percent of Florida's gasoline and jet fuel, which makes the petroleum berths and the tank farms behind them a permanent inspection load rather than a project one. The port puts its regional economic impact above $15.1 billion and its supported employment above 80,000 jobs.

Gulf Marine Repair works 50 waterfront acres with 3,200 linear feet of bulkhead and four drydocks, supported by tugboats, track cranes, machine, pipe, prefabrication, electrical and blast-and-paint shops. Its customer list is the Tampa profile in one line: large ocean-going commercial vessels, tugs and barges, dredges, harbour tugs, and Coast Guard, MARAD, Army Corps of Engineers and NOAA hulls. It also performs gas freeing and tank cleaning dockside.

International Ship Repair operates the largest number of working drydocks in Florida from a 25-acre main yard with seven outfitting piers and close to 4,000 feet of berthing. Its docks run from a 600-ton unit through 17,600 and 22,000-ton docks that combine to 39,600 tons across 843 feet. Tampa Ship adds graving dock capacity on Hookers Point. Mosaic's marine terminal carries the phosphate export trade.

The firm that buys ASNT Level III consulting in this market is rarely the yard itself. It is the twelve-to-forty-person inspection contractor working out of Ybor or Riverview that holds standing orders with two yards and three terminals, and that gets told without warning that a class surveyor will not accept its gauging report, or that a terminal operator now requires a documented written practice before the next turnaround. That firm already has the technicians and the instruments. What it lacks is a Level III to sign.

sections.heading: Tampa's governing regime is class and code, not a Navy agreement
paragraphs: A Master Ship Repair Agreement is centralised at NAVSEA headquarters and is written for yards capable of overhauling an FFG or larger, performing 55 percent or more of a job with their own workforce, with a Navy-certified dry dock in the immediate geographic area. That is a Hampton Roads or Mayport conversation. Tampa's government work arrives through Coast Guard, MARAD, Army Corps and NOAA channels, and its commercial work arrives through class and flag.

For a Tampa inspection firm, the approval that unlocks bidding is the IACS UR Z17 service supplier certificate. Section 4.2 states the rule directly: where a surveyor uses your results in making decisions affecting classification, your firm must be approved and verified by that society. That is the sentence that turns thickness gauging from a commodity service into a certificated one, and it is the sentence most Tampa firms discover late.

The scope in section 4.1.2 covers thickness measurements on ships and mobile offshore units with two exclusions: non-ESP ships under 500 gross tonnage, and all fishing vessels. Given how much of the Tampa Bay fleet is harbour tugs and inland barges, reading those exclusions correctly is a commercial decision, not a technical footnote. Read them too narrowly and a firm spends a year and an audit cycle chasing an approval no customer asked for. Read them too broadly and a surveyor refuses the readings on a bulk carrier with the tide already booked.

sections.heading: What Z17 approval demands, item by item
paragraphs: Section 5.1 lists the submission: an outline of the company and its management structure, the list of agents, subsidiaries and subcontractors, documented experience in the specific service area, a list of operators with training, experience and qualifications, an equipment description with an operator guide, training programmes, checklists and record formats, the quality manual, conflict-of-interest disclosure, a record of customer claims and corrective actions, and signed code-of-conduct acknowledgements.

Section 5.2 then sets the people bar. Operators need a minimum of one year of tutored on-the-job training. The responsible supervisor needs at least two years of experience as an operator, technician or inspector within the activity the approval covers. Section 5.2.8 requires documented work procedures covering all services supplied, and section 5.2.9 extends the same requirements to any subcontractor performing part of the service.

Annex 1 section 1 adds the technical requirements specific to thickness measurement: pulsed-echo or multiple-echo instruments on coated surfaces, single-echo confined to cleaned and ground uncoated surfaces, procedures covering inspection preparation, test-location selection and identification, surface preparation, protective coating preservation, calibration checks and report content, and the attending surveyor's signature verifying each separate job. We build that document set through /consulting/written-practice-development and /consulting/ndt-technical-procedure-development.

Two further clauses catch firms that have modernised faster than they have documented. Section 5.2.5 requires a record of the equipment used carrying maintenance, calibration and verification results, and empowers the society to assess and act on the validity of previous measuring results where equipment is found not to conform. Section 5.2.6 requires the ability of any software used to acquire, process, record, report or assess data to be documented and confirmed before first use, with commercial off-the-shelf tools in general use treated as already validated.

sections.heading: The shoreside half: phosphate and petroleum fixed equipment
paragraphs: The tanks, jetty piping and loading arms behind Port Tampa Bay's petroleum berths and Mosaic's phosphate terminal generate a steady inspection load that has nothing to do with class survey. Floor scanning, shell course ultrasonics, weld examination on repairs and settlement work are all NDT scope, and they are all qualified under the owner's or contractor's written practice against the applicable API inspection programme rather than against IACS rules.

This is where Tampa firms most often run a single, undifferentiated programme and hope it holds. It does not survive a serious owner audit, because the acceptance criteria, the reporting format and the technician authorisation basis differ from the class-side documents. The written practice has to name which scope each certification covers and on what evidence, and the procedures have to cite the correct acceptance standard.

Atlantis does not sell API 510, 570 or 653 training. What we do on the terminal side is programme work: reviewing the inspection programme against the code it claims to follow through /consulting/api-510-program-audit, and building the risk basis that decides inspection interval and extent. The NDT layer underneath all of it is the same layer that serves the yards: a written practice, qualified procedures, certified technicians, and a Level III who signs. What changes between the tank farm and the drydock is the acceptance standard, not the qualification machinery.

sections.heading: Dredges, Coast Guard hulls and the Jones Act fleet
paragraphs: Gulf Marine Repair names dredges, Coast Guard, MARAD, Army Corps and NOAA vessels explicitly, and that mix changes the inspection profile. Government-owned hulls arrive with contract-specified inspection requirements that reference federal standards rather than class rules, and the acceptance authority is a government representative who will ask to see the written practice and the procedure qualification record rather than a class certificate.

The 2026 US Maritime Administration Small Shipyard Grant programme distributed $35.1 million across 45 shipyards in 24 states and the US Virgin Islands. Gulf Marine Repair's award of $1,007,678 funds three berth improvements in its south slip, new wheel loaders, and equipment for its training centre. Federal capital going into qualification infrastructure at a Tampa yard is a direct statement about where the constraint sits.

For an inspection firm serving that yard, the implication is that the customer's own auditors are getting more capable, not less. A programme that passed on familiarity three years ago will be read against its documents now, by someone who has just been trained to read documents. That is the argument for putting the Level III function on a contracted, documented footing rather than an informal one, and for holding the qualification evidence before a purchase order makes it urgent.

sections.heading: New construction and fabrication brings UR W35 into Tampa
paragraphs: IACS UR W35 Rev.1 applies to NDT on new construction of classed ships and offshore structures, and it applies to two kinds of organisation: independent NDT companies, and internal NDT departments of fabricators such as shipyards and hull block or section fabricators. A Tampa fabrication shop cutting and welding sections for a classed hull is inside that scope whether or not it calls itself an NDT service supplier.

Section 2.4 is the provision that matters commercially. A supplier normally employs a full-time Level 3 supervisor, but W35 recognises that a supplier may not employ a Level 3 in every method practised, and permits employing an external Level 3 certified by an accredited certification body in the methods not held in house. It further allows a full-time supervisor certified to Level 2 alongside contracted external Level 3 services for procedure development, approval, consultancy and review.

Section 2.7 requires written procedures for every method applied, written, verified or approved by the supplier's Level 3, internal or external, defining defect evaluation against the society's acceptance criteria, with all procedures acceptable to the society. Section 2.9 requires reports to give a conclusive accept or reject statement and to be signed by personnel with the appropriate certification level and signatory status.

Section 2.3 carries a trap for any fabricator relying on employer-based certification. Where an operator holds a certificate issued under an employer scheme, that certification is deemed revoked when employment is terminated by either party. A Tampa shop that loses two certified inspectors to a competing yard has not lost two people; it has lost two certifications, and the replacement hires arrive with nothing the shop can use until its own Level 3 has examined and certified them under its own written practice.

sections.heading: Where Tampa programmes fail an audit
paragraphs: The first failure is the practical demonstration. Firms assemble an excellent document pack and then discover that Z17 section 5.4 makes certification conditional on demonstrating the service and reporting it satisfactorily. A technician who has never had a surveyor watch him take and log a reading against the firm's own procedure is a liability on audit day, however good his certificate looks.

The second is subcontracting. Section 5.2.9 requires the supplier to disclose subcontracting arrangements and requires subcontractors providing the approved service to meet the same section 5 requirements. Tampa firms flex crews between yards during dock-window peaks and frequently hold no controlled record of which subcontracted technician worked which job under whose procedure. Annex 1 section 1.7 compounds it by requiring the attending surveyor's signature verifying each separate job, so an unattributable job is also an unverifiable one.

The third is the change notification. Section 8.2.3 allows cancellation where alterations have been made to the quality system relevant to the certificate without written notification to the society, and section 7.1 requires immediate notification of any alteration to the certified service operating system. Re-audit can follow. A quiet revision to the written practice after a Level III departs is exactly the kind of alteration that triggers it.

sections.heading: How an outsourced Level III engagement runs in Tampa Bay
paragraphs: The work starts with a scope decision rather than a document: which of your jobs put a surveyor in the acceptance chain, which sit inside the Z17 exclusions, and which are shoreside fixed equipment. That decision sets how many written practices you need and what each has to say. Building it backwards, from a template written practice, is why so many firms hold documents that do not match the work they sell.

From there the sequence is written practice, method procedures with qualification evidence, technician examination and certification, and a rehearsed practical demonstration before the society audit. The supervisor qualification gap is closed either by contracting the Level III function or by qualifying an internal candidate under independent examination, which is what /consulting/ndt-level-3-exam-oversight covers. Where a Level III has already left and the certificate is exposed, interim contracted coverage restores the signing authority while the internal candidate is developed.

The full role definition sits at /consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services. Firms weighing Tampa against a Navy-contract market should compare /consulting/maritime-ndt-consulting-jacksonville, where a single shiplift takes both Mayport warships and classed commercial tonnage and the same inspection crew works under two rulebooks in one week. Ask us for a demo of the document set, or a quote scoped to your method mix and headcount, through /contact.

faq.q: Is an ASNT Level III certificate enough to act as the responsible supervisor under Z17?
faq.a: Z17 Annex 1 section 1.2 requires the responsible supervisor to be qualified to a recognised national or international industrial NDT standard, and gives ISO 9712 Level II as an example. Section 5.2.3 separately requires two years of experience as an operator, technician or inspector within the approved activity. Certification and documented ship-side experience are both assessed.

faq.q: How long does class approval last once we have it?
faq.a: For firms engaged in thickness measurements, Z17 section 6.2 sets renewal or endorsement at intervals not exceeding three years by verification that the original conditions are maintained. Other service categories run to five years by audit. Individual societies are entitled to require shorter intervals and intermediate audits, and a missed intermediate audit is grounds for cancellation.

faq.q: Does Atlantis sell API 653 training for Tampa terminal work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not sell API 510, 570 or 653 training. Our terminal-side work is consulting: reviewing the fixed-equipment inspection programme against the code it claims to follow, designing the risk basis for interval and extent, and qualifying the NDT procedures and personnel that feed it under your written practice.

faq.q: We use subcontract technicians during dock peaks. Does that break our approval?
faq.a: Not by itself. Z17 section 5.2.9 requires you to disclose subcontracting arrangements and requires subcontractors providing the approved service to meet the same requirements you do, with the society emphasising your quality management of those subcontracts. What breaks approval is undisclosed subcontracting or an absent record of who worked which job under which procedure.

faq.q: What can an outside Level III sign for us, and what can it not?
faq.a: An outside Level III can write, verify and approve procedures, examine and certify your technicians, and act as the external Level 3 that IACS UR W35 section 2.4 expressly permits. It cannot substitute for your quality system, your equipment calibration control, or your records, and it cannot make your firm an approved service supplier without the society's audit and practical demonstration.

title: In Hampton Roads, NDT Certifications Do Not Move With the Technician
description: Norfolk has the densest naval repair market in the US. Why NAVSEA bars certification transfer between yards, and what an outsourced ASNT Level III does about it.
h1: Outsourced ASNT Level III Support for Norfolk and Hampton Roads Ship Repair Firms
answer: Hampton Roads technicians rotate between BAE Norfolk, NASSCO-Norfolk, Colonna's, Lyon, MHI and East Coast Repair every cycle. NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 section 1.6.9 prohibits transferring NDT certifications between activities, and section 1.7.4 prohibits transferring procedures. Every hire is a fresh qualification event that only the receiving firm's own Level III Examiner can close.
expansion: Hampton Roads is the densest naval repair market in the United States, and the density is the problem. Norfolk Naval Shipyard, founded in Portsmouth in 1767, is the Navy's oldest and its largest multifaceted industrial facility, with roughly twelve thousand civilian personnel. Naval Station Norfolk is the world's largest naval complex. BAE Systems Norfolk Ship Repair works 109 acres with four piers totalling 3,015 feet, the 52,500-ton Titan drydock and the 14,000-ton Old Dominion drydock. General Dynamics NASSCO-Norfolk repairs carriers and amphibious hulls across two yards under a Master Ship Repair Agreement. Colonna's Shipyard covers 120 acres with three drydocks, a marine railway and a thousand-tonne travelift. Newport News Shipbuilding employs more than twenty thousand. Technicians move between these employers constantly, and NAVSEA's rules mean none of their certifications travel with them.
source: Verified against NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 Revision 1 (11 September 2014), sections 1.5 to 1.8; NAVSEA Standard Item 009-04; NAVSEA Master Ship Repair Agreement and Agreement for Boat Repair application guidance; IACS UR Z17 Rev.21 (2025) for the commercial comparison; published facility data from BAE Systems Norfolk Ship Repair, General Dynamics NASSCO-Norfolk and Colonna's Shipyard; Hampton Roads Alliance published figures for Norfolk Naval Shipyard, Naval Station Norfolk, Newport News Shipbuilding and the Virginia Maritime Association.

table.caption: Navy-contract work against commercial class work in the same Hampton Roads yard
rows: Which document governs NDT?
NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 Rev 1, invoked through the contract and NAVSEA Standard Items
IACS UR Z17 for service suppliers in survey; IACS UR W35 for new construction
Who certifies the technician?
The employing activity's own Level III NDT Examiner, under the activity's written practice
The employer under a written practice the society has reviewed and accepted, or an accredited certification body
Does a certification from the previous employer count?
No. Transfer between activities is prohibited except as authorised by NAVSEA
No. Under an employer-based scheme the certification is deemed revoked when employment ends
How often is recertification required?
Operators and inspectors every 3 years; Examiners every 5 years, with continued-performance recertification prohibited
Operator qualification re-evaluated annually by the supervisor under UR W35
Can a procedure be reused from another yard?
No. Procedures are not transferable between activities without specific NAVSEA approval
Procedures must be written, verified or approved by the supplier's own Level 3 and be acceptable to the society
Who may hold the senior technical role?
A Level III Examiner examined by the activity, ASNT or another outside agency, with the specific examination set independently
An external Level 3 is expressly permitted where the supplier does not employ one in every method practised
table.note: Columns reflect the current published texts of NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 Revision 1 and IACS Unified Requirements Z17 Rev.21 and W35 Rev.1. A Hampton Roads firm holding both scopes maintains two document sets, not one amended set.

facets.q: Why can't a Norfolk firm reuse certifications from a technician's previous yard?
facets.a: Section 1.6.9 of NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 states that transfer of NDT certifications to other activities is prohibited except as authorised by NAVSEA. Section 1.5.3 defines an activity as all sites under the same quality assurance management using the same quality assurance plan. A move from BAE Norfolk to Colonna's crosses that line, so the certification does not follow the technician.

facets.q: What is a Master Ship Repair Agreement and does every Hampton Roads yard hold one?
facets.a: No. An MSRA is issued and controlled centrally by NAVSEA headquarters for firms primarily engaged in ship repair with facilities capable of overhauling an FFG or larger, performing 55 percent or more of a job with their own workforce and facilities, and with access to a Navy-certified drydock in the immediate geographic area. Smaller boat work runs under an Agreement for Boat Repair instead.

facets.q: Can our Level III be shared across two Hampton Roads sites?
facets.a: Only if both sites sit under the same quality assurance management and use the same quality assurance plan, which is how section 1.5.3 defines a single activity. Two legally separate firms, or two sites with separate quality plans, are two activities. Each needs its own written practice, its own procedures and its own certification records signed by the cognizant Examiner.

facets.q: Does NAVSEA accept recertification on continued satisfactory performance?
facets.a: No. Section 1.6.4 requires recertification by examinations as comprehensive as those used for initial certification, and states that recertification by evidence of continuing satisfactory technical performance, or on the basis of ASNT certifications granted without examination, is not permitted. The only relief is that the basic examination for Examiners need not be readministered while a method certification is maintained.

facets.q: What proves an NDT procedure is qualified for Navy work?
facets.a: Section 1.7.2 requires each procedure to have been qualified by proving that known discontinuities, natural or artificial, can be reliably detected and evaluated, with the discontinuities representative of expected flaw types and sized near the acceptance and rejection threshold. The demonstration data must be produced to the Government inspector on request. Section 1.7.1 puts the certifying statement inside the procedure, signed by the cognizant Examiner.

facets.q: How does commercial work at Colonna's or Lyon differ from BAE Navy work?
facets.a: Commercial classed work puts a class surveyor in the acceptance chain, which triggers IACS UR Z17 approval for the firm producing thickness readings, renewed at intervals not exceeding three years. New construction triggers UR W35, which permits an external Level 3. Navy work puts a Government inspector in the chain under a technical publication that permits neither shortcut.

sections.heading: The Hampton Roads market is dense enough to change the rules
paragraphs: Naval Station Norfolk is the world's largest naval complex, home to seventy-five ships and one hundred thirty-four aircraft across fourteen piers. Norfolk Naval Shipyard in Portsmouth, founded in 1767, is the Navy's oldest shipyard and the largest and most multifaceted industrial facility the Navy owns, carrying roughly twelve thousand civilian personnel. Up the peninsula, Newport News Shipbuilding employs more than twenty thousand and is the only yard in the country able to build nuclear aircraft carriers.

The private repair tier around them is deep. BAE Systems Norfolk Ship Repair holds 109 acres, four piers totalling 3,015 feet, the 52,500-ton Titan drydock and the 14,000-ton Old Dominion drydock, an apprenticeship programme running since 1936, and ISO 9001:2015. General Dynamics NASSCO-Norfolk maintains carriers and the amphibious fleet from a Ligon Street yard with a 40,000-ton drydock and a 60-acre Harper Avenue yard in Portsmouth, under a Master Ship Repair Agreement.

Below that sit Colonna's Shipyard, with 120 acres, three drydocks, a marine railway, a thousand-tonne travelift and thirty-one thousand tons of total lift capacity across nine piers, alongside East Coast Repair and Fabrication, Fairlead, Lyon Shipyard and MHI Ship Repair. The Virginia Maritime Association counts more than four hundred member companies employing over seventy thousand Virginians. Technicians circulate through all of it.

The buyer for outsourced Level III support is not Norfolk Naval Shipyard. It is the sixty-person structural and machinery subcontractor in Chesapeake or South Norfolk holding purchase orders into two of those prime yards, whose entire NDT programme runs on one Level III and whose next availability depends on him staying. When that person retires, resigns, or is hired by the yard he has been serving, the firm discovers how many signatures were attached to a single name.

sections.heading: Certification density is exactly why NAVSEA locked the doors
paragraphs: In a market this concentrated, a certified UT technician can change employers three times in five years without changing his commute. Section 1.6.9 of NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 closes that loop: transfer of NDT certifications to other activities is prohibited except as authorised by NAVSEA. Section 1.5.3 defines an activity as all sites of an organisation under the same quality assurance management using the same quality assurance plan.

Section 1.7.4 applies the same bar to documents. Procedures shall not be transferred from one activity to another without the specific approval of NAVSEA. The instinct to bring a proven procedure over from a previous employer, adjust the header and issue it is not a shortcut. It is a finding, and it puts the technician's inspection results in question along with the procedure.

The operational consequence for a Norfolk firm is that headcount growth and qualification capacity are the same problem. Hiring five experienced technicians in a quarter creates five examination and certification events, each requiring a written examination, a practical examination, a vision test and a signed certification statement from the cognizant Examiner. Without an Examiner with capacity, the hires cannot work the scope they were hired for.

The same definition catches acquisitions. Two Hampton Roads firms merging on paper do not become one activity until they operate under the same quality assurance management and the same quality assurance plan. Until that consolidation is real and documented they hold two written practices, two procedure sets and two Examiner delegations, and personnel certified by one cannot simply be worked on the other's contracts. Planning the certification consolidation belongs in planning the acquisition, and it is routinely discovered afterwards instead.

sections.heading: The Level III Examiner role, as NAVSEA defines it
paragraphs: Section 1.5.5 names the Level III NDT Examiner as the individual to whom the activity delegates responsibility and authority to examine and certify NDT personnel, and to whom the activity assigns responsibility for approving NDT procedures and workmanship standards. The publication states the Examiner is equivalent to the Level III in ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Administration and grading of examinations can be delegated to a recorded representative; the delegating authority cannot.

Section 1.6.2 permits Examiner testing by the employing activity, by ASNT, or by another outside agency. Section 1.6.2.1 then requires a specific examination for each method covering the specifications, equipment, techniques and procedures applicable to the employer's products, plus administration of the employer's written practice, and requires the employing activity, independent of the Examiner being tested, to prepare, approve and administer it.

That independence clause is where a single-Level-III firm stalls. The incumbent cannot examine himself, and cannot examine his own successor into the role without an independent party preparing and approving the examination. Section 1.6.6 adds that the Government inspector can require a written or practical examination at any point there is reason to believe an individual cannot perform at the level certified. We supply the independent hand through /consulting/ndt-level-3-exam-oversight, preparing and approving the method-specific examination against your own products and procedures rather than a generic bank.

sections.heading: When the Level III leaves, in this market, they are usually going next door
paragraphs: A Level III resignation in Hampton Roads is rarely a retirement. It is a move to another yard within the same harbour, often to a customer or a competitor on the same availability. The receiving firm gains nothing transferable and the departing firm loses the only person who can approve procedures, certify personnel and sign the certification statements the Government inspector will ask for.

The immediate exposure is not theoretical. Every procedure in the controlled set carries a certifying statement signed by the cognizant Examiner under section 1.7.1. Every operator and inspector certification carries the Examiner's signature under section 1.6.8. New work cannot be authorised, expiring certifications cannot be renewed, and the annual oversight required by section 1.6.10 has no one qualified to perform it.

The recovery sequence matters more than the panic. Interim coverage by a contracted Level III restores signing authority, an internal candidate is developed and independently examined into the role, and the handover is documented so nothing in the controlled set carries a gap in its approval chain. Certifications the departed Examiner already issued do not evaporate, but nothing new can be issued and nothing expiring can be renewed until the delegation is re-established in writing. That sequence is laid out at /consulting/ndt-level-3-resigned-what-to-do.

sections.heading: The quality system the SUPERVISOR audits alongside the NDT programme
paragraphs: NAVSEA Standard Item 009-04 requires the contractor to establish and maintain a documented quality management system, with acceptance handled as a one-time submittal unless the Standard Item, its references or the contractor's status change. The system is subject to audit by the SUPERVISOR throughout the contract, which means the NDT programme is inspected in place rather than reviewed once at award.

Process control procedures invoked by NAVSEA Standard Items, military standards, drawings, technical publications and specifications are submitted to and approved by the SUPERVISOR a minimum of fourteen working days before use, independent of the quality management system. For a Hampton Roads subcontractor picking up scope mid-availability, that lead time is the schedule constraint that decides whether the work can be taken at all.

The practical answer is to hold a qualified, approved procedure set before it is needed rather than after. The same Standard Item requires a test and inspection plan and records of the tests and inspections accomplished, which is where an NDT programme is either legible to an auditor or is not. We build and qualify the procedure documents alongside the personnel programme through /consulting/written-practice-development, so the two document sets reference each other rather than contradict each other and a single change is reflected in both.

sections.heading: The commercial side of Hampton Roads still runs on class rules
paragraphs: Colonna's serves commercial and government markets and runs a barge business alongside its steel fabrication and machining divisions. Lyon Shipyard and MHI work commercial tonnage as well as government hulls. For any of that work where an ABS, DNV or Lloyd's Register surveyor relies on your thickness readings in a classification decision, IACS UR Z17 section 4.2 requires your firm to be approved and verified by that society.

Z17 Annex 1 sets a different bar from NAVSEA. The responsible supervisor is qualified to a recognised national or international NDT standard such as ISO 9712 Level II, operators are certified at Level I with enough ship-structure knowledge to select representative reading positions, and certification for thickness-measurement firms renews at intervals not exceeding three years. Section 5.4 makes initial certification conditional on a practical demonstration and satisfactory reporting.

For new construction and block fabrication, IACS UR W35 governs, and section 2.4 expressly permits an external Level 3 certified by an accredited certification body in methods the supplier does not hold in house. That is the opposite of the Navy position, and it is why a Hampton Roads firm working both sides needs two written practices rather than one broad document.

The contrast is worth stating plainly to a shop that works both. On the class side an external Level 3 is an approved structure written into the rule, and section 2.8 requires only that the arrangement be disclosed so the society can assess the subcontractor's quality management. On the Navy side the activity carries responsibility for the programme itself under section 1.6.3, and the outside Level III holds a documented delegation rather than independent standing. Same person, same competence, two different legal footings.

sections.heading: The findings that repeat across Hampton Roads programmes
paragraphs: Inherited certifications lead the list, for the reasons above. Second is procedure qualification evidence: firms hold the procedure but not the section 1.7.2 demonstration record proving that representative discontinuities sized near the acceptance threshold were reliably detected and evaluated. The Government inspector is entitled to that data on request, and to request a demonstration during initial review or at any point results are in doubt.

Third is annual oversight. Section 1.6.10.1 requires at least one witnessed in-process inspection, reinspection of previously inspected product, or technical performance evaluation, documented every twelve months by the last day of the twelfth month. Section 1.6.10.2 requires a technical performance evaluation on production hardware or specimens containing discontinuities before the end of the second year of the certification cycle for anyone performing acceptance inspections.

Fourth is vision. Section 1.6.7 requires annual testing to J1 letters on a standard Jaeger chart at between twelve and sixteen inches, met by one or both eyes, with colour differentiation where the work requires it at initial certification, and section 1.6.8 requires the records for the current and preceding certification period. Corrective aids used for the test must be used during examination and all subsequent inspections.

sections.heading: How an outsourced Level III engagement runs in Hampton Roads
paragraphs: We start by separating the scopes. Navy availability work, commercial class work and any fabrication work each get their own written practice, their own procedure set and their own authorisation matrix, so no technician is working outside the scheme that certified him. In a market where crews move between yards mid-availability, that matrix is the document that keeps the programme defensible under audit.

Then we close the qualification backlog. Examinations are prepared, approved and administered independently of the person being examined, procedures are qualified with demonstration records rather than assertions, and the annual oversight programme is put on a calendar with named responsibility and a documented method. Certification statements are signed as the evidence closes, not in advance of it, and the authorisation matrix is updated the same day so the shop floor and the document set never disagree.

The role definition sits at /consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services. Firms comparing markets should read /consulting/maritime-ndt-consulting-jacksonville, where one shiplift takes both Mayport warships and classed commercial tonnage, and /consulting/maritime-ndt-consulting-tampa, where an approved service supplier certificate rather than a Master Ship Repair Agreement is the gate on the work. Technicians moving into these roles are trained on site against your own written practice rather than a generic syllabus. Ask for a demo of the document set or a quote through /contact.

faq.q: We just hired three certified technicians from another Hampton Roads yard. Can they work tomorrow?
faq.a: Not on Navy scope. Section 1.6.9 prohibits transfer of NDT certifications between activities except as authorised by NAVSEA, so each technician needs qualification and certification under your written practice, examined by your Level III Examiner, with training and experience records, a current vision test and a signed certification statement before performing acceptance inspections.

faq.q: Does an ASNT Level III certificate make someone our Examiner?
faq.a: No. It satisfies part of the requirement. Section 1.6.2.1 additionally requires a specific examination for each method covering your products, procedures and the administration of your written practice, prepared, approved and administered by the employing activity independent of the Examiner being tested. The certificate is a prerequisite; the delegation and the specific examination make the Examiner.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train our technicians toward API 510, 570 or 653 in Norfolk?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not sell API 510, 570 or 653 training. Our Hampton Roads work is ASNT Level III consulting, written practice development, NDT procedure development and qualification, examination oversight and audit readiness, plus corporate NDT training delivered on your Hampton Roads site and mapped to your own written practice so the hours logged count toward the scheme that governs the work.

faq.q: Is an outside Level III acceptable to a Government inspector?
faq.a: The publication requires the activity to delegate the Examiner role and to be responsible for the adequacy of the NDT programme under section 1.6.3. A contracted Level III can hold that delegation where the appointment, authority and independence are documented in the written practice. What cannot be delegated away is the activity's own responsibility for the programme.

faq.q: How quickly can a new procedure be put to work on an availability?
faq.a: The procedure has to be written, qualified with demonstration evidence, and carry the cognizant Examiner's certifying statement. Where NAVSEA Standard Item 009-04 applies, process control procedures are submitted to and approved by the SUPERVISOR a minimum of fourteen working days before use. Building the qualified set ahead of the availability is the only way to take mid-availability scope.

title: Houston Marine NDT Approval Runs on Class, Not API Certification
description: Houston Ship Channel and Galveston Bay yards qualify NDT under class rules and 46 CFR Subchapter M, not API. What an outsourced ASNT Level III has to sign.
h1: Maritime and Shipyard NDT Consulting for Houston and Galveston Bay
answer: Houston shipyard and barge work is governed by class society rules and 46 CFR Subchapter M, not API. An outsourced ASNT Level III writes the marine written practice, qualifies gaugers to IACS UR Z17, approves the hull-weld procedures an ABS Surveyor will accept, and administers the examinations that make your Level II certifications valid.
expansion: The Houston Ship Channel complex runs more than 200 private terminals alongside eight public ones and moves roughly twelve percent of all United States waterborne tonnage. That traffic creates three separate NDT markets, and most local firms try to serve all three with one certification programme: hull thickness gauging for ocean-going ships under class survey, weld inspection at Galveston Bay repair and newbuild yards, and structural work on the tank barge fleet run out of Channelview and the upper channel. Each answers to a different controlling document. Class gauging sits under IACS UR Z17. Hull welds sit under the classification society's own rules and NDT guide. Tank barge structure sits under 46 CFR Subchapter M. All three demand procedures written and signed by a certified Level III, and technicians qualified under a written practice that names the marine techniques explicitly. Most Houston firms hold a written practice built for refinery piping instead.
source: Verified against IACS UR Z17, Procedural Requirements for Service Suppliers, sections 4.2 to 5.2 and Annex 1 section 1; the ABS Guide for Nondestructive Inspection of Hull Welds, Section 1 sections 5, 7 and 9; 46 CFR 137.210, 137.300 and 137.135; Port Houston and Greater Houston Port Bureau tonnage figures for 2023 and 2025; Kirby Corporation and Higman Barge Lines company disclosures; and WorkBoat reporting on Davie Defense's December 2025 acquisition and modernisation of the Gulf Copper yards at Galveston and Port Arthur.
