table.note: SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice. These numbers become binding on you through your own written practice, which is the document an auditor reads first and holds you to.

facets.q: How many questions does a defensible NDT question bank actually hold?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A sets the examination length, not the bank size. A 40-question general examination drawn at a five-to-one ratio needs 200 live items, and three non-overlapping parallel forms need 120 as an absolute floor. Build to the higher figure. Anything tighter means candidates who resit see questions they already answered, and the bank stops measuring competence within two years.

facets.q: Can we use questions from a published Level III study guide in our bank?
facets.a: Use them as calibration, never as your live bank. Published guides circulate widely and candidates study them directly, so an examination built from them measures recall of a book. ANSI/ASNT CP-105 topical outlines are the correct source: they define the body of knowledge by method and level, and you write original items against each topic line.

facets.q: Who is allowed to administer and grade the examinations?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A Section 8.1 makes the NDT Level III responsible for administering and grading examinations, with a designated representative permitted after documented instruction. Paragraph 8.1.1 closes the loophole: no certification examination is administered by the candidate or by a subordinate of the candidate. That single sentence is why a one-Level-III shop cannot certify its own Level III in-house.

facets.q: What is the pass mark, and how is the composite calculated?
facets.a: A composite grade of at least 80 percent, with no individual examination below 70 percent. The composite is a simple average of the general, specific and practical results at Level I and II, and of the basic, method and specific results at Level III. Where an outside agency examination is accepted, common written practice records that pass as 80 percent for compositing.

facets.q: Are our examinations open book or closed book?
facets.a: Closed book. Reference material such as graphs, tables, charts and code extracts is supplied where the question tests whether the candidate can use the reference rather than whether they memorised it. An acceptance criteria question handing over the code table is testing judgement; the same question without the table is testing recall of a number the technician will always look up on site.

facets.q: How long do graded examination papers have to be kept?
facets.a: SNT-TC-1A Section 9 requires the certification record to hold the current examination copies or suitable evidence of successful completion, along with composite grades, the individual's education and experience, training completion, vision results, and the Level III signature verifying certification. The retention period is set by your written practice, so it becomes an obligation you wrote for yourself.

sections.heading: One programme, six banks — the count people get wrong first
paragraphs: Firms describe the examination bank as a single object, and that framing is the root of most findings. An employer-based programme running six methods at two working levels feeds a general bank and a specific bank per method per level, a practical checkpoint set per method, and three more banks at Level III. Six methods produce dozens of distinct question sets, each tied to a different source of content and a different signature. Treating them as one file is how the specific examination ends up containing general questions.

The separation matters because the banks age at different rates. General questions track the physics and the CP-105 outline, and stay valid for years. Specific questions track your instrument fleet, your procedure revisions and the acceptance codes on your current contracts, so they expire whenever a procedure is reissued or a flaw detector is replaced. A bank that mixes the two guarantees that a procedure revision silently invalidates part of every examination you administer.

The practical examination is a third species entirely and carries no question count. SNT-TC-1A asks for a minimum of ten different checkpoints evaluating the candidate's understanding of the NDT variables and the employer's procedural requirements, exercised on approved specimens where the candidate is required to detect the specified discontinuities. Its bank is a set of specimens with documented flaw truth plus the checkpoint sheets that go with them, and it is the bank most often found to consist of one plate and a photocopy.

sections.heading: Where general-examination content legitimately comes from
paragraphs: ANSI/ASNT CP-105 is the standard that defines the body of knowledge for training, qualifying and certifying NDT personnel, published as topical outlines by method and by level. The 2024 edition is current and brought in changes including machine learning within acoustic emission and updates to computed tomography and computed radiography. It is the document your general bank should be built against, line by line, because it is also the document a training provider and an auditor will both recognise.

The method is unglamorous and effective. Take the CP-105 outline for the method and level, list every topic line, and write a target number of items against each. Physics and principles carry the most weight, equipment and technique next, then interpretation. Map each finished question back to its outline reference in a spreadsheet column, and the coverage gaps become visible instead of theoretical. That map is also the fastest possible answer when an auditor asks how you know the examination covers the syllabus.

What the general bank must not be is a photocopy of a published study guide. Those books circulate, candidates read them, and an examination assembled from them measures how recently somebody bought the book. Use published material to calibrate difficulty and phrasing, then write original items. This is the single largest quality gap we find when reviewing programmes alongside [written practice development](/consulting/written-practice-development), and it is invisible until a candidate with a good memory passes an examination they cannot perform against.

sections.heading: The specific examination is where employer banks collapse
paragraphs: The specific examination addresses the equipment, operating procedures and test techniques the candidate will encounter on assignment. That is the whole point and it is also why the bank cannot be bought. A 20-question specific examination for UT Level II should name your flaw detectors, your calibration blocks, your couplant, your scanning plan, your reporting form, your acceptance code and the exact paragraph in your own procedure that sets the reference level. Nothing generic survives that test.

Most collapsed banks share one symptom: the specific paper reads like a second general paper. Questions about the velocity of sound in steel belong in the general bank. Questions about which of your four procedures governs a 12 mm carbon steel butt weld to a named client specification belong in the specific bank. When we audit programmes, we count how many specific-examination questions could be answered by a competent technician who had never seen your documents. Any answer above zero is a finding waiting to be written.

There is a maintenance obligation attached. Because specific questions cite procedure numbers, revisions and equipment models, every procedure reissue triggers a bank review. Record the procedure revision each question was written against in the bank itself, and reissuing a procedure becomes a filter query rather than a re-read. Firms that skip this discover during an audit that their current examinations test a revision withdrawn eighteen months earlier.

sections.heading: Practical examinations: checkpoints, specimens and flaw truth
paragraphs: The practical examination is assessed against a minimum of ten different checkpoints covering the NDT variables and the employer's procedural requirements. At Level I those checkpoints centre on performing the examination as directed and recording what is found. At Level II they extend to selecting the technique, performing it, and interpreting and evaluating the results against acceptance criteria. In both cases the candidate is required to detect the discontinuities the specimen holds.

That last requirement quietly demands documented flaw truth. If the specimen's flaws were never independently characterized, there is no way to state that the candidate detected them, and the grade becomes an opinion. Keep an as-built drawing or reference examination record per specimen, kept apart from the examination room, held by the administering Level III alone. This is the same discipline that governs [procedure qualification by demonstration](/consulting/ndt-procedure-qualification-demonstration), and the same failure mode applies when it is missing.

Specimen population is the other constraint. One plate examined by every candidate for three years is a specimen whose flaw locations are common knowledge before anyone picks up a probe. Rotate specimens, keep more than the minimum, and log which specimen each candidate examined so repeat candidates get a different one. Where a firm cannot justify buying specimen sets for every method, prioritise the methods it sells most, and cover the rest through an outside examination agency.

sections.heading: How big a bank has to be before it is defensible
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A sets examination length, never bank depth, so the sizing decision falls to you and it deserves arithmetic rather than instinct. Start from the draw ratio. A 40-question general examination drawn from 200 live items gives a five-to-one ratio, which means two candidates sitting the same examination share roughly eight questions by chance and a resitting candidate sees mostly new material. At two-to-one, a resit is close to a repeat.

Parallel forms give the second constraint. Three non-overlapping 40-question forms need 120 items before any margin, and a fourth reserve form for resits pushes it to 160. Add retirement: any item that more than 90 percent of candidates answer correctly has stopped discriminating and should be pulled, which historically removes a tenth of a bank in its first two cycles. Building to 200 live items per general examination absorbs that attrition without emergency writing sessions.

Specific banks scale differently because the population is smaller and the content is yours. A 20-question specific examination supported by 80 to 100 live items covers the same ratio logic while staying maintainable against procedure revisions. Level III banks are smaller again in item count but heavier per item, since the method examination alone needs 30 fundamentals, 15 technique-establishment and 20 code-interpretation questions before any draw ratio is applied.

sections.heading: Writing items that survive a Level III review
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A requires that examination questions be approved by the NDT Level III, which makes item review a formal gate rather than a courtesy read. The gate is worth using properly. A reviewable item has one defensible answer, distractors that a partially-informed candidate would find plausible, no negative stems, no all-of-the-above, and a citation to the source paragraph or outline line that justifies the key. Items without a citation cannot be defended when a candidate challenges a grade.

Difficulty distribution matters more than difficulty. A bank of uniformly hard questions fails competent technicians; a bank of uniformly easy ones passes everyone and tells you nothing. A workable spread places roughly a fifth of items as straightforward recall, the bulk as application, and a fifth requiring the candidate to work through a calculation or a code table. Track the actual pass rate per item once you have a dozen sittings, and the outliers identify themselves.

Language is a quiet source of failure in international crews. Long compound stems, double negatives and idiomatic phrasing test English rather than NDT. Keep stems short, put the question in the stem rather than the options, and use the terminology your procedures use. This is worth doing before an examination is challenged, because a candidate who fails on a badly-written item has a legitimate grievance and the Level III who approved it owns the outcome.

sections.heading: Grading: the 70/80 arithmetic and what a composite hides
paragraphs: The rule is a composite grade of at least 80 percent with no individual examination scoring below 70 percent. Both halves bind. A candidate scoring 95, 95 and 68 has a composite of 86 and still fails, because one part fell below 70. A candidate scoring 79, 79 and 79 passes every part and still fails, because the composite falls short of 80. Written practices that state only one of the two conditions produce certifications an auditor can challenge on arithmetic alone.

The composite is a simple average of the parts — general, specific and practical at Level I and II; basic, method and specific at Level III. Where an outside agency examination is accepted in place of one part, common written practice records that result as 80 percent for compositing purposes, and the practice has to say so explicitly rather than leaving the grader to improvise. Write the rule down, including how a retake grade replaces the original.

What the composite hides is the practical. A candidate can average their way to 80 while barely clearing 70 on the hands-on examination, which is the part that predicts field performance. Nothing prevents an employer setting a higher internal bar than the recommended practice, and firms selling inspection services into demanding clients routinely do. Set that bar in the written practice and it becomes auditable; leave it in a manager's head and it becomes inconsistent.

sections.heading: Security: a bank the candidates have seen is worthless
paragraphs: A question bank is an asset whose entire value is confidentiality. Once circulated, it measures memory rather than competence, and every certification issued from it becomes indefensible in an incident investigation. Yet banks routinely live on shared drives, in email attachments to trainers, and in printed masters left in the examination room. Treat the bank the way you treat pricing or client drawings: access list, version control, and a named owner who is the Level III responsible for the programme.

Practical controls are cheap. Keep the live bank separate from the training material and never let the same file serve both. Print papers on demand rather than keeping a stock of prepared copies. Number every paper, issue and collect them against the number, and shred spoiled copies rather than binning them. Where examinations run at multiple sites, do not send the bank — send the assembled paper, and have it returned. Rotate a portion of items every cycle so a leak has a limited half-life.

Detection is possible and worth building in. When a group's scores jump sharply on specific items without a corresponding change in training, the bank has leaked. When candidates finish a 40-question paper in ten minutes, the bank has leaked. Log item-level results and the pattern shows up before the certifications do. Independent administration removes the largest exposure, which is why [Level III examination oversight](/consulting/ndt-level-3-exam-oversight) is usually the cheapest security control a small firm can buy.

sections.heading: Administration and proctoring in practice
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A Section 8.1 makes the NDT Level III responsible for administering and grading examinations, and allows a designated representative to do so after receiving documented instruction. Paragraph 8.1.1 adds the constraint everyone eventually collides with: a certification examination is never administered by the candidate or by a subordinate of the candidate. In a firm with one Level III who reports to the owner and supervises everyone else, that sentence rules out most of the obvious arrangements.

The consequences run further than people expect. The Level III cannot administer their own Level III specific examination. A supervisor cannot proctor the Level II examination of a technician who reports to them. A quality manager who signs the written practice cannot grade the paper of someone in their own chain. Each of these turns up as a finding because the examination record carries a grader signature and the organisation chart is in the same audit pack.

Proctoring itself has no code text behind it, which means the written practice has to supply the rules. State who invigilates, whether phones leave the room, what reference material is issued, the time allowed, and what happens if a candidate is caught with unauthorised material. ANSI/ASNT CP-189 tightens several of these expectations relative to SNT-TC-1A, and firms working to that standard should read our [CP-189 compliance notes](/compliance/ansi-asnt-cp-189) alongside [SNT-TC-1A](/compliance/asnt-snt-tc-1a) before drafting.

sections.heading: Retention: what stays in the file after the paper is graded
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A Section 9 lists what the personnel certification record holds: the individual's name; the certification level, NDT method or technique and any limitations; educational background and experience; a statement that training was completed to the written practice; current vision examination results; current examination copies or suitable evidence of successful completion; composite grades; the signature of the Level III verifying certification; and the certification and expiry dates. The retention period is whatever your written practice states.

Two of those entries carry hidden weight. Current examination copies or suitable evidence means the graded papers themselves are the default, and firms that discard papers must be able to point at the alternative evidence they kept. Limitations, if any, is the field that records a technician certified for a restricted scope, and a blank field asserts unrestricted competence in the method. Both fields are checked in audits far more often than the training hours everybody worries about.

Recertification closes the loop. SNT-TC-1A recommends a maximum interval of five years, and each cycle asks whether the individual's competence still holds. A programme with a well-maintained bank handles recertification as a normal draw; a programme without one improvises a paper the week before the certificate expires. If your bank cannot support the next five years of recertifications without repeating itself, it is undersized — and rebuilding it is one of the standard workstreams in our [outsourced Level III consulting](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services). Affordable, accessible and fully customizable: [request a quote](/contact).

faq.q: Can we buy a ready-made NDT question bank instead of writing one?
faq.a: You can buy general-examination material and calibrate against it, but the specific examination cannot be purchased because it has to name your procedures, your instruments and your acceptance codes. A programme built entirely on a bought bank fails on the specific paper the moment an auditor reads it. The realistic split is purchased or commissioned general items, plus specific items written against your own document set.

faq.q: Our only Level III is also the owner. Who administers his specific examination?
faq.a: Somebody outside the reporting line. SNT-TC-1A 8.1.1 prevents a candidate administering their own examination, and no subordinate can administer a superior's either. The normal solution is an outside Level III engaged to administer and grade, or an ASNT examination accepted in place of the basic and method parts. The employer still issues the certification; only the administration moves outside.

faq.q: How often should the question bank be revised?
faq.a: Review the general banks against the current CP-105 edition on a fixed annual cycle, and review specific banks whenever a referenced procedure is reissued or an instrument model is replaced. Retire items that nearly every candidate answers correctly, since they no longer discriminate. Recording the procedure revision and the outline reference against each item turns both reviews into a filter query rather than a full re-read.

faq.q: Does the practical examination need its own bank?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the bank most often missing. It consists of the flawed specimens with documented flaw truth, the checkpoint sheets covering the minimum of ten checkpoints, and a log recording which specimen each candidate examined. Without the flaw truth record you cannot demonstrate that the candidate detected the specified discontinuities, which is what the standard actually asks you to show.

faq.q: Can ASNT certificates replace parts of our in-house examinations?
faq.a: Written practices commonly accept a valid ASNT or ACCP certificate in place of the general examination where the Level III determines it meets the requirements, and accept the ASNT NDT Level III Basic and method examinations in place of those parts. The employer still administers the specific examination, because no external body can examine a candidate on your procedures and equipment.

title: Signing Outside Your Method: The Level III Scope Audit Finding
description: Why a UT Level III cannot approve an RT procedure, how method scope is recorded, how firms cover methods their Level III lacks, and how auditors find it.
h1: One certificate, one method — and the signature block that gives you away
answer: A Level III certificate is issued per method. Signing an RT procedure on a UT certificate is the most common Level III audit finding there is, because SNT-TC-1A makes the Level III responsible only for the operations for which qualified. Cover the gap with a second method-certified Level III, written delegation, or by sitting the ASNT method exam.
expansion: ASNT issues the NDT Level III credential method by method: one Basic examination of 135 questions over four hours, then a separate method examination for each method held — 135 questions and four hours for UT, RT, ET, LT and AE, 90 questions and two hours for MT, PT, VT, IR and MFL. SNT-TC-1A mirrors that structure and makes the Level III responsible for the NDT operations for which qualified. Certification records must state the level, the method or technique, and limitations if any. Nothing in that chain lets a UT Level III approve an RT technique sheet, grade an RT practical, or certify an RT Level II. Firms close the gap by contracting a method-certified Level III, by written delegation under NAS 410, or by sending their own Level III to the ASNT method examination.
source: ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2020), Sections 5, 8 and 9; ANSI/ASNT CP-189 (2024); ASNT Certification Services published NDT Level III examination schedule; NAS 410 paragraph 4.5 Responsible Level 3; PRI Nadcap AC7114 audit criteria; documented ASME Section V and SNT-TC-1A audit non-conformances discussed on ndt.net.

table.note: An auditor does not need your organisation chart to find this. Every one of these documents carries a signature and a date, and every Level III certificate carries a method list. The cross-reference takes under an hour.

facets.q: Can a UT Level III approve an RT procedure if he is experienced in radiography?
facets.a: No. SNT-TC-1A makes the Level III responsible for the NDT operations for which qualified, and qualification is evidenced by a method certification. Experience without certification in the method leaves the approval unsupported, and the auditor reads the certificate rather than the CV. NAS 410 practice is explicit on the same point: a person cannot be designated responsible for a method they are not certified in.

facets.q: How does a firm cover a method its Level III does not hold?
facets.a: Four routes work. Contract an outside Level III certified in that method to approve procedures and administer examinations. Send the in-house Level III to the ASNT method examination and add the method. Delegate in writing to another qualified Level III where the governing standard permits it. Or stop offering the method until one of the first three is in place. Undocumented informal review is not a route.

facets.q: Does one person have to hold every method the company offers?
facets.a: No, and almost nobody does. A firm running six methods commonly holds two or three in-house and contracts the rest. NAS 410 practice recognises a single Responsible Level 3 certified in one or more methods used by the employer, with written delegation to method-certified Level 3s for the remainder. The requirement is coverage of every method by somebody certified, not concentration in one person.

facets.q: Which methods generate this finding most often?
facets.a: Visual testing and leak testing, because both feel like inspection rather than NDT. A documented audit non-conformance on ndt.net records exactly that: a visual examination written practice prepared by a welding inspector, no SNT-TC-1A reference in the training and certification records, and no evidence that an ASNT NDT Level III held current certification in visual testing. VT is a Section V method with its own article.

facets.q: Where is method scope actually recorded?
facets.a: On the certification record. SNT-TC-1A Section 9 requires it to state the level of certification, the NDT method and technique as applicable, and limitations if any. That limitations field is not decorative — it is where a restricted scope is captured, and a blank field asserts full competence in the method. Auditors read it, and so should the Level III signing the record.

facets.q: Does CP-189 change the answer?
facets.a: It tightens it. ANSI/ASNT CP-189 requires that Level III personnel hold ASNT NDT Level III certification in the method for which certification is sought, so the method-scope question has an external certificate behind it rather than an employer's judgement. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer decides how the Level III demonstrated method competence; under CP-189 the certificate is the evidence.

sections.heading: The finding, as auditors actually write it
paragraphs: The wording changes but the shape does not: no objective evidence that the NDT Level III who approved this procedure holds current certification in the applicable method. It is written against fabrication shops, inspection contractors, and in-house inspection departments, by ISO 9001 registrars, API auditors, Nadcap auditors and clients' technical authorities alike. It is not an interpretation dispute. It is a document comparison, and the documents are both in the audit pack you handed over.

A published example makes the mechanics concrete. In an audit discussed on ndt.net against ASME Section V and SNT-TC-1A, an auditor raised a non-conformance because the visual testing written practice had been prepared by a welding inspector rather than by NDT personnel, SNT-TC-1A references were absent from the training and certification records, and there was no evidence that an ASNT NDT Level III held current certification in visual testing. The firm disputed adjacent points about hydrostatic testing; that first one it could not.

What makes this finding expensive is its blast radius. A procedure approved by somebody without the method certification puts every examination performed to that procedure into question, along with every report issued from those examinations and every certification signed off on that basis. A single signature block can reopen two years of deliverables, which is why closing it is worth more than the hour it takes to find.

sections.heading: For which qualified — the four words doing the work
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A describes the NDT Level III as capable of establishing techniques, interpreting codes, standards, specifications and procedures, and designating the methods, techniques and procedures to be used — and as responsible for the NDT operations for which qualified and assigned. The qualifier at the end is the whole argument. Capability language describes what a Level III does in general; the responsibility clause bounds it to the methods the individual actually holds.

This reading is not a strict interpretation invented by auditors. It is how the certification structure is built. ASNT issues the NDT Level III credential on a Basic examination plus one or more method examinations, and each method passed adds that method to the credential. If the intent were that a Level III in any method could act across all methods, the separate method examinations would serve no purpose. The credential is method-scoped by construction.

The practical translation for a QA manager is short. List every NDT method your company performs, sells or certifies people in. Against each, name the individual whose method certification covers it. Any method with a blank against it is an open finding, whether or not an auditor has arrived yet. Firms taking this seriously do the exercise annually alongside an [NDT programme audit and gap assessment](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) rather than in the week before a surveillance visit.

sections.heading: Your certification record has a limitations field, and it is not decorative
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A Section 9 sets out what the personnel certification record holds, and the second item on the list is the level of certification, the NDT method and technique as applicable, and limitations if any. That last clause is the mechanism the standard gives you for recording a bounded scope, and it is chronically left empty. A blank limitations field on a certificate is a positive assertion that the individual is competent across the full method, which is a claim somebody has to be willing to defend.

Limitations are useful in both directions. A Level II certified in UT but restricted to thickness measurement, or in RT but restricted to interpretation and not radiation-producing operations, is a real and defensible arrangement provided the record says so. Where the field is left blank to avoid awkward conversations, the firm has traded a documented restriction for an undocumented exposure, and the exposure surfaces during an incident rather than during an audit.

The same discipline applies at Level III. A Level III certification record listing UT and MT is a clean document; the problem arises when the same individual's signature appears on RT and PT procedures with nothing in the file explaining why. Getting the record fields right is one of the standard corrections we make when rebuilding a programme's [written practice](/consulting/written-practice-development), because the record and the practice have to describe the same scopes.

sections.heading: Four documents where method scope actually bites
paragraphs: Procedures and technique sheets are the obvious one. Every NDT procedure carries an approval block, and that approval has to come from a Level III certified in the method the procedure describes. This includes the derived documents: RT technique sheets and shooting sketches, UT scan plans, MT technique variations for different part geometries. Firms that get the master procedure right frequently miss the technique sheets, which are approved on the shop floor under time pressure.

Examination administration is the second, and it is enforced explicitly in aerospace. Nadcap AC7114 criteria require practical examinations to be administered by the Responsible Level 3 or by an examiner certified in the applicable test method. The logic is unarguable — an examiner who cannot perform the method cannot judge whether the candidate performed it correctly — and the same logic applies outside aerospace even where the text is softer. Our [examination oversight](/consulting/ndt-level-3-exam-oversight) engagements exist largely to fill this gap.

The third is certification sign-off itself, where the Level III signature verifying a Level II's certification has to come from someone certified in that method. The fourth is report and interpretation review, where a Level III adjudicating a disputed call or countersigning a final report is exercising method judgement. Each of these leaves a dated signature in a file, and each is checked. The [boundaries of an outside Level III's authority](/consulting/outside-ndt-level-3-can-and-cannot-do) apply identically to an employed one.

sections.heading: Why a UT Level III genuinely cannot approve an RT procedure
paragraphs: Strip away the compliance framing and the technical case stands on its own. Approving a radiographic procedure means judging source selection and activity, source-to-film distance against geometric unsharpness, film system class and screen selection, density and contrast requirements, IQI type, placement and the essential hole or wire to be resolved, exposure calculations, back-scatter control, and the radiation safety envelope around all of it. None of that knowledge is contained in ultrasonic qualification, and none of it is acquired by proximity.

The examination structure prices the difference. ASNT sets its NDT Level III RT method examination at 135 questions over four hours, the same weight as UT, ET, LT and AE, while MT, PT, VT, IR and MFL run 90 questions over two hours. Those are not administrative distinctions; they reflect how much method-specific body of knowledge sits behind each credential. A UT Level III has demonstrated the UT body of knowledge and nothing else.

The reverse case is equally real and less often discussed. An RT Level III approving a phased array procedure is making judgements about focal laws, wedge selection, encoder calibration, scan plan coverage and sizing technique that radiographic qualification never touched. The finding is symmetrical, and firms that have grown from one method into several accumulate it in whichever direction they expanded.

sections.heading: Covering a method your Level III does not hold — four routes that work
paragraphs: Route one is contracting. Engage an outside Level III certified in the missing method to review and approve those procedures, administer and grade those examinations, and countersign the certification records. This is the fastest route and the one most small firms use, and it does not transfer responsibility away from the employer — the employer still certifies its own people. Our [interim and ongoing Level III cover](/consulting/interim-ndt-level-3) is built for exactly this pattern.

Route two is adding the method. Send the in-house Level III to the ASNT method examination for the missing method — 135 questions and four hours for UT, RT, ET, LT and AE, 90 questions and two hours for MT, PT, VT, IR and MFL, with the Basic examination already behind them. This is the strongest long-term answer for a method the firm sells regularly, because it removes an external dependency from routine work.

Route three is written delegation, where the governing standard supports it. NAS 410 practice allows a Responsible Level 3 to delegate in writing to another Level 3 for specified methods while retaining final approval authority over the written practice and the training and examination programme. The delegation has to be documented, method-specific and current. Route four is the honest one: withdraw the method from your scope of supply until one of the first three is in place.

sections.heading: The multi-Level-III arrangement, and who stays responsible
paragraphs: Larger organisations run several Level IIIs with a defined split, and the arrangement is entirely normal — separate individuals holding MT, RT and UT, with one of them named as the responsible or corporate Level III for the programme as a whole. The responsible role is supervisory and programme-wide: approving the written practice, owning the examination system, interfacing with auditors and regulators. Method authority sits with whoever holds the method.

The failure mode in these arrangements is ambiguity rather than absence. Two Level IIIs, both competent, neither named against specific documents, and a procedure set where the approval signatures were whoever was in the office that week. The fix is a one-page authority matrix in the written practice: method down the left, named individual and certificate number across, with the delegation reference where the individual is external. Auditors accept clarity; they write findings against vagueness.

Outside Level IIIs slot into that matrix on the same terms as employees, with one boundary that stays fixed. An outside agency or contracted Level III qualifies and examines; the employer certifies. That division holds under SNT-TC-1A and under NAS 410 practice, and it means a contracted method specialist strengthens your programme without ever taking your certification decisions away from you.

sections.heading: CP-189 and NAS 410 raise the bar above SNT-TC-1A
paragraphs: SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice, and it leaves the employer to decide how a Level III demonstrated method competence — an ASNT certificate, or an employer-administered basic, method and specific examination sequence. ANSI/ASNT CP-189 removes the discretion. Under CP-189 the Level III candidate has to hold ASNT NDT Level III certification in the method for which certification is sought, which converts the method-scope question into a certificate check with no room for interpretation.

That single difference reshapes the compliance picture for anybody whose client contracts invoke CP-189 rather than SNT-TC-1A. A firm whose Level III was qualified in-house across four methods under a well-written practice can find that only the two methods carrying ASNT certificates survive the transition. Reviewing your contract stack for which standard each client actually invokes is worth doing before a client does it for you, and our [CP-189 compliance notes](/compliance/ansi-asnt-cp-189) set out the differences against [SNT-TC-1A](/compliance/asnt-snt-tc-1a).

Aerospace applies a third pattern through NAS 410 and Nadcap. The Responsible Level 3 has to be certified in one or more methods the employer uses and be well versed in the codes and specifications the employer works to, and practical examinations have to be administered by that person or by an examiner certified in the applicable method. A firm holding both an ISO 9001 registration and a Nadcap accreditation is answering to the stricter of the two on every method it runs.

sections.heading: How auditors detect the mismatch in under an hour
paragraphs: The procedure is mechanical and any competent auditor knows it. Collect the Level III certificates and note the methods and expiry dates on each. Collect the procedure index and note the approver and date on every procedure and technique sheet. Cross-reference. Any procedure whose approver has no certificate covering that method on that date is a finding, and the audit trail is two documents long. No interviews, no interpretation, no argument.

The second pass goes to examinations. Pull a sample of certification records, look at the grader signature on the practical checkpoint sheets, and compare against the same certificate list. Then look at the limitations field on each record, and at whether the record's method matches the methods the individual actually performs on site. The third pass is the written practice: does it name who is authorised for which method, and does the naming match reality.

Everything an auditor needs is in the pack you supply voluntarily, which means you can run the same three passes yourself first. Firms that do this discover the gaps at a point where all four coverage routes are still open, rather than during a closing meeting where only the expensive ones are. Atlantis runs this cross-reference as a fixed-scope review — affordable, accessible and fully customizable — and returns the authority matrix along with it. [Request a quote or a demo](/contact).

sections.heading: Visual and leak testing: the two methods that generate the finding
paragraphs: Visual testing is where this goes wrong most often, because it does not feel like NDT. It is performed by welding inspectors, described in weld inspection procedures, and treated as a craft skill. ASME Section V disagrees: VT is a method with its own article and its own procedure variables table, and a VT procedure needs approval by a Level III certified in VT like any other. The documented audit case above turned on precisely that mismatch.

Leak testing collects the same problem from a different direction. Bubble, pressure change, halogen diode and mass spectrometer techniques are treated as pressure testing rather than examination, and end up in mechanical completion procedures signed by process engineers. Where a construction code routes leak testing to Section V Article 10, the procedure needs a Level III certified in LT. Where it does not, the argument is worth having with the auditor from a documented position rather than an improvised one.

Both cases share a root cause: methods that arrived through operations rather than through the NDT department were never brought under the written practice. The corrective action is the same in both — add the method to the written practice, name a certified Level III against it, bring the procedure under the same approval route as every other method, and update the certification records so the method appears where an auditor expects to see it.

faq.q: Our Level III holds UT and MT. We also run PT and VT. Are we non-compliant today?
faq.a: You have an open gap in PT and VT until somebody certified in those methods approves the procedures, administers the practical examinations and signs the certification records. The gap is closeable in days by contracting a method-certified Level III, and closeable permanently by adding the methods to your own Level III's credential. What you cannot do is leave the existing signatures in place and hope the sampling misses them.

faq.q: Can our Level III approve a procedure in a method he is qualified but not certified in?
faq.a: No. Qualification without certification leaves nothing for an auditor to verify, and the certification record is the evidence the standards ask for. NAS 410 practice states the point directly: a person cannot be designated as responsible for a method without being certified in it, regardless of certification held in other methods. The distinction between qualified and certified is exactly what the finding turns on.

faq.q: Does an outside Level III take on our liability for the methods they cover?
faq.a: No. The employer certifies its own personnel and owns the certification decisions under SNT-TC-1A, and that does not transfer to a contracted Level III. What the arrangement transfers is the technical authority to approve method-specific documents and administer method-specific examinations, backed by a certificate an auditor can verify. Record the delegation in the written practice so the authority and the responsibility are both visible.

faq.q: How do we prove method coverage quickly during an audit?
faq.a: Hand over a one-page authority matrix: NDT method down the left, the named Level III and their certificate number and expiry across, and the delegation or contract reference where the individual is external. Auditors work from documents, and a matrix that reconciles to your procedure approval blocks and certification records removes the entire line of questioning in one exchange.

faq.q: Is a Level III certificate from a previous employer still valid at ours?
faq.a: Under SNT-TC-1A the certification is employer-based and lapses when employment ends unless the individual holds a third-party certification. An ASNT NDT Level III certificate travels with the person and evidences method competence; the employer-issued certification does not. This is why the ASNT credential matters so much to the method-scope question — it is the portable evidence your new written practice can rest on.

faq.q: We are adding phased array. Does our UT Level III cover it?
faq.a: UT certification covers the method, and PAUT sits within it, but the technique carries its own competence question. Add a documented technique-level qualification for the individuals involved, record it in the technique field of the certification record, and make sure the scan plans and procedures are approved by someone who can actually judge focal laws and coverage. The record fields exist for exactly this distinction.

title: When You Can't Re-Inspect: Independent NDT Report Validation
description: Independent Level III review of NDT reports already issued: procedure, personnel, calibration, technique and acceptance criteria tested against the governing code.
h1: Independent validation of NDT reports you are being asked to rely on
answer: NDT report validation is an independent Level III review of an inspection report that already exists. It tests seven things: procedure compliance, personnel qualification on the date of work, calibration traceability, technique adequacy for the expected flaw, acceptance criteria correctly applied, results correctly interpreted, and completeness against the governing code. The verdict is sound, deficient in disposition, or deficient only in documentation.
expansion: Validation is bought at a decision point: accept the report, pay the invoice, close the claim, sign the purchase, or go to hearing. The reviewer works only from the record and its supporting evidence — procedure and revision, certification files current on the examination date, calibration certificates with traceability, technique sheets, calibration records, and the raw data or radiographs where they exist. Each element is tested against the code the job was contracted to, not against a house preference. Three outcomes are possible. The report is sound and supports its disposition. The report is deficient in a way that changes the disposition, meaning the accept or reject call is not supported. Or the report is deficient only in documentation — the examination was adequate but the record does not prove it. The third outcome carries the least technical risk and the most commercial risk, and it is where most disputes actually live.
source: ASME BPVC Section V, Article 1 (T-120(e) personnel qualification, T-150 procedure demonstration, T-190 records and documentation); ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2020) recertification and vision examination requirements; ANSI/ASNT CP-189; IACS UR Z17 procedural requirements for service suppliers; Atlantis NDT Level III review practice.

table.note: A validation is bought at a decision point. If no decision is waiting on the answer, a programme audit is the better instrument.

facets.q: How is report validation different from having a second contractor re-inspect?
facets.a: Re-inspection tells you what is in the material now. Validation tells you whether the examination already performed was adequate and correctly interpreted. They answer different questions, and only validation can settle a dispute about a report produced two years ago on an asset that has since been closed up, painted, insulated, or sold to somebody else.

facets.q: Can a report be validated without the raw data or radiographs?
facets.a: Yes, with a stated limitation. Procedure compliance, personnel currency, calibration traceability, criteria selection and report completeness are all testable from the record alone. Interpretation is not — without the radiographs, A-scans or scan files, the review can confirm that the interpretation was recorded competently but cannot independently re-read the data. The report states which of the two it did.

facets.q: Who signs the validation, and does the signature matter?
facets.a: An ASNT Level III certified in each method under review signs it, and the signature is the product. A validation signed by somebody without scope in a reviewed method carries the same defect it is looking for. Where a package spans four methods, either one signer holds all four or the report names a reviewer per method on its face.

facets.q: What happens if the validation finds the original report was correct?
facets.a: You get a written finding that says so, with the evidence recorded for each element tested. That is the outcome in a large share of validations and it is a usable result: it closes a rejection, releases a retention, supports a claim, or lets a purchase proceed. An opinion that could only come back negative would not be worth commissioning.

facets.q: How old can a report be and still be worth validating?
facets.a: Age limits the evidence, not the review. What degrades is retrievability — certification files, calibration certificates and technique sheets get lost when contractors change or archives are purged. A report from several years ago with an intact evidence pack is more validatable than one from last quarter whose supporting records were never collected. Ask what still exists first.

facets.q: Does report validation work outside the United States?
facets.a: It works anywhere the governing code is written down. ASME Section V paragraphs read the same in Rotterdam as in Houston, ISO 9712 certificates are verifiable from any country, and class requirements under IACS unified requirements apply by flag rather than by geography. The work is document-based, so nothing mobilises and the asset's location does not affect the scope.

sections.heading: Validation starts where the examination ended
paragraphs: A report validation begins after the examination is finished, the crew has demobilised, and the document is sitting in somebody's inbox waiting to be accepted, paid for, or argued about. No probe goes back on the weld. What gets examined is the record: the procedure it invokes, the people who signed it, the equipment it names, the technique it describes, the criteria it cites, and the disposition it reaches. The output is a written opinion from an [ASNT Level III](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) on whether that record supports the conclusion printed on its front page.

This is a different product from inspection, sold to different people for different reasons. An inspection company sells you a finding. A validation sells you an answer about somebody else's finding. That distinction is commercial as well as technical: the validating party has no stake in the original result and no scope of its own to defend. It also changes how the work is done. A validator reads for internal contradiction, missing linkage and code compliance — not for flaws in steel.

The service exists because the alternative is often unavailable. The vessel is closed, the line is buried, the coating is back on, the fabricator has been paid and demobilised, the ship has sailed. When re-examination is impossible, disproportionate, or too slow for the decision in front of you, the record is the only evidence that exists — and somebody has to be able to say whether it is worth anything. The full trade-off is set out in [third-party review versus re-inspection](/report-validation/third-party-review-vs-re-inspection).

sections.heading: Six triggers, and each one asks a different question
paragraphs: The asset owner's trigger is distrust plus impossibility. A contractor has handed over a report that clears a weld, a shell course or a run of supports, something about it reads thin, and the asset is back in service. The question is not whether there was a flaw — it is whether this document justifies releasing retention and closing the work order. A validation answers that from the paper, and does it in days rather than waiting for an outage window.

The EPC or fabricator's trigger runs the other way. Their client's reviewer has rejected a report, and the fabricator believes the rejection is wrong: the criteria applied were never in the contract, or the reviewer misread a technique that the code permits. Here the buyer wants the report defended. An honest validator will sometimes tell them it cannot be, and that is exactly why the opinion carries weight when it goes back across the table.

Four more triggers behave differently again. An insurer or underwriter assessing a claim whose outcome turns on an inspection record needs to know whether that record is evidence or noise. A purchaser in due diligence on a plant, vessel or fleet is buying the inspection history along with the steel. A party in litigation or arbitration needs a record tested before it is relied on. And a Level III who has inherited a programme needs to know what the previous regime actually produced, which is closer to a [programme audit](/consulting/ndt-program-audit-gap-assessment) run backwards through the files.

sections.heading: The seven checks a validation runs
paragraphs: Procedure compliance comes first. The report must invoke a procedure by number and revision, that procedure must cover the configuration and thickness actually examined, and it must have been qualified or demonstrated where the referencing code requires it. Personnel qualification comes second, and it is checked against the date the work was done. A certificate that is valid today proves nothing about a scan performed eighteen months ago under a certification that had already lapsed at the time.

Third is equipment and calibration traceability: the instrument identified by serial number, the calibration status current at the time of examination, and a chain back to a recognised standard rather than a sticker with a date on it. Fourth is technique adequacy for the flaw type expected. A shear-wave setup optimised for planar weld defects will not reliably characterise volumetric porosity, and a technique that cannot orient to the expected flaw is inadequate regardless of how well it was executed on the day.

Fifth, the acceptance criteria must be the right ones, stated with code and edition, and taken from the construction or in-service code rather than from Section V, which prescribes methods rather than accept or reject limits. Sixth, the results must have been correctly interpreted against those criteria. Seventh, the report must be complete against what the governing code requires it to contain — the element list is set out in full on [what makes an NDT report defensible](/report-validation/what-makes-an-ndt-report-defensible).

sections.heading: Qualification is tested on the date of the work, not the date of the review
paragraphs: In the ASME world, NDT personnel are certified by their employer, not by an outside body. ASME BPVC Section V requires qualification in accordance with the employer's written practice, and that written practice is built on ASNT [SNT-TC-1A](/compliance/asnt-snt-tc-1a) or ANSI/ASNT CP-189. In the 2023 edition of Section V, the personnel requirements that had lived in Mandatory Appendices III and IV were moved into T-120(e). A validation therefore starts by asking to see the written practice, not just the certificate.

The 2020 edition of SNT-TC-1A sets recertification for all three levels at five-year intervals, near-vision acuity examination annually — Jaeger Number 2 or equivalent at a distance of not less than 12 in. (30.5 cm) — and colour contrast differentiation at initial certification and at five-year intervals after. Three separate clocks run on every technician. The finding that turns up repeatedly is a certification file that is complete on the day it was scanned and short a vision record on the day of the scan.

Outside ASME, the model changes and so does the check. Marine work under [IACS UR Z17](/compliance/iacs-ur-z17) expects the responsible supervisor for thickness measurement to hold a recognised national or international qualification such as ISO 9712 Level II, with operators certified to Level I and holding adequate knowledge of ship structures. ISO 9712 is third-party certification, so the evidence is a certificate from a certification body rather than an employer's internal file — a different document, tested a different way.

sections.heading: Three verdicts, and the third is the one people misread
paragraphs: Verdict one: sound. The examination described was adequate for the flaw type expected, the criteria applied were the contracted ones, the interpretation follows from the data, and the record proves it. The disposition stands. This verdict is written to be usable — it names what was checked and what evidence supported each check, so the party who commissioned it can put it straight in front of the party who doubted the report.

Verdict two: deficient in a way that changes the disposition. The accept or reject call is not supported. This covers the wrong acceptance criteria, a technique incapable of detecting the flaw type the component is prone to, an indication recorded but evaluated against a limit that does not apply, or coverage that never reached the volume the code required. This verdict has commercial consequences and is written to survive being contested by a competent opponent.

Verdict three: deficient only in documentation. The examination was plausibly adequate, but the record does not prove it — a missing revision number, an unrecorded couplant, a calibration block never identified, a lighting check absent from a fluorescent examination. Nothing about the steel changed. What changed is that the report can no longer defend itself, and a client, auditor or opposing expert can reject it without ever disputing the technician's work. Most of what a validation finds sits here.

sections.heading: A validation that confirms the report was right is a result, not a failure
paragraphs: Report validation is not a defect-finding exercise pointed at contractors. A significant share of validations conclude that the original report was correct, adequately documented and properly disposed. That outcome is worth paying for, because the buyer did not purchase a criticism — they purchased a defensible answer, and "this report holds" is a defensible answer that ends the argument, closes the claim, or lets the purchase proceed on schedule.

This shapes how the work is run. A reviewer paid, structurally or psychologically, to find problems will find them. The discipline is to test each element against the code and record the outcome either way, including the elements that passed. A validation report that lists only failures is a complaint; one that lists what was tested, what passed and what did not is evidence, and only the second kind is any use in front of a tribunal or an underwriter.

It matters to the contractor on the other side too. A fabricator whose report has been rejected by a client's reviewer commissions validation precisely hoping for verdict one, and the value of getting it is that the same document would have said otherwise had the evidence pointed that way. An opinion that can only come back one way is worth nothing to either party, and everyone reading it knows that.

sections.heading: The deliverable, and what you can do with it
paragraphs: The deliverable is a signed technical opinion, element by element. Each of the seven checks appears as a heading with the evidence examined, the finding, and the code paragraph or contract clause the finding rests on. The verdict is stated in one line at the top. Where a deficiency is documentary rather than technical, it says so explicitly, because the remedy is different, the timescale is different, and the commercial consequence is different.

Attached to it is the evidence pack: the procedure revision reviewed, the certification records with their dates, the calibration certificates and their traceability chain, the technique sheets and calibration records, and the raw data, radiographs or scan files where they exist. The pack matters as much as the opinion, because it lets a third party — an auditor, an underwriter, a tribunal — re-run the reasoning without having to re-run the review from scratch.

Where the finding is that documentation is short, the deliverable states what would close each gap and whether it can still be closed after the fact. Some gaps can: a certification file can be produced, a calibration certificate retrieved, a technique sheet located in an archive. Some cannot: a lighting verification never performed cannot be reconstructed a year later. Saying which is which is the practical half of the report, and the half buyers act on first.

sections.heading: Independence: who can validate, and who cannot
paragraphs: The validator must not have produced the thing being validated. A firm that wrote the procedure, trained the technicians, or performed the original examination cannot review its own work and call the result independent. Where Atlantis has previously supported a client with procedure development or programme work, the validation is ring-fenced from that engagement or declined outright — the answer is only worth as much as the independence standing behind it.

Independence is not the only limit. An outside Level III operates inside a defined authority: reviewing, evaluating and rendering opinion, but not assuming the employer's certifying responsibility unless that has been formally delegated in the written practice. The boundaries are set out in [what an outside NDT Level III can and cannot do](/consulting/outside-ndt-level-3-can-and-cannot-do), and they apply to validation work exactly as they apply to any other outside engagement.

Method scope is the third limit. A Level III validates in the methods they hold, and a validation touching UT, RT, MT and PT across the same weld package needs qualification across all four or a named reviewer per method. A report that quietly reviews a method outside the signer's scope has the same defect it is accusing the original report of having, and an opposing expert will find it in the first hour.

sections.heading: United States first, and worldwide because the codes are
paragraphs: The primary market is the United States, where ASME BPVC construction and in-service codes, API in-service inspection practice, and employer-based certification under SNT-TC-1A create the exact conditions that make report validation buyable: a document-driven regime where the paper is the proof. Most of the disputes that reach a validator are about whether the paper does its job, not about whether the metal underneath it is sound.

The service travels because the codes travel. A Section V examination performed in Jubail, Rotterdam or Singapore is examined against the same paragraphs it would be in Texas, and an ISO 9712 certification is verifiable from anywhere. Reviews are conducted on documents, so time zone and mobilisation stop being cost drivers — which is why validation reaches assets that no inspector would realistically be flown out to look at.

What changes across jurisdictions is the referencing code and the contract. A European fabrication under EN and ISO invokes different acceptance criteria and a different certification model from a US pressure vessel, and a marine survey under class rules invokes another again. The seven checks stay constant; the documents they are tested against are read out of the contract. Send the report and the governing code, and the scope defines itself — [start here](/contact).

faq.q: What do you need from us to start a validation?
faq.a: The report itself, the procedure it invokes at the revision in force on the examination date, the certification records for the personnel who signed it, the calibration certificates for the equipment named, and the governing code or contract that set the acceptance criteria. Raw data, radiographs or scan files where they still exist. If parts are missing, say so — a missing evidence class is itself a finding, and knowing early changes how the scope is written.

faq.q: Can you validate a report produced by a contractor we are currently in dispute with?
faq.a: Yes, provided Atlantis has no relationship with that contractor and did not write the procedure, train the personnel, or perform the original examination on that job. Conflicts are declared before scope is agreed, and an engagement that cannot be run independently is declined rather than caveated. The independence has to survive the other side's scrutiny, not just ours.

faq.q: Which methods can you validate?
faq.a: UT including phased array and TOFD, RT, MT, PT, VT and ET, with the reviewing Level III certified in each method that appears in the scope. Where a package spans methods outside the signer's certification, the report names an additional reviewer for those methods rather than reviewing them anyway. The methods reviewed and the scope behind each signature are stated on the face of the report.

faq.q: Will the validation stand up if it is challenged?
faq.a: It is written to be challenged. Every finding is tied to a code paragraph, a contract clause or a document in the evidence pack, so an opposing reviewer can test the reasoning rather than argue with the opinion. That construction is deliberate for insurance, due diligence and arbitration work, where the report will be read by somebody whose job is to disagree with it.

faq.q: Is this the same as an NDT programme audit?
faq.a: No. A validation examines specific reports and reaches a verdict on each. A programme audit examines the system that produces reports — written practice, procedures, qualification records, calibration control — and reports on capability rather than on individual jobs. Buyers who find the same defect repeating across several validations usually move to an audit next, because the fix is upstream of any single report.

title: Nine Things an NDT Report Must Carry to Survive Scrutiny
description: The record elements an NDT report must carry — component ID, procedure revision, certification, calibration traceability, technique detail, criteria and disposition.
h1: What a defensible NDT report has to carry, element by element
answer: A defensible NDT report identifies the component and the exact area examined, names the procedure and its revision, names the examiner with certification level, method and certifying authority, records equipment with traceable calibration status, states technique detail sufficient to reproduce the examination, cites acceptance criteria by code and edition, reports results against those criteria, and states a disposition.
expansion: Defensibility is not a style question. ASME BPVC Section V places records and documentation under the referencing code section and makes the Manufacturer, fabricator or installer responsible for producing them, then prescribes article by article what each examination record must contain. Those lists are the floor. A report that omits a named item has failed a code requirement, whatever the quality of the examination behind it. The nine elements below are the order a validation tests in, and the order a client's reviewer reaches for when deciding whether to reject. Three of them fail more often than the rest: the procedure revision, the acceptance criteria line, and the technique detail that would let a stranger reproduce the setup. All three are short to write at the time and close to impossible to reconstruct afterwards, which is why a report is either built defensible on the day or is never defensible at all.
source: ASME BPVC Section V: Article 1 T-120(e), T-150, T-190; Article 2 T-276, T-277, T-282, T-291, T-292; Article 4 T-491, T-492; Article 6 T-672, T-691, T-692; Article 7 T-762, T-792, T-793. ASNT SNT-TC-1A (2020); ANSI/ASNT CP-189.
