table.note: Sizes computed from the published record layouts at 100 million points carrying XYZ, intensity and colour: 17 bytes per point for a scaled-integer E57, 34 bytes for LAS point data record format 3, 40-60 bytes per line of ASCII. Embedded imagery, 1024-byte page overhead and null grid rows add to these.

facets.q: Which point cloud format should I name in the contract?
facets.a: Name two. E57 per ASTM E2807 as the archive deliverable, undecimated, with each scanner setup preserved and the structured grid retained. Then one indexed working copy matching the software you own: RCP with its RCS folder for Autodesk sites, POD for Bentley sites, an AVEVA Point Cloud Manager dataset for E3D sites, LAZ where the work is georeferenced.

facets.q: Can I convert an RCP back to E57?
facets.a: No. ReCap indexing is one-way. An RCP references RCS files that hold points restructured into an octree, and any decimation applied at import to make the file manageable is gone permanently. Export tools produce a new cloud from the indexed data, not the original file. A survey delivered only as RCP cannot be re-purposed outside the Autodesk family later.

facets.q: Does E57 or LAS give me the smaller file?
facets.a: E57 is smaller uncompressed and LAZ beats both. A point with scaled-integer XYZ, intensity and colour costs about 17 bytes in E57 against 34 bytes in LAS point data record format 3. LAZ then compresses the LAS losslessly to roughly 7-20% of its size, which makes LAZ the smallest option and the right archive companion for georeferenced work.

facets.q: Why will Revit not open my E57 directly?
facets.a: Revit links RCP and RCS files, not E57. The E57 goes through ReCap indexing first, or through a third-party importer from the Autodesk App Store. That conversion is a real step with real hours attached, and it is where scope disputes start: the contractor delivered a valid standards-based file, the modelling team cannot open it, and nobody priced the indexing.

facets.q: What does a structured point cloud mean in a deliverable?
facets.a: Structured means each point keeps its row and column index in the scanner's sweep, so the cloud remembers the grid the instrument fired in. That grid is what lets software compute reliable surface normals, generate a panoramic view from the setup position, and separate a real surface from a mixed-pixel artefact at an edge. E57 and PTX preserve it. LAS and a merged export destroy it.

facets.q: Is LAZ compression lossy?
facets.a: No. LASzip is lossless entropy coding: decompress a LAZ and you get back the exact LAS it came from, byte for byte. It stores points in chunks that decompress independently, so software still random-accesses the file. What people call lossy compression in point clouds is almost always decimation — points deleted to hit a spacing target — which is irreversible and unrelated to the codec.

sections.heading: Read the extension before you read the invoice
paragraphs: A scan delivery lands as a folder of files with six or seven different extensions, and the useful sort is not best-to-worst. It is master, derivative and legacy. E57 and LAS/LAZ are exchange formats: anyone can read them with free software, and they can regenerate everything else. RCP/RCS and POD are vendor working formats — fast, indexed and one-way. PTX and PTS are ASCII text from the Leica lineage, kept alive by a handful of old workflows. Establish which file in the folder is the master before you archive anything.

The master is the file that can rebuild every other deliverable five years from now, after the scanning contractor has changed software and the technician who ran the job has left. That file has to carry each scanner setup separately, with its own position and orientation, at full captured density, in a documented coordinate system. If the only file in the handover is an indexed vendor project, the master does not exist and the survey is now hostage to one software vendor's licence renewal.

Three checks settle the question at handover: which file holds the undecimated per-setup data, which coordinate system and units the numbers are in, and whether the scanner's own structure survived the export. Everything else — colour, panoramic imagery, classification — is recoverable or replaceable. Those three are not. Run the checks in the week the data arrives, while the crew can still remobilise, rather than during the outage where the model is needed.

sections.heading: E57 is the only one published by a standards body
paragraphs: E57 is standardised as ASTM E2807, Standard Specification for 3D Imaging Data Exchange, Version 1.0, originally approved in 2011 and kept current by reapproval rather than revision. The edition most implementations cite is E2807-11(2019), and ASTM's catalogue lists a further reapproval of the same 2011 text as the active version, so a scope clause reading "E57 per ASTM E2807" stays correct without naming a year. It is the only format in this list published by a standards body rather than by the company that sells the software that reads it.

The file is a hybrid. Binary point data is written in fixed 1024-byte pages, each carrying a checksum, and described by an XML section. That layout is why a reader can navigate a 40 GB E57 without loading it and why partial corruption stays legible. Each scanner setup is stored as its own section with a 4x4 pose, so the registration lives inside the file rather than in a separate transform list. Photographs — spherical panoramas and pinhole images — sit alongside, which is how a colourised cloud keeps the imagery that coloured it.

Two E57 features matter for plant work and get lost in casual exports. The structured grid stores each point with its row and column index in the scanner's sweep, which is what lets software compute reliable normals, build a panorama and separate a real surface from a mixed-pixel artefact at an edge. The invalid-state flag records where the scanner fired and got no return, which is the difference between "nothing there" and "not measured". Compression is a lossless bit-packing codec that shrinks integer fields to their actual range.

sections.heading: LAS and LAZ carry geometry and throw the rest away
paragraphs: LAS comes from airborne LiDAR and the American Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing, and it shows. The current published edition is LAS 1.4, revision R15. Coordinates are stored as 32-bit signed integers with a scale factor and offset declared once in the header, so precision is a header decision rather than a format limit: at a scale factor of 0.001 the integer range spans roughly 2,147 km either side of the offset, which covers any plant on any state plane grid at millimetre resolution. Getting that header wrong is the commonest way a LAS delivery quietly loses precision.

What LAS holds per point is fixed by the point data record format, and the byte counts set your file sizes. Format 0 is 20 bytes. Format 1 adds GPS time at 28, format 2 adds colour at 26, format 3 carries both at 34. The 6-to-10 family rebuilt the record for 15 returns and 256 classes: format 6 is 30 bytes, format 7 adds colour at 36, format 8 adds near-infrared at 38. Intensity is present everywhere. Colour is present only in formats 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 and 10, so a request for "LAS with colour" has to name the record format.

What LAS does not hold is the reason it makes a poor master for terrestrial plant scanning. There is no scanner pose, no imagery and no structured grid, so the deliverable arrives as one merged cloud in a single frame with the setups blended together. Point Source ID, and Scanner Channel in the newer formats, are the only provenance left. LAZ fixes the size problem without touching content: LASzip is lossless, lands at roughly 7-20% of the LAS it came from, and chunks the data so readers still random-access it.

sections.heading: RCP and RCS are a working copy, never an archive
paragraphs: RCS and RCP are Autodesk ReCap's pair. An RCS holds one spatially indexed scan — coordinates, colour and intensity restructured into an octree so a workstation streams level-of-detail instead of loading three billion points. An RCP holds no points at all: it is a project file that references a set of RCS files and adds registration transforms, scan regions, recorded distances and annotations. Move or rename the RCS folder and the RCP opens empty, which is the most common support call in scan-to-BIM work and the reason an RCP delivery needs a folder-structure note.

This pair is what Revit, AutoCAD, Civil 3D and Navisworks attach natively. Revit does not link an E57 out of the box: the E57 goes through ReCap indexing first, or through a third-party importer from the Autodesk App Store. That conversion step is where scope disputes start, because the contractor delivered a valid standards-based file, the modelling team cannot open it, and neither party priced the indexing. Name the indexing in the scope and name who performs it.

Treat RCP and RCS as derivatives. Indexing is one-way — there is no route back to the E57 it was built from — and any decimation applied at import to make the file manageable is gone permanently. A survey delivered only as RCP is usable for two years in one software family and cannot be re-purposed afterwards. The same logic governs every indexed vendor container, which is the point of writing a proper [deliverables specification](/3d-scanning/point-cloud-to-cad-deliverables) rather than accepting whatever the contractor's software exports.

sections.heading: POD, PTX, PTS and the plant-specific containers
paragraphs: POD is Bentley's equivalent. MicroStation, OpenPlant and OpenRoads import a long list of formats — LAS, E57, PTS, PTX, FLS, RXP and more — but only POD attaches natively to a DGN through the point cloud engine, so everything else is converted on the way in. The one-way rule holds: POD is a working copy. AVEVA E3D consumes clouds through AVEVA Point Cloud Manager, formerly LFM Server, which builds its own indexed dataset from the same source formats and serves it to the design session.

PTX and PTS are Leica Cyclone's ASCII exports, and they are text files. PTX keeps the useful part — each scan section carries a 4x4 transformation matrix and the structured grid survives — while PTS is a flat list with no pose and no grid. Because the grid is preserved as text, PTX writes a row for every shot the scanner fired, including the ones that returned nothing, so the file is dramatically larger than the data inside it. Both formats are in decline as E57 absorbs their role.

Neither belongs in a modern scope except as a named compatibility copy for one named legacy tool. If a stress package, an old piping design seat or a subcontractor's viewer needs PTX, write that single requirement in and generate it from the E57 master. Making PTX the general deliverable multiplies your storage several times over and hands the next contractor a text file to re-parse.

sections.heading: Where the data actually disappears
paragraphs: Compression is not where point cloud data is lost. LAZ is lossless entropy coding and E57's bit-packing is lossless integer packing; both return the numbers they were given. Data disappears in three other places. Decimation removes points at export or index time to hit a spacing target, and it is irreversible. Quantisation sets how finely coordinates are stored — the LAS scale factor, the E57 scaled-integer precision — and a coarse setting rounds real geometry away. Structure loss merges the setups into one undifferentiated cloud and destroys pose, grid and per-setup provenance in a single operation.

Structure loss is the one buyers never see coming, because the merged cloud looks correct on screen. The cost shows up later. Normals become unreliable, so surface fitting and automatic pipe extraction degrade. Panoramic views are gone, so a remote reviewer cannot look around from a setup position. A noisy scan cannot be isolated and re-weighted, because nobody can tell which points came from which setup. Any of those failures pushes work back to a field remobilisation months after the crew demobilised.

One rule prevents all three: the archive deliverable is undecimated, per-setup and structured, in E57. Every optimised, merged and decimated file in the delivery is a derivative of that one, generated for a named tool and regenerable at will. Once that is written into the scope, working formats stop being contentious, because losing one costs an afternoon of re-conversion rather than a re-scan. If the cloud is heading into an operational [digital twin](/digital-twins), that rule is what keeps the geometry re-usable when the twin platform changes.

sections.heading: File sizes at real plant densities
paragraphs: Size follows from bytes per point and the arithmetic is short. A point with XYZ as three 4-byte scaled integers, 2-byte intensity and 3-byte colour costs 17 bytes, so 100 million points is about 1.7 GB before imagery and page overhead — roughly what a well-written E57 costs. The same 100 million points in LAS point data record format 3 is 34 bytes each, or 3.4 GB. Compress that to LAZ and it lands around 250-700 MB. PTX, as text, runs 40 to 60 bytes per line and clears 4 GB, plus the null rows for every non-return.

Those numbers decide who can open your data. A 2 GB E57 opens in free software on a laptop. A 40 GB merged E57 from a full process unit opens only in software that streams from disk, which is precisely what the indexed formats exist to solve — an RCP or POD is sized by its indexing settings rather than by the raw point count, and it is the file an inspector or a project engineer will actually use. Deliver both and the archive question stops competing with the usability question.

Storage cost is the weakest reason to decimate. A full unit survey held as lossless LAZ plus a per-setup E57 master fits inside the storage a mid-size operator already pays for, and it is smaller than the video footage from one turnaround. What justifies a decimated copy is the field tablet and the review session, and both are derivatives generated on demand. Never let a workstation performance problem become an archive policy.

sections.heading: What to write into the scope of work
paragraphs: A deliverable clause that prevents every dispute above fits on one page. Name the archive format as E57 per ASTM E2807, with each scanner setup preserved, undecimated, structured grid and invalid-state retained. Name the coordinate system, the units, the vertical datum and the plant grid or benchmark the survey ties to. Require the registration report with cloud-to-cloud and target residuals rather than a pass statement. Require the panoramic imagery inside the E57 rather than as a separate folder of JPEGs that no software will ever re-associate with the points.

Then name the working copy after the software you already own. Autodesk sites ask for RCP with the RCS folder intact and a note on relative paths. Bentley sites ask for POD. AVEVA sites ask for the Point Cloud Manager dataset. Georeferenced and drone-integrated work asks for LAZ. One named working format is enough — a scope that lists five is a scope that pays for five conversions and archives none of them properly. If the cloud will feed an operational [digital twin](/digital-twins), name that consumer too.

Close with the mechanics: a file manifest with checksums, a naming convention that encodes unit, setup number and date, and a statement that the deliverable must open in a licence-free reader. That last line is the enforcement mechanism for everything above it. Keep the [modelling scope](/3d-scanning/scan-to-cad-modelling-levels-lod) as a separate section rather than folding it into the scanning clause, because modelling effort is the real cost driver and it deserves its own acceptance criteria.

sections.heading: The twenty-minute handover check
paragraphs: Twenty minutes with free software settles acceptance. Open the master E57 in CloudCompare, which reads E57, LAS, LAZ, PTX and PTS without a licence. Confirm the setup count matches the field log. Confirm colour and intensity are present. Measure something you know — flange face to flange face, a nominal pipe outside diameter, a column bay — and check it against the drawing. Read the coordinates of a known benchmark and confirm they land where the plant grid says they should.

Then convert one scan yourself into your working format. If you can index one E57 into an RCS, or bring one into POD, the whole set will follow and you have proven you are not dependent on the contractor to use your own data. That single test separates a survey you own from a survey you licensed, and it applies the same evidence logic that makes [an NDT report defensible](/report-validation/what-makes-an-ndt-report-defensible): traceable, repeatable, independently readable. Book it before the retention payment, not after.

What comes next is a separate decision with a larger number attached — how much of that cloud becomes modelled geometry, and at what level. That question drives more cost than the scanning does, and it is answered on the [modelling levels page](/3d-scanning/scan-to-cad-modelling-levels-lod). If the geometry is heading into an operational model that inspection data will hang off, the [twin side of the workflow](/digital-twins/inspection-data-on-a-twin-what-it-changes) sets what the model has to support. To scope a survey against the tools you already run, [ask for a quote](/contact).

faq.q: What software opens an E57 file for free?
faq.a: CloudCompare is the standard answer: it is free and open source, runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and reads E57, LAS, LAZ, PTX, PTS, PLY and around twenty other formats. It also converts between them, which makes it the right acceptance tool at handover. Autodesk ReCap, Leica Cyclone, FARO SCENE and Trimble RealWorks all read E57 as well, under licence.

faq.q: How large is the point cloud for a full process unit?
faq.a: Work it from bytes per point. A well-written E57 costs about 17 bytes per point carrying XYZ, intensity and colour, so a billion points is roughly 17 GB before embedded imagery. The same data as LAS point data record format 3 is 34 bytes per point. LAZ compresses that to roughly 7-20%. A congested unit surveyed at production density runs to tens of gigabytes in the master file.

faq.q: What is the difference between an RCP and an RCS file?
faq.a: An RCS holds the points for one scan, spatially indexed into an octree. An RCP holds no points at all — it is a project file pointing at a set of RCS files, plus registration transforms, scan regions, recorded distances and annotations. Both must be delivered together with the folder structure intact, because moving or renaming the RCS folder makes the RCP open empty.

faq.q: Should I accept a single merged cloud as the deliverable?
faq.a: Not as the archive. Merging the setups into one cloud destroys the per-setup pose, the structured grid and the provenance of every point, and none of it comes back. Surface normals degrade, panoramic review from a setup position becomes impossible, and a noisy scan can no longer be isolated. Accept a merged file as a convenience derivative alongside a per-setup E57 master.

faq.q: Which standard defines the E57 format?
faq.a: ASTM E2807, Standard Specification for 3D Imaging Data Exchange, Version 1.0. It was approved in 2011 and has been carried forward by reapproval rather than revision, so the technical content is unchanged: the edition commonly cited is E2807-11(2019), with a later reapproval of the same text listed as active. Writing "E57 per ASTM E2807" in a scope stays correct without naming a year.

title: Scan-to-CAD Modelling Levels: What Each LOD Step Costs in Hours
description: Scan-to-CAD levels compared: LOD 200 to intelligent piping, the relative modelling hours behind each, and how to tell when a drawing set was the real need.
h1: How much of the point cloud actually needs to become a model?
answer: Modelling level drives as-built cost more than scanning does. Two scales apply: BIMForum LOD describes how much detail is modelled, USIBD LOA describes how accurately it matches reality. Effort roughly triples from generic solids to spec-driven intelligent piping. Buy intelligent objects only where something downstream reads the attributes; otherwise a dimensioned drawing set delivers the same answer.
expansion: Two published scales govern the answer and they are not interchangeable. The BIMForum Level of Development Specification — current edition 2025, which added an optional LOD 250 between approximate and accurate geometry — describes how much of an element is modelled and how far it can be relied on. The USIBD Level of Accuracy Specification, document C120 version 3.0, describes how close the result sits to the real steel, in five bands running from coarser than 5 cm at LOA10 to finer than 1 mm at LOA50, stated at 95% confidence. LOD without LOA buys detail without tolerance. Effort scales with element and connection count, so a congested process area costs multiples of an open one at the same level, and small-bore pipe dominates the hours. The decision that saves the most money is the earliest one: identify who opens the file and in what software, then buy only the level that consumer can read. [Deliverable formats](/3d-scanning/point-cloud-to-cad-deliverables) follow from that.
source: BIMForum Level of Development (LOD) Specification, 2025 edition (LOD 100-500, LOD 350 for trade coordination, optional LOD 250 introduced 2025, organised by CSI UniFormat). AIA E201-2022, which succeeded AIA G202-2013 as the contractual LOD reference. USIBD Level of Accuracy (LOA) Specification, document C120, version 3.0 (2019), five bands at 95% confidence, tolerance ranges derived from DIN 18710, distinguishing measured from represented accuracy. Effort ratios are planning figures for congested process areas, expressed relative to an LOD 200 baseline and intended to be calibrated on a pilot bay. Verified August 2026.

table.note: Effort figures are planning ratios against an LOD 200 baseline for congested process areas, dominated by element and connection count rather than by area or point count. Calibrate against one 15-20 m pilot bay before pricing a unit. Open areas, tank farms and racks fall well below these ratios.

facets.q: What is the difference between LOD and LOA?
facets.a: LOD is how much of the element is modelled and how far you may rely on it — BIMForum's 100 to 500 scale. LOA is how close the modelled surface sits to the real steel — USIBD's five bands at 95% confidence. A model can be highly developed and dimensionally wrong, or crude and exact. Specify both, per discipline, or you have bought detail without tolerance.

facets.q: Which LOD should I ask for in an as-built plant model?
facets.a: LOD 300 covers most operational needs: accurate geometry with real dimensions, locations and orientations fitted to the cloud. Step to LOD 350 only where tie-ins must be buildable, because that level adds supports, connections and penetrations and carries the largest hour increase on the ladder. Set the level per discipline — pipe, steel, equipment, electrical — rather than applying one level across a whole unit.

facets.q: Do I need intelligent piping objects or will a mesh do?
facets.a: A mesh wins whenever the consumer is a person looking: walkdowns, access reviews, scaffold planning, rigging studies, contractor familiarisation. Intelligent objects earn their cost only where software reads the attributes — isometric extraction, material take-off, spec-driven clash, or anchoring inspection records to components. Count the downstream consumers first, because the modelling cost is fixed and the return is entirely in reuse.

facets.q: What does LOD 500 mean for an operating plant?
facets.a: LOD 500 means field-verified as-built, which is a statement about verification rather than about geometric detail. A scope asking for "LOD 500 as-built" without naming what was verified, by whom and against what tolerance has bought a phrase. Write the requirement properly instead: LOD 300 geometry, verified against the registered point cloud, delivered with a deviation map and a stated tolerance band.

facets.q: How do I price a scan-to-CAD modelling job?
facets.a: Model one pilot cell — a single congested bay of 15 to 20 metres — at the level you think you want, and count the hours. Multiply by element density across the unit. That number prices the job more reliably than any per-square-metre rate, and it surfaces the occlusion and small-bore problems while they are still cheap to solve. Area rates hide the two things that actually drive cost.

facets.q: How accurate is a model built from a laser scan?
facets.a: Two numbers govern it, and they fail independently. Measured accuracy is how close the registered cloud sits to the real object, evidenced by the registration report's residuals. Represented accuracy is how close the model sits to that cloud, evidenced by a deviation analysis. A 4 mm registration feeding a model fitted by eye produces errors nobody can trace. Ask for both numbers in writing.

sections.heading: Two scales, one decision
paragraphs: Two published scales govern an as-built model and they answer different questions. The BIMForum Level of Development Specification says how much of the element is modelled and how far you may rely on it — LOD 100 through 500, with LOD 350 added for trade coordination and an optional LOD 250 introduced in the 2025 edition to close the gap between approximate and accurate geometry. The USIBD Level of Accuracy Specification says how close the modelled surface sits to the real steel. A model can be highly developed and inaccurate, or crude and dimensionally exact.

Buyers ask for LOD 300 and assume they have specified accuracy. They have not. LOD 300 means accurate geometry with size, shape, location and orientation modelled, and it says nothing about the tolerance those dimensions were held to. That is a separate clause, and USIBD C120 exists to write it. Two contractors can both deliver a defensible LOD 300 model of the same pipe rack with a centimetre of difference between them, and both are right against the scope you wrote.

The contractual reference for LOD moved from AIA G202-2013 to AIA E201-2022, and legacy documents still cite the older form. For an operating plant neither AIA form is the point — the BIMForum specification's organisation by CSI UniFormat is what makes it usable, because it lets you set a different level for pipe, for structural steel, for equipment and for electrical inside one scope. Set them separately. Nothing forces one level across a whole unit, and applying one everywhere is the fastest route to overpaying.

sections.heading: The LOD ladder read for an operating plant
paragraphs: LOD 100 is a placeholder, a symbol standing in for something whose real size is unknown. It has almost no place in an as-built scope, because the survey already knows the size. LOD 200 is generic geometry at approximate quantity, size, shape and location: pipe as centrelines at nominal diameter, equipment as blocks with correct envelopes, steel as generic members. For a rig study, an access review or a rough clash check, LOD 200 answers the question completely and costs less modelling time than anything above a mesh.

LOD 300 is where most useful as-built work sits: accurate geometry, real dimensions, real locations, fitted against the cloud rather than transcribed from the P&ID. LOD 350 adds the interfaces — supports, connections, penetrations, the things that make a tie-in buildable and that the fabricator has to hit. The step from 300 to 350 is where a modelling team stops drawing pipe and starts drawing everything the pipe touches, which is why the hour count moves more between those two levels than anywhere else on the ladder.

LOD 400 is fabrication-level and belongs to the fabricator, not to the as-built survey. LOD 500 is the level that gets misused: it means field-verified as-built, a statement about verification rather than about detail. A scope asking for "LOD 500 as-built" without saying what was verified, by whom, against what tolerance, has bought a phrase. Write it properly instead — LOD 300 geometry, verified against the registered cloud, reported with a deviation map and a stated tolerance.

sections.heading: Accuracy is a separate purchase
paragraphs: The USIBD Level of Accuracy Specification, document C120, defines five bands at 95% confidence. LOA10 is coarser than 5 cm. LOA20 spans 5 cm to 15 mm. LOA30 spans 15 mm to 5 mm. LOA40 spans 5 mm to 1 mm. LOA50 is finer than 1 mm. The bands were drawn from the tolerance ranges in DIN 18710, and the version to cite is 3.0, published in 2019. Each band is an achievable procurement target rather than a marketing claim, which is exactly why it belongs in the scope.

The specification separates measured accuracy — how close the survey sits to the real object — from represented accuracy, how close the model sits to the survey. Those are two different failures. A registration with 4 mm residuals feeding a model built by eye against a coarse cloud produces a 30 mm error nobody can trace to either cause. Ask for both numbers. The registration report gives you the first, a deviation analysis of the finished model against the cloud gives you the second, and that analysis is a short automated output almost nobody requests.

Set the band by consequence rather than by ambition. A tie-in flange face that a prefabricated spool must land on needs LOA30 or better plus a field-verified check before fabrication release. A rack elevation used for access planning is satisfied at LOA20. Equipment envelopes for a layout study are satisfied at LOA10. Applying LOA30 across an entire unit because one flange needed it is the accuracy version of the same overspend that a proper [deliverables specification](/3d-scanning/point-cloud-to-cad-deliverables) exists to prevent.

sections.heading: Where the modelling hours actually go
paragraphs: Modelling effort tracks element count and connection count, not floor area and not point count. Ten thousand square metres of open tank farm models in a fraction of the time of one congested compressor house, because the hours are spent identifying, fitting and connecting discrete objects. Small-bore pipe is the dominant cost in every process unit: it is numerous, it is poorly captured because it hides behind larger pipe and structure, and it demands the same object-by-object attention as a 24-inch header while carrying a fraction of the value.

The second driver is occlusion. A point cloud holds only what the scanner saw, and a modeller working a shadowed region either interpolates, flags it, or asks for a return visit. Interpolation is fast and silently wrong. Flagging is honest and generates a punch list. The return visit is the only complete answer and it costs a mobilisation. Deciding that policy up front — flag and schedule, never interpolate — changes the quoted hours and changes what the finished model can be relied on for.

The third driver is attribute population. Geometry is a one-time fit; attributes are data entry against a source of truth. Line numbers, service, specification, insulation, material and inspection references have to come from a register that is itself correct, and reconciling a piping line list against what the scan actually shows is often the largest single line in a model quote. Where that register already lives in an [asset system](/erp), the reconciliation is worth doing once and keeping.

sections.heading: When intelligent piping objects pay for themselves
paragraphs: An intelligent piping object knows it is a 6-inch, 150-pound, carbon steel elbow in a named line, and it inherits from a specification. That knowledge earns money in four places: automatic isometric extraction, material take-off, spec-driven clash and interference checking, and attribute anchoring for anything downstream that reads the model. If the project pulls isometrics or an MTO from the model, intelligent objects pay for themselves on the first package, because the alternative is a draughtsman producing the same isometrics by hand.

The fourth use is the one that compounds. When corrosion and inspection records hang off the geometry, they hang off objects with identity — this spool, this line, this component — and that identity is what makes [inspection data on a twin](/digital-twins/inspection-data-on-a-twin-what-it-changes) navigable rather than decorative. A dumb surface can display a heat map. It cannot answer "show me every 6-inch line in this service with less than five years of remaining life", because it does not know what any of its triangles are.

Reuse across studies is the multiplier. A spec-driven model that feeds a stress package, a [fitness-for-service assessment](/consulting/fitness-for-service-api-579) and an [RBI programme](/consulting/rbi-program-design) is paid for three times against one modelling cost. A model built for one revamp and archived is paid for once. Count the downstream consumers before you buy intelligence, because the cost is fixed at the front and the return is entirely a function of how many times the model gets opened again.

sections.heading: When a dumb surface or a drawing set is the right answer
paragraphs: A mesh or dumb surface wins whenever the requirement is visual and spatial: virtual walkdowns, access and egress reviews, scaffold planning, crane and rigging studies, laydown and route checks, contractor familiarisation before a shutdown. It builds fast, opens on modest hardware, and it carries no attributes that can become wrong. A large share of the value operators attribute to 3D models is delivered entirely at this level, and buying intelligence for it converts a two-week deliverable into a three-month one.

A dimensioned 2D drawing set wins whenever the answer is a set of numbers on a page: a tie-in dimension pack, a platform or foundation check, a nozzle orientation record, an equipment replacement clearance study. The consumer is a person reading a drawing, and no intelligent model improves that experience. Extracting the sections and dimensions from a cloud costs a fraction of modelling the same region, and the deliverable opens in any PDF viewer on any device for the next twenty years.

Both of these are legitimate final deliverables rather than steps towards a real model. The industry habit of describing them as low levels pushes buyers upward for reasons of vocabulary rather than requirement. What decides it is the consumer: a person looking, a person dimensioning, or a piece of software reading attributes. Only the third case requires an intelligent model, and only the third case justifies its maintenance.

sections.heading: The expensive mistake, and the four questions that catch it
paragraphs: The recurring overspend is a full intelligent piping model bought for a project whose actual requirement was a dimensioned drawing set and a walkable cloud. It happens because the scope is written from the deliverable menu rather than from the consumer, and because "as-built model" sounds like one thing. The result is a three-month modelling programme producing an asset that gets opened twice, drifts out of date at the first shutdown, and is never trusted again by the people it was bought for.

Four questions prevent it. Who opens this file, by name and role? What software do they open it in, and do they hold a licence? What decision does it inform that a dimensioned drawing cannot? And who updates it after the next management-of-change? If the fourth question has no owner, the intelligent model is a wasting asset and the money belongs in a better cloud with better registration instead — a cloud does not go stale, it only gets old.

The reverse mistake is rarer and cheaper to fix: buying a mesh when isometrics were needed, discovering it in month two, and modelling the affected region properly. Under-buying is recoverable because the cloud is still there. Over-buying is not, because the hours are spent. That asymmetry is the whole argument for staging the purchase — cloud first, model the region that earns it, and keep the [master data formats](/3d-scanning/point-cloud-file-formats-e57-las-rcp) open so the second stage stays competitively priced.

sections.heading: Writing a modelling scope that can be priced and accepted
paragraphs: Start with a pilot cell. Pick one congested bay of 15 to 20 metres, model it at the level you think you want, and count the hours. That number, multiplied out by element density across the unit, prices the job more reliably than any per-square-metre rate, and it exposes the occlusion and small-bore problems while they are still cheap. Every as-built programme that lands on budget started with a pilot; the ones that overrun started with an area rate and a hopeful assumption about congestion.

Then write the four clauses that make acceptance objective: the modelling level per discipline, the accuracy band per discipline with the USIBD citation, the occlusion policy — flag and schedule, never interpolate — and the verification deliverable, which is a deviation analysis of the model against the registered cloud with a stated tolerance and a colour map. Add the attribute schedule as a named list of fields and the register each field is sourced from, and the argument about what "complete" means disappears before it starts.

Close with ownership. Name who holds the model, in what format, and what event triggers an update. A model attached to a live [digital twin](/digital-twins) with a management-of-change gate stays true; a model in a project folder decays from the first bolt turned. If nobody will own it, buy the drawing set and keep the cloud. To scope a specific unit, [request a quote](/contact) with the pilot cell defined and the consumer named.

faq.q: Is LOD 350 worth the extra cost over LOD 300?
faq.a: It is worth it in congested brownfield areas where a prefabricated tie-in has to land first time, because LOD 350 adds the supports, connections and penetrations that decide whether a spool fits. It is not worth it across a whole unit. Specify LOD 350 for the tie-in regions and the interfaces, LOD 300 for the surrounding as-built record, and let the rest sit lower.

faq.q: Can a point cloud be converted to CAD automatically?
faq.a: Automated extraction works well on straight, well-exposed cylindrical runs and degrades sharply with occlusion, insulation, small bore and fittings — which is where the hours are. Every production workflow uses automation for the easy 60% and human fitting for the rest, plus a human check on all of it. Treat vendor claims of full automation as claims about open racks, not about compressor houses.

faq.q: What is a deviation map and why should I ask for one?
faq.a: It is a colour rendering of the finished model measured against the registered point cloud, showing where modelled geometry departs from measured reality and by how much. It takes minutes to produce and it is the only objective acceptance test for represented accuracy. Without it, you are accepting a model on the contractor's word that it was fitted carefully rather than drawn approximately.

faq.q: Who owns the as-built model after the project?
faq.a: Whoever is named in the scope, and if nobody is named the answer in practice is nobody. Name the holder, the native format, the exchange format, and the event that triggers an update — most usefully any management-of-change that touches geometry. An unowned intelligent model is worth less than a maintained drawing set, because it looks authoritative while quietly going wrong.

faq.q: How long does an as-built model take?
faq.a: The pilot cell answers it. Model one congested 15 to 20 metre bay at the target level, count the hours, and scale by element density rather than by area. Congested process areas run several times the effort of racks and tank farms at the same level, and small-bore pipe dominates. Any schedule quoted before a pilot is an estimate of an area, not of the work.

title: Inspection Data on a Digital Twin: What Actually Changes at Work
description: What changes operationally when CML history sits on the model: finding the point, seeing the pattern, handing over context, and the link nobody maintains.
h1: What changes when CML history lives on the geometry, not a spreadsheet
answer: Four things change. The inspector finds the CML on the model instead of hunting a drawing index. Corrosion appears as a spatial pattern instead of a column of numbers. An incoming contractor inherits context rather than a folder. The next campaign is planned from where the wall is thinnest. What breaks it is the maintenance of the CML-to-object link.
expansion: The change is not visual. A CML is a designated area containing one or more examination points, and both API 510 and API 570 expect it to be marked on inspection drawings so that every campaign measures the same place — because the corrosion rate arithmetic subtracts one reading from another and attributes the whole difference to metal loss. When the location moves, the arithmetic still runs and reports a rate that is really a location difference. Putting the CML on the geometry fixes that repeatability assumption directly rather than decoratively. Three further changes follow: corrosion becomes a spatial pattern with a mechanism attached instead of a column sorted by an identifier nobody assigned for physical reasons, a new contractor inherits context rather than a folder of PDFs, and campaign scope is ranked by remaining life rather than by due date. What decides whether any of it survives is maintenance of the link between CML identity and model object, and the [thickness trending](/digital-twins/thickness-trending) view is where that link proves itself.
source: API 510 and API 570 terminology for condition monitoring locations, which replaced the earlier thickness measurement location designation; a CML is a designated area containing one or more examination points, expected to be marked on inspection drawings so measurements repeat at the same location. Corrosion rate and remaining life relationships as applied under API 510 and API 570: long-term rate from initial and current thickness, short-term rate from previous and current thickness, governing rate the higher of the two, remaining life from current thickness less required thickness divided by the governing rate. No clause numbers cited; requirements described against the codes' current editions as published by API. Verified August 2026.

Navigate to the object, confirm against surrounding geometry and a site photograph

The unit ranked by remaining life and damage activity
Hours move from calendar-due points to genuinely thin points

The new component silently inherits the old thickness history
Old CML closed, new CML opened with a new baseline
Fabrication differences stop being reported as corrosion rates
table.note: None of this improves the measurement itself. Reading quality remains governed by surface preparation, couplant, probe selection, temperature compensation, calibration and technician qualification.

facets.q: What actually changes when inspection data sits on a 3D model?
facets.a: Four things. Locating a CML becomes navigation instead of counting welds off an isometric. Corrosion becomes a spatial pattern with a mechanism attached instead of a sorted column. A new contractor inherits context on day one instead of learning the unit over two campaigns. And campaign scope gets ranked by remaining life rather than assembled from due dates.

facets.q: Do I need a new CML numbering scheme to build a twin?
facets.a: No, and creating one is the fastest way to fail. Use the register you already have. The build links existing CML identifiers to model objects and publishes an orphan list of the ones that do not resolve. That orphan list is the first real deliverable, because it measures the quality of the inspection data you actually hold rather than the data you assume you hold.

facets.q: What breaks a digital twin of an inspection programme?
facets.a: The link between CML identity and model object, in four reliable ways. A database migration renumbers CMLs while the model keeps the old identifiers. A replaced spool inherits the old thickness history. A management-of-change alters the plant and the geometry is not updated. Readings arrive with identifiers matching nothing and accumulate in an orphan pile with no owner and no deadline.

facets.q: Does a digital twin replace my inspection data management system?
facets.a: No, and it should not try. The IDMS or ERP module stays the system of record for CML identity, readings, calculations and intervals. The twin is the spatial index onto that record. One system owns identity and everything else references it — that separation is what keeps the twin honest when the register is migrated, extended or audited.

facets.q: Can a twin be built from a point cloud we already have?
facets.a: Yes, if the existing survey preserved per-setup structure and is readable outside the contractor's software. That is a file format question rather than a scanning one, and it is settled by checking whether an open master exists alongside the indexed working copy. Where the old cloud is per-setup and undecimated, no re-survey is needed to start on one unit.

facets.q: Does this help with an API 570 or API 510 audit?
facets.a: It shortens the answer. When an auditor asks why an interval was extended or why a CML was retired, the evidence is the geometry, the readings on it, the dates, the instruments and the qualifications of the people who took them — assembled once rather than reconstructed under time pressure. The codes and the calculations are unchanged; the retrieval time collapses.

sections.heading: A CML is a location before it is a number
paragraphs: API 510 and API 570 replaced the older thickness measurement location designation with the condition monitoring location. A CML is a designated area on the equipment where periodic examinations are performed to assess and monitor condition, and it contains one or more examination points — commonly a marked circle a few inches across on the surface. The codes expect CMLs to be marked on inspection drawings so that the same place is measured every campaign, because the entire corrosion rate calculation rests on repeatability of location.

That assumption is where spreadsheet-based programmes fail quietly. The formulas are unforgiving about it. The long-term rate is the initial thickness minus the current thickness divided by the years between them. The short-term rate is the previous thickness minus the current thickness divided by the years between those. The governing rate is the higher of the two. Remaining life is the current thickness minus the required thickness divided by that rate. Every term in both formulas assumes the two readings came from the same square inch of steel.

When a technician measures 40 mm from the weld instead of 200 mm because the drawing was ambiguous, the arithmetic still runs. It produces a corrosion rate that is a location difference wearing the costume of a metal loss trend, and nothing in the spreadsheet flags it. Attaching the CML to geometry is not a visualisation upgrade. It is a fix for the repeatability assumption that the codes require and that paper isometrics enforce weakly.

sections.heading: Change one: finding the CML
paragraphs: The current workflow is a drawing index. The inspector opens the register, reads a CML identifier, finds the isometric that identifier belongs to, locates the balloon on the isometric, walks to the line, counts welds or elbows from a reference point, and marks up. In a congested unit with parallel lines in the same service, that last step is the one that goes wrong, and it goes wrong most often with a contractor crew who did not set the CMLs originally and never met the person who did.

On a twin the CML is an object in space. The inspector navigates to it, sees it in context against the surrounding geometry — which elbow, which side, how far from which flange — and confirms the position visually before climbing. On a tablet at the job site that comparison takes seconds against a photograph of the actual pipe. The number of readings taken at the wrong location falls because the ambiguity that produced them is gone, not because anybody tried harder or was told to be careful.

The knock-on effect is in scaffolding and access. When the CMLs for a campaign can be selected spatially, the access plan is built from where the points are rather than from a list of line numbers, and points sharing a scaffold get grouped into one visit. That is a scheduling gain which lands in the shutdown budget rather than the inspection budget, which is why it is usually the number that justifies the programme to the people who approve it.

sections.heading: Change two: corrosion as a pattern, not a column
paragraphs: A thickness register is a column of numbers sorted by CML identifier, and identifiers are assigned in the order somebody walked the line. The sort order carries no physical meaning, so a pattern distributed in space is invisible in the table. Four readings thinning faster than their neighbours look like scatter in a column. Plotted on the geometry, the same four readings sit on the extrados of consecutive elbows, or at the six o'clock position along one run, or immediately downstream of an injection point.

Those three patterns are three different damage mechanisms with three different responses. Extrados thinning through elbows is erosion-corrosion driven by velocity and geometry. Six o'clock thinning along a run is under-deposit or wet-phase attack. A thinning band downstream of an injection point is exactly where API guidance says to concentrate monitoring. Each one changes where the next campaign looks and what the engineer does about it, and none of them is legible in a list sorted by an identifier.

The corollary is that spatial display exposes gaps as clearly as it exposes damage. A heat map with a dark region is not always good news — it is often a region with no CMLs at all, and a table sorted by identifier never shows an absence. Programmes that move onto a twin routinely find whole branches, dead legs and small-bore connections with no monitoring at all, which is a finding worth more than the visualisation that produced it. The [thickness trending](/digital-twins/thickness-trending) view is where that reads clearest.

sections.heading: Change three: handover context instead of a folder
paragraphs: Inspection contracts change hands, and today the handover is a folder — a data dump of PDF reports, a thickness spreadsheet, a set of isometrics of uncertain vintage, and the tacit knowledge of the outgoing inspector, which does not transfer at all. The incoming crew rebuilds an understanding of the unit over one or two campaigns, and the first of those campaigns is measurably worse: more repeat visits, more located-the-wrong-point corrections, more questions escalated to the owner's engineer at the worst moment.

When the history lives on the geometry, the handover is an access grant. The incoming inspector opens the unit, selects a line, and sees every reading ever taken on it — when, by whom, with what instrument, against which report — in place and in context. What previously took two campaigns to learn is available on the first morning. The value is largest exactly where turnover is highest, which is contract inspection, and it is the argument that gets the programme funded in organisations that outsource inspection entirely.

The same structure serves an audit. When a regulator or a client asks why an interval was extended, the answer is the geometry with the data on it, the readings that supported the decision, and the qualifications of the people who took them. That is the same evidence chain that makes [an NDT report defensible](/report-validation/what-makes-an-ndt-report-defensible), assembled once and kept, rather than reconstructed from four systems under time pressure while an auditor waits.

sections.heading: Change four: planning from the thin end
paragraphs: Campaign scope is normally built from intervals — this vessel is due, that circuit is due — and the resulting work list is a calendar artefact. Remaining life is calculated per CML and sits in the register, so the unit's thinnest points are already known and scattered across it. Rendered on the geometry, the same data ranks the unit by where the wall is actually thinnest, and the campaign is built from the top of that list downward until the budget runs out.

That reordering changes what gets inspected. Points with decades of remaining life stop consuming inspection hours on a calendar cadence, and points approaching their limit get earlier and denser coverage. It is the input side of a risk-based programme, and a spatially resolved thickness picture is the most credible corrosion-likelihood evidence an [RBI programme](/consulting/rbi-program-design) can be built from — considerably better than a generic circuit corrosion rate applied uniformly to everything in the same service.

It also changes what a finding triggers. When a reading drops below the required thickness, the surrounding CMLs are immediately visible as neighbours rather than as identifiers to look up, so the extent of the affected region is scoped in minutes instead of an afternoon. If a [fitness-for-service assessment](/consulting/fitness-for-service-api-579) follows, the assessor starts with the geometry and the local thickness field already assembled, rather than reconstructing both from a spreadsheet and an isometric of unclear vintage.

sections.heading: The maintenance burden that makes or breaks it
paragraphs: Everything above depends on one link staying true: the CML identifier in the inspection database pointing at the correct object in the model. That link has no natural custodian and four reliable ways to break. A database migration renumbers CMLs while the model keeps the old identifiers. A spool is replaced and the new component inherits the old thickness history, manufacturing a corrosion rate out of a fabrication difference. A management-of-change modifies the plant and the geometry is never updated. Readings arrive with identifiers matching nothing and land in an orphan pile.

The governance that holds it together is small and boring. One system owns CML identity and everything else references it — the [inspection data management side of the ERP](/erp) is the natural home, because that is where the register already lives and where the calculations already run. Any management-of-change that touches geometry raises a model update task in the same workflow that raises the drawing update. An orphan report runs after every campaign with a named owner and a deadline. Component replacement closes the old CML and opens a new one with a new baseline.

Programmes that skip this get eighteen good months and then a twin nobody trusts, which is worse than the spreadsheet because it looks authoritative. The failure is never dramatic. Someone notices a spool on the model that was cut out last turnaround, and from that day the whole model is treated as indicative. Budget the maintenance as an operating line with a named owner before the twin is built, not as a project closeout task assigned to whoever is left.

sections.heading: What it does not change
paragraphs: A twin does not make a reading correct. A UT thickness reading placed perfectly on a model is still governed by surface preparation, couplant, probe selection, temperature compensation, calibration against a block of the right material and velocity, and the qualification of the technician who took it. Placing a wrong number accurately produces a confidently wrong corrosion rate, and the spatial display makes it more persuasive rather than less. The measurement quality problem sits upstream and it stays upstream.

That is why the data-quality layer belongs alongside the twin rather than after it. Reading-level validation catches what a spreadsheet accepts silently: instrument calibration in date, technique sheet followed, technician certified to the method and level, values inside physically plausible bounds against the previous reading at the same point. Independent report review and [Level III oversight](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) do the same job for the reports those readings arrive in, before the numbers reach a trend line.

It also does not change the code. Intervals, required thickness calculations, corrosion rate selection and remaining life all run exactly as they did, on the same formulas, subject to the same engineering judgement and the same authorised inspector. What the twin changes is how quickly the right data reaches the person applying them, and how confident everyone is that the readings came from where the record says they did.

sections.heading: A rollout that survives the first turnaround
paragraphs: Start with one unit and the CML register you already have. No re-survey, no new numbering scheme, no attempt to model the whole site. The geometry can come from an existing scan, and whether that scan is reusable is settled on the [point cloud formats page](/3d-scanning/point-cloud-file-formats-e57-las-rcp) rather than by asking the original contractor. Load the existing register, link what links, and publish the orphan list. The orphan list is the first deliverable and the first honest measure of the inspection data you actually hold.

Prove it in one turnaround. Run the campaign with the twin alongside the existing process rather than replacing it, and count three things: readings taken at a location the inspector had to query, scaffold visits that served more than one CML, and hours spent by the incoming crew locating points. Those three numbers are the business case, and all three are measurable inside a single outage rather than inferred from a vendor's benefits slide.

Then extend by service severity rather than by unit boundary. The circuits with the shortest remaining life and the most active damage mechanisms earn the geometry first; the tank farm waits. Atlantis builds this on the [Digital Twins platform](/digital-twins) against your existing inspection register — affordable, accessible, and fully customisable to the data you already keep. [Request a demo](/contact) with one unit's register and one existing scan, and the orphan list comes back before anything is committed.

faq.q: Is a digital twin the same as a 3D model?
faq.a: No. A 3D model is geometry. A twin is geometry with live operational data bound to it and a process that keeps the binding true. The difference is entirely in the maintenance: a model is delivered once and decays, a twin has an owner, a management-of-change trigger and an orphan report. A model with a heat map painted on it once is a screenshot with ambitions.

faq.q: How long does it take to link an existing CML register to a model?
faq.a: The pacing item is register quality, not software. Identifiers that resolve cleanly link in bulk. What takes the time is the orphan set — CMLs whose location description is ambiguous, whose line no longer exists, or whose component was replaced without closing the record. Publishing that orphan list early turns an open-ended data cleanup into a bounded, countable task with a named owner.

faq.q: What happens to the twin when a spool is replaced?
faq.a: The old CML closes and a new CML opens on the new component with a new baseline thickness. Letting the new spool inherit the old history is the single most damaging data error in thickness trending, because it subtracts a new wall from an old one and reports the fabrication difference as corrosion. Make component replacement a mandatory step in the management-of-change workflow.

faq.q: Do inspectors need CAD skills to use it?
faq.a: No. The field interface is navigation and selection on a tablet — find the point, confirm it against the surrounding geometry and a photograph, enter the reading. The CAD skills sit with whoever maintains the geometry after a management-of-change, which is a different person on a different cadence. If the field tool requires CAD competence, the tool is wrong for the job.

faq.q: Can it hold RT, PT, MT and PAUT results, not just thickness?
faq.a: Yes, and the spatial argument is stronger for them. A weld map with radiographic and penetrant results attached to specific joints shows repair concentrations by fabricator, position and procedure — patterns that a report index cannot surface. Phased array C-scans anchored to a component carry their scan extent with them, so the next campaign knows exactly which area was covered and which was not.

title: Crew Dispatch Software That Checks NDT Certification First
description: Dispatching an NDT crew is a certification problem before a calendar problem. The eight constraints US inspection firms hit, and why field-service tools miss them.
h1: Which certified technician can legally take this job today?
answer: Dispatching an NDT technician is a qualification check before it is a calendar check. The scheduler must confirm the method certification is current for the level and method the scope calls for, that the assigned instrument is in calibration, and that site access credentials are valid. Generic field-service software tracks people and trucks, not certification matrices, so it books jobs the technician cannot sign.
expansion: The constraint set is larger than most schedulers hold in their head. A five-day refinery outage crew needs current UT and PT certification at Level II, a Level III on call to approve the technique, a calibrated thickness gauge, TWIC cards that have not lapsed, site-specific safety orientation, and enough remaining hours in the week that nobody hits an overtime cliff on day four. Miss any one and the crew arrives and cannot start. What makes this different from plumbing dispatch is that the qualification is per-method and per-level, it expires, and the client's inspector is required to verify it. API 510, Eleventh Edition, October 2022, clause 4.5.3 puts the duty on the examiner's employer to hold certification records and make them available to the inspector. Scheduling that reads the same certification matrix the auditor reads stops the failure before the truck leaves.
source: Verified August 2026 against: API 510, Pressure Vessel Inspection Code, Eleventh Edition, October 2022, clause 4.5.3 (the examiner's employer shall maintain certification records of examiners employed, including dates and results of personnel qualifications, and make them available to the inspector). 10 CFR 34.25(b)(1) (radiation survey instruments calibrated at intervals not to exceed 6 months and after servicing other than battery changes); 10 CFR 34.43(a) (radiographers certified through a certifying entity meeting Part 34 Appendix A criteria); 10 CFR 34.43(d) (refresher safety training at intervals not to exceed 12 months); 10 CFR 34.43(e) (observation of job performance during actual radiographic operations at intervals not to exceed 6 months). 49 CFR 395.3 (property-carrying driver: 11 driving hours within a 14-hour window after 10 consecutive hours off duty; 30-minute interruption before more than 8 cumulative driving hours; 60/7 and 70/8 limits with 34-hour restart) and the FMCSA short-haul exception (150 air-mile radius, same reporting location, 14-hour duty period, relief from RODS and ELD). ASNT published guidance on Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A (2024 edition): all NDT personnel shall be recertified periodically, recommended maximum interval five years. GSA FY2026 CONUS standard per diem: $110 lodging plus $68 meals and incidental expenses, effective 1 October 2025 through 30 September 2026. California Department of Industrial Relations overtime rules. TSA TWIC programme: five-year card validity, enrolment lead time guidance. Third-party fees and rates are cited as published by those bodies and are not Atlantis rates.
