Employer Written Practices and Agreement State rules are frequently stricter than the federal floor — dispatch against yours, not against the minimum.

facets.q: Why does generic field-service software fail on NDT scheduling?
facets.a: Field-service platforms model qualification as a permanent skills tag. NDT certification is granted per method at a specific level under an employer's Written Practice, it expires, an annual vision examination can suspend it, and a client's inspector is entitled to audit it for the date the work was performed. A checkbox stores none of that, so the software confidently books assignments the technician cannot legally sign.

facets.q: What does a certification matrix need to contain to drive dispatch?
facets.a: Person by method by level, with the certification date, the expiry date, the Written Practice or standard it was issued under, the examination records behind it, and the annual near-vision examination date held separately. Equipment needs the same treatment: instrument identity, calibration certificate, calibration expiry. Dispatch queries both against the job date rather than against today, so a booking three weeks out is validated against the state it will be in.

facets.q: How does equipment calibration status change the schedule?
facets.a: It makes equipment a qualified resource rather than inventory. For industrial radiography, 10 CFR 34.25(b)(1) requires radiation survey instruments to be calibrated at intervals not to exceed six months and after servicing other than battery changes. When that certificate lapses the crew is grounded even though every technician is current. Reading calibration expiry against the forward schedule surfaces the block weeks before the job rather than at the gate.

facets.q: Do NDT technicians fall under DOT hours-of-service rules?
facets.a: They do when the crew operates a commercial motor vehicle, which includes radiography trucks carrying placarded radioactive material. 49 CFR 395.3 allows eleven driving hours inside a fourteen-hour window that begins after ten consecutive hours off duty, with a thirty-minute interruption before more than eight cumulative driving hours. The short-haul exception covers work inside a 150 air-mile radius returning to the same reporting location within fourteen hours.

facets.q: What happens when a certification expires in the middle of a job?
facets.a: Work performed after the expiry date is work performed by an uncertified examiner, and it is the client's inspector who finds it — during review, or during an audit months later. The schedule must validate certification against every day of a multi-week assignment, not against the start date alone. Long turnarounds are where this failure concentrates, because the crew was current on day one.

facets.q: How do travel and per diem affect which technician you send?
facets.a: Two equally qualified technicians can differ by thousands of dollars over a five-day job once travel, lodging and subsistence are counted. GSA's FY2026 standard CONUS rate is $110 lodging plus $68 for meals and incidental expenses per day, effective 1 October 2025 through 30 September 2026, with non-standard localities higher. Surfacing that difference at dispatch turns an invisible margin decision into a deliberate one.

sections.heading: Dispatch is a qualification decision that happens to have a date on it
paragraphs: The scheduler's question is never "who is free Tuesday". It is "who is free Tuesday, holds current certification in the method and level this scope calls for, has an instrument that is in calibration, can get through the gate, and will not run out of legal hours on the drive home". Every one of those is a hard constraint. A calendar answers the first and none of the rest, which is why a schedule built on availability alone produces crews that arrive and cannot start work.

The cost of getting it wrong is not a rescheduling fee. It is a mobilised crew, a day of per diem, a client whose outage window just moved, and — where the technician performed work they were not certified for — a report the client's inspector will reject on review. Rework of that kind is diagnosed months later as a quality problem, which is why the scheduling defect that caused it is rarely traced back and rarely fixed.

The fix is structural. The certification data that the client's inspector audits and the availability data the dispatcher uses have to be the same record. When they are two systems — a spreadsheet of expiry dates beside a scheduling calendar — the spreadsheet is always the one that is out of date. [Certification tracking](/erp/ndt-personnel-certification-tracking) that feeds dispatch directly removes the reconciliation step where the error lives.

sections.heading: Certification currency is per method, per level, and it expires
paragraphs: An NDT technician is not certified as a technician. They are certified in UT at Level II, in PT at Level II, in MT at Level I, and possibly not at all in RT. Assigning them to a scope that calls for a method outside that set is not a stretch assignment, it is an unqualified examination. The certification record therefore has to be a matrix — person by method by level — rather than a single expiry date sitting on a personnel file.

Under [ASNT Recommended Practice No. SNT-TC-1A](/compliance/asnt-snt-tc-1a) the employer's Written Practice sets the qualification and recertification requirements, and ASNT's published guidance states that all NDT personnel shall be recertified periodically, with a recommended maximum interval of five years. Near-vision acuity is examined annually and recorded. That gives every technician two independent clocks — one long, one annual — and either of them can ground the person on a day the schedule says they are available.

Level constrains what the technician may do, not only which method they may touch. A Level I performs specified calibrations and examinations and records results under the direction of higher-level personnel; interpretation and evaluation sit with Level II and above. A schedule that treats levels as interchangeable seniority produces reports signed at the wrong level. The [scope limits that attach to a Level III](/consulting/level-iii-method-scope-limitations) matter for the same reason, because approving a technique in a method the Level III is not certified in is the identical defect one tier up.

sections.heading: The instrument carries its own certificate, and it travels with the crew
paragraphs: Equipment availability is two constraints wearing one label. The first is physical: there are four thickness gauges and three crews. The second is documentary: the gauge assigned to Tuesday's job has a calibration certificate with an expiry date, and an examination performed on an out-of-calibration instrument is invalid regardless of who held the probe. Scheduling that models only the physical constraint will happily assign a gauge whose certificate lapsed in March.

Radiography makes the documentary constraint explicit in federal regulation. 10 CFR 34.25(b)(1) requires radiation survey instruments to be calibrated at intervals not to exceed six months and after instrument servicing other than battery changes. That is a hard six-month clock attached to a physical object which moves between crews and trucks. If the survey meter's calibration is the binding constraint on Thursday, no amount of technician availability unblocks the job.

The design consequence is that equipment needs the same treatment as people: an identity, a qualification state, an expiry date, and a booking. Firms that keep calibration in a maintenance log and bookings in a calendar rediscover the conflict at the gate. Firms that hold both in one record see the calibration expiry as a scheduling block three weeks out, while there is still time to send the instrument away and get it back before the job.

sections.heading: Site access is a separate credential with its own lead time
paragraphs: Getting to the work is its own qualification stack. MTSA-regulated marine and port facilities require a Transportation Worker Identification Credential, valid for five years, and TSA advises enrolling — renewals included — well ahead of the date you need the card, because processing runs long. Refineries and chemical plants add site-specific orientation, contractor safety programmes, background checks, drug and alcohol testing windows, and a badge that frequently expires on a different cycle from everything else.

None of these appear on a certification matrix, and none of them are optional. A UT Level II with impeccable certification and a lapsed TWIC is unschedulable at a marine terminal. Because the lead times differ so widely — a same-week drug screen against a multi-week credential — the scheduling system has to distinguish constraints it can clear inside the booking window from constraints it cannot, and escalate the second category much earlier.

Where the client operates under OSHA's process safety management standard, your inspection work sits inside the client's [mechanical integrity programme](/consulting/osha-psm-mechanical-integrity-ndt) and their contractor requirements attach to your crew. That relationship is worth modelling explicitly in the schedule, because access refusals at PSM-covered sites are rarely arbitrary — they trace to a document the contractor was supposed to have on file and did not.

sections.heading: Hours, overtime and driving rules cap the day before your calendar does
paragraphs: Two separate legal clocks run on a field day. Wage and hour rules set what the day costs: the federal Fair Labor Standards Act pays overtime past forty hours in a workweek, and California requires one and one-half times the regular rate for hours past eight in a workday up to twelve, double time past twelve, time and a half for the first eight hours on the seventh consecutive day and double time beyond that. A schedule that ignores the daily rule builds ten-hour days that cost more than the quote assumed.

The second clock is the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration's hours of service, which binds when the crew operates a commercial motor vehicle — including radiography trucks carrying placarded sources. Under 49 CFR 395.3 a property-carrying driver may drive eleven hours within a fourteen-hour window that starts after ten consecutive hours off duty, with a thirty-minute interruption in driving required before more than eight cumulative driving hours, inside a sixty-hour seven-day or seventy-hour eight-day limit.

The short-haul exception reshapes regional work specifically. A driver operating within a 150 air-mile radius who starts and ends the duty period at the same reporting location, inside fourteen hours, is relieved of records of duty status and the electronic logging device requirement. That radius is a scheduling boundary with a real cost step on the far side of it, and it belongs in the dispatch model rather than in a driver's memory.

sections.heading: Why generic field-service management software breaks here
paragraphs: Field-service platforms are built around a skills tag: mark the technician "HVAC" and route HVAC tickets to them. The tag is descriptive and permanent. NDT certification is neither. It is granted per method at a specific level, it is granted by an employer under a Written Practice, it expires, it can be suspended by a failed vision examination, and a third party is entitled to audit it. Modelling that as a checkbox discards every property that makes it a constraint.

The second failure is the equipment model. Field-service tools treat equipment as inventory a technician carries. NDT equipment is a qualified instrument with a certificate, a calibration due date, and in radiography a set of licence conditions attached to it. Inventory logic assigns the nearest gauge; qualification logic has to assign the nearest in-calibration gauge, and refuse the booking outright when there is none available for the job dates.

The third failure is documentary. When the client's inspector asks who performed the examination and whether they were qualified, the answer must be reconstructable for the date of the work, not for today. API 510, Eleventh Edition, October 2022, clause 4.5.3 requires the examiner's employer to maintain certification records of examiners employed, including dates and results of personnel qualifications, and to make those records available to the inspector. Field-service systems store current state. This requires history.

sections.heading: What changes when the scheduler reads the certification matrix
paragraphs: The first change is that unqualified assignments become impossible rather than discouraged. If a scope line calls for UT Level II and PT Level II, only technicians holding both and current on the job date appear as candidates. The dispatcher stops carrying the matrix in their head, which matters most at the moment it always fails — a Friday afternoon callout with the usual crew unavailable and a client waiting on the phone.

The second is that expiries become forward-looking rather than retrospective. Certifications, vision examinations, calibration certificates, site badges and refresher training all have dates. Read against the forward schedule instead of against today, they surface as a list of bookings that will break, with enough lead time to book the recertification or send the instrument out. A recurring emergency becomes a maintenance task with a queue.

The third is that the schedule itself becomes evidence. Every dispatch decision carries the qualification state that justified it at the time it was made. When a report is challenged eighteen months later, the question "was this technician certified in this method on this date" is answered from the record rather than from a drawer of scanned certificates. That is the same evidence chain a programme audit asks for, assembled as a by-product of scheduling.

sections.heading: Travel, per diem and the cost of the crew you chose
paragraphs: Two qualified technicians are rarely equal in cost. One lives ninety minutes from the site and drives home; the other flies in and draws per diem for five nights. GSA's FY2026 standard CONUS rate — $110 lodging plus $68 for meals and incidental expenses, effective 1 October 2025 through 30 September 2026 — is the published reference most US contractors anchor travel policy to, and non-standard localities are set higher, with Gulf Coast outage season higher again in practice.

Because that cost difference never appears on the schedule, dispatchers optimise for availability and the margin difference emerges a month later on the accounts. Scheduling that surfaces the cost consequence of each candidate — drive time, per diem nights, mileage — lets the dispatcher make the trade deliberately instead of accidentally. The downstream half of the same problem is worked through on [inspection job costing](/erp/inspection-job-costing-profitability).

Recording travel and per diem against the job at the point of dispatch, rather than reconstructing it from expense claims three weeks afterwards, also removes the reconciliation work that makes accurate job costing feel expensive. The same entry that books the technician books the nights. [Timesheet capture](/erp/timesheet-software-for-ndt-companies) closes the loop on the hours side, so the job record is complete when the crew demobilises.

sections.heading: When nobody qualifies: subcontracting, and the record you still owe
paragraphs: Some weeks the matrix returns nothing. The scope calls for phased array at Level II, both certified technicians are committed, and the client's window does not move. Subcontracting is the answer, and it is where certification discipline most often collapses, because the subcontractor's technician is not in your personnel system. The obligation does not move with the work. If the report goes out on your letterhead, the qualification evidence is yours to hold and yours to produce.

Treat subcontracted technicians as scheduled resources with certification records attached, collected before dispatch rather than at invoice time. That means the sub's Written Practice, the technician's method certifications with dates, and the calibration certificate for whatever instrument they bring to site. It is the same evidence set your own crew carries, and the client's inspector applies exactly the same test to both.

Firms that cannot staff a method repeatedly have a capability decision to make rather than a scheduling one. Building it in house runs through [ASNT method training](/training) and, for technique approval and Written Practice ownership, through [outsourced Level III support](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services). Either route beats the third option, which is declining work you were otherwise qualified to win. Atlantis builds the scheduling and certification model on Odoo — affordable, accessible, fully customisable. Demo or quote on request.

faq.q: Can I dispatch a Level I technician if a Level II reviews the report afterwards?
faq.a: Level I personnel perform specified calibrations and examinations and record results under the direction of higher-level personnel; interpretation and evaluation of results sit with Level II and above. A Level II reviewing afterwards does not convert a Level I's independent interpretation into a qualified one. Scope the assignment so the interpreting work is performed by someone certified to interpret it, and let the schedule enforce that split.

faq.q: How far ahead should certification and calibration expiry warnings fire?
faq.a: Far enough to complete the remedy, which differs by constraint. Recertification examinations, annual vision examinations and instrument calibration each carry their own turnaround, and site credentials have the longest lead of all — TSA advises enrolling for a TWIC, renewals included, well before you need the card. Set the warning horizon per constraint type rather than using one global figure for everything.

faq.q: Does the client have a right to see my technicians' certification records?
faq.a: Under API 510, Eleventh Edition, October 2022, clause 4.5.3, the examiner's employer shall maintain certification records of the examiners employed, including dates and results of personnel qualifications, and those records shall be available to the inspector — who is responsible to the owner-operator for determining that all NDE examiners are properly qualified for the work they perform. Plan to produce them on demand.

faq.q: Does Atlantis sell API 510, 570 or 653 certification training?
faq.a: No. Atlantis delivers ASNT method training in UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET, TOFD and phased array, outsourced ASNT Level III services, NDT report validation, and the ERP that runs scheduling and certification tracking. The API individual certification programmes are administered by API, and independent prep providers price those courses separately from anything Atlantis offers.

faq.q: Can scheduling and certification tracking live in the same system?
faq.a: They should. The failure mode in every firm running them separately is identical: the certification spreadsheet drifts out of date relative to the schedule, and the discrepancy is discovered at the gate on the morning of the job. One record, read by dispatch as a constraint and by the auditor as evidence, removes the reconciliation step where the error is created.

title: Inspection Job Costing: Report Hours and Per Diem Hide Margin
description: Inspection firms lose money in two places their accounting never shows: uncosted report preparation and per-diem-heavy turnaround work. Cost a job so the leak shows.
h1: Why the job that looked profitable at 38% closed at 11%
answer: Inspection jobs lose margin in two components that rarely reach the job record: report preparation hours, which are booked as overhead rather than to the job that generated them, and per diem, which is a cost on every field day but is folded into a blended rate. Cost both to the job and the profitable clients separate from the unprofitable ones immediately.
expansion: The pattern is consistent across US inspection contractors. Revenue is captured perfectly, because it is one invoice produced by one process. Cost arrives in fragments from payroll, accounts payable, a fuel card, a subcontractor purchase order and a Level III's Tuesday evening, and only some of those fragments carry a job number. The gross margin the accounting system reports is therefore revenue minus the costs that happened to be coded — a systematically flattering number. It flatters unevenly, which is the damaging part. The two largest uncoded components, report preparation and travel-linked cost, both scale with the work that looks most attractive on a revenue report: complex multi-method scopes and out-of-town turnarounds. Firms consequently chase more of the work that is quietly losing money. Attaching every cost a job causes to that job, at the moment it is incurred, is the whole fix.
source: Third-party rates cited on this page, verified August 2026: GSA FY2026 CONUS standard per diem, $110 lodging plus $68 meals and incidental expenses, effective 1 October 2025 through 30 September 2026, with non-standard localities set higher (GSA per diem bulletin FTR 26-01). IRS 2026 business standard mileage rate: 72.5 cents per mile for 1 January through 30 June 2026, and 76 cents per mile for 1 July through 31 December 2026 (IRS newsroom announcements). Overtime: the federal Fair Labor Standards Act, and California Department of Industrial Relations overtime rules — one and one-half times the regular rate past eight hours in a workday up to twelve and for the first eight hours on the seventh consecutive day, double time past twelve hours in a workday and past eight hours on the seventh consecutive day. Recurring radiography qualification costs: 10 CFR 34.25(b)(1) survey instrument calibration at intervals not to exceed 6 months; 10 CFR 34.43(d) refresher safety training at intervals not to exceed 12 months; 10 CFR 34.43(e) observation of job performance at intervals not to exceed 6 months, as published on eCFR. These are published third-party and federal figures and are not Atlantis rates. Atlantis does not publish pricing.

GSA non-standard localities exceed the CONUS standard, and Gulf Coast markets during outage season exceed the federal lodging figure in practice — use your actual settlement, with the federal rate as the floor for policy.

facets.q: Why is report preparation time almost never costed to the job?
facets.a: Because the people doing it are salaried and their hours are treated as company overhead. Data reduction, drafting, technique documentation, Level III technical review, client comments, revision and re-issue all happen after the field timesheet closed. Report burden scales with scope complexity and client revision behaviour rather than with revenue, so pooling it hides the exact variation that separates profitable clients from unprofitable ones.

facets.q: How does per diem distort margin analysis on turnaround work?
facets.a: Per diem is incurred every day a technician is away, billable or not, and it is coded to a travel pool rather than to the job. Pooled, it is spread evenly across all jobs, so local work subsidises travel work and both report the wrong margin. GSA's FY2026 standard CONUS rate is $110 lodging plus $68 meals and incidentals per day; non-standard localities are higher.

facets.q: What goes into a loaded technician rate?
facets.a: Base wage plus employer payroll taxes, workers' compensation, health benefits, paid time off, PPE, vehicle, phone, and the non-billable hours the firm pays for — travel, safety orientations, training and recertification. Build it from your own twelve months of employment cost divided by billable hours actually delivered, not by 2,080 hours, because the denominator is where firms assume a utilisation rate they never achieve.

facets.q: How do you tell which clients are actually profitable?
facets.a: Attach every cost a client causes to that client's jobs: loaded field hours, premium hours, per diem nights, mileage, consumables, subcontractor invoices, coordination time and report hours including revisions. Then rank accounts by margin rather than by revenue. The common finding is that the largest account by revenue sits near the bottom by margin, because rate concessions were granted and delivery burden was never priced in.

facets.q: Why does subcontracted work hide negative margin?
facets.a: The visible arithmetic is clean — purchase order out, invoice in, markup applied. The invisible cost is coordination: scheduling the sub, collecting and filing their certification records, receiving and reviewing their report, integrating it into yours, and defending it when the client queries it. That is Level III and project management time, rarely charged to the job, and on a thin markup it exceeds the margin entirely.

facets.q: Does QuickBooks give you job-level inspection profitability?
facets.a: It gives you the financial half. QuickBooks runs the general ledger, payroll, payables and receivables, and it can carry a job or class dimension. What it never sees is the operational fact set — who was dispatched, for how long, with which instrument, drawing how many per diem nights, generating how many report hours. Job costing needs both halves, captured where each one happens.

sections.heading: Revenue is visible. Cost is not. That is the whole problem.
paragraphs: Every inspection firm knows what a job invoiced. Almost none know what it cost. The invoice is one document produced by one process. The cost is fifteen fragments produced by payroll, accounts payable, a fuel card, a purchase order to a subcontractor, and a Level III's Tuesday evening. Only some of those fragments carry a job number, so the gross margin the accounting system reports is revenue minus the costs that happened to be coded — a different number from the one the owner needs to make decisions with.

The gap is neither small nor random. It concentrates in two components, report preparation and travel-linked cost, and both of them scale with exactly the work that looks most attractive on a revenue report: complex multi-method scopes and out-of-town turnarounds. The result is a firm that pursues more of the work that is quietly losing money, because every report it runs says that work is its highest-revenue segment.

Fixing this does not require replacing the accounting system. It requires the job to become the unit of record, with every cost a job causes attaching to it at the moment it is incurred rather than being reconstructed at month end. The [inspection ERP](/erp) holds the operational half; the ledger keeps the financial half. Neither pretends to be the other, and the boundary between them is a design decision rather than an accident.

sections.heading: The loaded rate: what a field hour actually costs you
paragraphs: A technician's hourly wage is the smallest part of what an hour of their time costs. On top of it sit employer payroll taxes, workers' compensation — priced high for industrial inspection — health benefits, paid time off, PPE, vehicle, phone, and the non-billable hours the firm pays for: travel between sites, safety orientations, training and recertification. Costing a field hour at base wage understates it by a margin wide enough to turn a reported profit into a real loss on a thin job.

Build the loaded rate from your own numbers rather than a rule of thumb. Take twelve months of total employment cost for the technician group — wages, taxes, insurance, benefits, allowances, training and certification cost — and divide by the billable hours actually delivered in that period, not by 2,080. The denominator is where most firms flatter themselves, because dividing by a full year of hours silently assumes a utilisation rate that no inspection firm achieves.

Premium hours need their own treatment. Federal law pays overtime past forty hours in a workweek. California pays one and one-half times the regular rate for hours past eight in a workday and up to twelve, double time past twelve, time and a half for the first eight hours on the seventh consecutive day and double time beyond that. Turnaround schedules generate those hours by design, so a twelve-hour-day scope costed at flat rate is wrong before the crew mobilises.

sections.heading: Per diem is a daily cost, not a travel expense
paragraphs: Per diem is coded to travel, approved by whoever approves expenses, and never seen again. It is in fact one of the largest direct costs on any out-of-town job, incurred every single day the technician is away, whether or not that day was billable. GSA's FY2026 standard CONUS rate is $110 for lodging plus $68 for meals and incidental expenses, effective 1 October 2025 through 30 September 2026; non-standard localities are set higher, and Gulf Coast turnaround markets during outage season price accommodation well above the federal figure.

The distortion this creates is specific and directional. A five-day local job and a five-day out-of-town job at the same day rate look identical on a revenue report and differ by the entire travel and subsistence stack in reality. When per diem sits in an overhead pool, that difference is spread evenly across all jobs, which subsidises travel work with margin generated by local work and makes the local work look worse than it actually is.

Allocate per diem to the job, per day, at the point the travel is scheduled rather than when the expense claim lands. Two things follow immediately. Bidding on out-of-town work starts from the real cost floor rather than from a day rate. And the comparison between clients becomes honest, because the client who calls you only for distant emergency work stops being credited with margin that local clients generated.

sections.heading: Mobilisation and mileage on regional work
paragraphs: Mobilisation is frequently invoiced as a line item and almost never costed as one. The real cost is drive hours at the loaded rate, vehicle running cost, and — where the drive is long enough to require it — an overnight before the shift starts. Firms that bill a flat mobilisation charge across a wide service radius are cross-subsidising the far edge of that radius with the near edge, and the further they let the radius grow, the worse the trade becomes.

For vehicle cost, the IRS business standard mileage rate is the accessible published reference: 72.5 cents per mile for 1 January through 30 June 2026, rising to 76 cents per mile for 1 July through 31 December 2026. It is a tax and reimbursement rate rather than a costing rate, but it is published, defensible, and far closer to true cost than a fuel receipt, which excludes depreciation, tyres, insurance and maintenance entirely.

The scheduling side of the same decision — which qualified technician is closest, and what that choice costs — is covered in [crew dispatch](/erp/inspection-scheduling-crew-dispatch-software). Costing and dispatch read the same data from opposite ends: dispatch needs the cost consequence before the assignment is made, costing needs the assignment record afterwards. Holding both in one system removes the reconstruction step, and mileage stops being an argument at month end.

sections.heading: Consumables, equipment and the cost of staying qualified
paragraphs: Consumables are expensed at purchase and disappear into overhead: couplant, penetrant and developer, film and chemistry, batteries, wedges, transducers, magnetic particle media. Each is caused by a specific method on a specific job. Radiographic and penetrant scopes consume materially more than a UT thickness survey, so pooling consumables into overhead makes RT and PT look cheaper than they are and makes UT carry cost it never incurred.

The cost of remaining qualified belongs to the methods that require it, not to the company at large. Radiography carries a stack of recurring obligations under 10 CFR Part 34: survey instruments calibrated at intervals not to exceed six months under 34.25(b)(1), refresher safety training for each radiographer at intervals not to exceed twelve months under 34.43(d), and observation of each radiographer's job performance during an actual radiographic operation at intervals not to exceed six months under 34.43(e).

Those are real, recurring, method-attributable costs. Allocated to the RT line, they change the answer to "should we keep doing radiography in house or subcontract it". Left in overhead, that question cannot be asked at all, because the cost of holding the capability is invisible against the revenue it produces. The same logic applies to instrument depreciation and calibration on every other method you run.

sections.heading: Report preparation: the cost nobody meters
paragraphs: This is the largest silent cost in the industry. Field work ends and report work begins: data reduction, drafting, sketching, photographs, technique documentation, Level III technical review, quality review, client comments, revision, re-issue. On a complex multi-method scope, that work consumes a meaningful fraction of the field hours it documents. Almost none of it reaches a timesheet with a job number on it, because the people doing it are salaried and their time is treated as overhead.

The consequence is systematic rather than random. Report burden does not scale with revenue — it scales with scope complexity, component count, number of findings, and how much a particular client revises. Two jobs at identical revenue can differ several-fold in report hours. Costing that lands report time in overhead reports both jobs at the same margin and gives the sales team no signal that one client's work is structurally more expensive to deliver.

Metering it costs almost nothing. Report hours are captured the same way field hours are — against the same job number, by the same people, on the same [timesheet](/erp/timesheet-software-for-ndt-companies). What changes is the analysis: revision cycles become a visible cost per client, and the argument for fixing report quality upstream turns into arithmetic instead of opinion. That argument is made in full on [what makes an NDT report defensible](/report-validation/what-makes-an-ndt-report-defensible).

sections.heading: Subcontracted methods and pass-through margin
paragraphs: Subcontracting is where negative margin hides best, because the transaction looks clean. A purchase order goes out, an invoice comes back, the client is billed at a markup, and the arithmetic appears to work. What that arithmetic omits is the coordination: scheduling the sub, verifying and filing their certification records, receiving and reviewing their report, integrating it into your deliverable, and answering for it when the client queries a finding.

That coordination is your [Level III's](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services) time and your project manager's time, and it is rarely charged to the job. On a thin markup it exceeds the margin outright. Firms discover this as a pattern long before the accounting shows why — the same method, the same subcontractor, consistently the job nobody in the office wants to run.

Cost the sub's invoice to the job, and cost the internal hours the sub generates to the same job. The markup that clears both is the real minimum. Where a method is subcontracted repeatedly at a loss, the decision to build the capability in house finally has a number behind it — including the recurring qualification cost that the method will carry once you own it.

sections.heading: Reading profitability by client, by job type and by technician
paragraphs: With costs attached to jobs, three cuts become available that no revenue report can produce. By client: which accounts pay for the delivery they demand. By job type: which method mixes and scope sizes clear the loaded rate. By crew: which combinations complete scopes inside estimate and which consistently overrun, which is a training and estimating signal rather than a disciplinary one.

The client cut usually produces the most uncomfortable finding. Firms routinely discover that their largest account by revenue sits near the bottom by margin, because volume was won on rate concessions and the delivery burden — revision cycles, short-notice callouts, distant sites, extra reporting formats — was never priced. The response is not necessarily to resign the account. It is to reprice the specific behaviours that cost money, which requires knowing which ones they are.

The job-type cut drives quoting. When the historic cost of a five-day, two-technician multi-method turnaround is known with report hours and per diem included, the next quote for that shape of work starts from evidence instead of instinct. Firms quoting from a day rate and a guess are running an uncontrolled experiment on every bid, and only the accounting system ever learns the result.

sections.heading: Where the ledger stops and the job record starts
paragraphs: The accounting system's job is the general ledger, payroll, accounts payable and receivable, tax and the financial statements. It is good at those, and it is not built to be a job-costing engine for a field services firm, because it never sees the operational facts — who was dispatched, for how long, with what instrument, drawing how many per diem nights, generating how many hours of report preparation and review.

The workable architecture keeps both systems and gives each one the job it is good at. Operational cost is captured where it happens, in the job record: dispatch, timesheets, per diem, mileage, consumables, subcontractor purchase orders and report hours. Financial postings synchronise to the ledger. The mechanics of that synchronisation are set out on the [QuickBooks integration](/erp/ndt-software-quickbooks-integration) page, and [invoicing](/erp/invoicing-software-for-ndt-companies) draws from the same job record, so what you bill and what you costed reconcile by construction rather than by effort.

Atlantis builds this on Odoo, configured for inspection work rather than generic professional services — affordable, accessible and fully customisable to your method mix and cost structure. Ask for a demo run against one of your own recent turnaround jobs. Re-costing a job you have already closed and invoiced is the fastest way to find out whether the leak described on this page is yours, or [request a quote](/contact) scoped to your crew size.

faq.q: Should per diem be billed to the client or absorbed into the day rate?
faq.a: Either works commercially. Neither works if per diem is not costed to the job. Firms folding it into a blended day rate must still know the per-day subsistence cost of each job to know whether that rate clears; firms billing it separately must still cost it, because unbilled days, partial days and travel days accumulate quietly. The costing decision is independent of the billing decision.

faq.q: How do you capture report hours without adding admin burden?
faq.a: The same way field hours are captured — a job number on a timesheet. The change is cultural rather than technical: report time is invisible today because nobody is asked to record it, not because recording it is difficult. Start by metering Level III technical review and revision cycles, which is where the variation between clients concentrates and where the commercial signal is strongest.

faq.q: How far back should we re-cost historic jobs?
faq.a: Twelve months is enough to expose the pattern and recent enough that the operational facts are still recoverable. Pick a representative mix — a local single-method job, an out-of-town multi-method turnaround, and a job with heavy revision traffic — and rebuild all three fully. The difference between the reported margin and the rebuilt margin is the size of your blind spot.

faq.q: Does costing by technician turn into performance management?
faq.a: It is a capability signal, not a disciplinary one. Consistent overruns on a scope type point at training, technique or an estimate built on wrong assumptions far more often than at effort. Used to reprice work and target training, the cut is valuable. Used to rank people, it degrades the data, because timesheets stop being honest the week the ranking is published.

faq.q: Does Atlantis publish rates for this?
faq.a: Atlantis positions on affordable, accessible and fully customisable, and scopes each deployment to the firm's crew size, method mix and existing accounting system. Demo or quote on request. The third-party figures cited on this page — GSA per diem and IRS standard mileage rates — are published federal rates included because they are useful costing references, and they are not Atlantis pricing.

title: Inspection Report Portals: Revision Control, Not a Document Dump
description: Clients do not want a folder of PDFs. They want this asset's current report, with status and revision history. What a portal must structure and control.
h1: What a reliability engineer needs from your report portal at 2am
answer: A client portal for inspection reports must answer one question: what is the current, approved report for this asset, and what is its status. That requires reports indexed by equipment identifier rather than by delivery date, an explicit revision state so superseded issues are visibly superseded, and per-contact access control so a contractor sees only their scope.
expansion: Most inspection portals are built as delivery mechanisms — somewhere to put the PDF instead of attaching it to an email — when what the client needs is a retrieval mechanism organised the way they think about their plant. The difference between the two is not a feature list. It is the index. A client never searches for a filename; they search for an asset, a date range, or an open finding, because that is how a regulator, an insurer, a turnaround planner or a failure investigation frames the question. The fields that make asset-first retrieval possible already exist inside every compliant report. API 510, Eleventh Edition, October 2022, clause 7.8.2(b) requires the equipment identifier, the inspection date, the next scheduled inspection date, the examiner's name, a description of what was performed and the results. Making those structured fields rather than text on page one is what converts a document into a queryable record.
source: Clause references verified August 2026 against: API 510, Pressure Vessel Inspection Code, Eleventh Edition, October 2022 — clause 4.5.3 (examiner's employer shall maintain certification records including dates and results of personnel qualifications, available to the inspector); clause 7.8.1 (owner-operators shall maintain permanent and progressive records, permanent throughout the service life of each equipment item); clause 7.8.2(b) (inspection reports shall document the date of each inspection or examination, the date of the next scheduled inspection, the name of the person who performed it, the serial number or other identifier of the equipment inspected, a description of the inspection or examination performed and the results, and shall indicate the disposition of each inspection recommendation including why a recommendation was not implemented); clause 7.8.4 (documented results shall be approved by the responsible owner-operator inspector, engineer or qualified designee and should be posted into the appropriate inspection data management system within 90 days of completion of the inspection or startup). API 653, Tank Inspection, Repair, Alteration, and Reconstruction, Fifth Edition, November 2014, with Addendum 3, November 2023 — clause 6.8 (owner-operator shall maintain a complete record file of construction records, inspection history and repair/alteration history) and clause 6.9.1 (inspection reports, inspector recommendations and documentation of disposition shall be maintained by the owner/operator for the life of the tank). 29 CFR 1910.119(j)(4)(iv), as published on eCFR — the employer shall document each inspection and test performed on process equipment, recording the date, the name of the person who performed it, the serial number or other identifier of the equipment, a description of the inspection or test performed, and the results.

Retention obligations sit with the owner-operator, not with the inspection contractor — but a portal that indexes correctly is doing part of that work for them.

facets.q: What do clients actually search for in a report portal?
facets.a: An asset, a date range, or an open finding — never a filename. The four recurring triggers are an auditor or insurer asking for evidence on specific equipment, turnaround planning across a list of assets, a failure investigation needing history, and an invoice query. Every one of those starts from the plant's structure, which is why an index built on your job numbers and delivery dates fails on the first real question.

facets.q: Why does a shared drive fail as a client portal?
facets.a: Three reasons. Its index is the folder tree, which encodes your job numbering rather than the client's asset register. It carries no status, so the client emails to ask what is in progress and what has been superseded. And it has one permission set, while a real client account has a planner, a reliability engineer, a plant manager, an insurer's engineer and sometimes a repair contractor, all with different scopes.

facets.q: How should revisions be handled so the client always sees current?
facets.a: As a revision chain on one record, not as separate files in a folder. Every superseded issue carries a visible superseded marker and a link to the current revision, and contacts who downloaded an earlier version are notified when it is replaced. The failure to design against is a client making an engineering decision in September from a revision that was corrected in March.

facets.q: How does access control work across multiple client contacts?
facets.a: On three axes: identity, asset scope, and permitted actions — view, download, comment, approve, and whether commercial information is visible at all. Third parties such as an insurer's engineer or a repair contractor receive scoped read access to an asset group with an expiry date. Grant is administered by the client's own administrator, so your project manager never decides who inside the client may see what.

facets.q: What does a client portal do to your admin workload?
facets.a: It removes the highest-volume categories from the coordinator's inbox: report requests, status enquiries, version checks, re-sends to a new contact, and bulk requests for everything on a unit. Those arrive during your working hours regardless of when the client actually needed them, and each consumes time twice — once finding the file, once replying. Self-service moves that time to billable work.

facets.q: How long does the client have to keep inspection reports?
facets.a: Long. API 510, Eleventh Edition, October 2022, clause 7.8.1 requires pressure vessel owner-operators to maintain permanent and progressive records, permanent throughout the service life of each equipment item. API 653, Fifth Edition with Addendum 3, November 2023, clause 6.9.1 requires inspection reports, inspector recommendations and documentation of disposition to be maintained for the life of the tank.

sections.heading: The client's question is never "send me the file"
paragraphs: A reliability engineer opens your portal for one of four reasons: a regulator, insurer or auditor has asked for evidence on a specific piece of equipment; a turnaround is being planned and they need the last inspection across a list of assets; something failed and they need the history; or finance is querying an invoice. Every one of those starts from an asset, a date range or a finding. None of them starts from a filename or a job number.

That is the entire design brief, and it explains why so many portals disappoint the people who paid for them. They are built as delivery mechanisms — a place to put the PDF instead of attaching it to an email — when the client needs a retrieval mechanism organised the way they think about their plant. The gap between the two is not a feature list. It is the index the whole thing is built on.

The client is also working to their own recordkeeping obligation, not to yours. Under API 510, Eleventh Edition, October 2022, clause 7.8.1, pressure vessel owner-operators shall maintain permanent and progressive records — permanent throughout the service life of each item, progressive so new information is added as it arrives. Your portal either feeds that obligation cleanly or creates fresh work for the client every single time you deliver something.

sections.heading: The document dump, and why the shared folder fails
paragraphs: The default portal is a folder tree: client, year, month, job number, PDF. It fails on the first real query. Asked for the current report on vessel V-1204, the engineer must already know which job number covered that vessel, which month the work was performed, and whether a revision was issued afterwards under a different job. None of that lives in the folder structure, so retrieval collapses into a filename search — which works only if your naming convention has never changed.

The second failure is status. A folder shows what has been delivered. It does not show what is in progress, what is awaiting Level III review, what has been issued pending client comment, and what has been superseded. The client compensates by emailing to ask, which is precisely the traffic the portal was bought to eliminate. The portal then costs you a licence fee and saves you nothing at all.

The third is that a folder has one permission set. Real client accounts have a maintenance planner, a reliability engineer, a corrosion specialist, a plant manager, an insurer's engineer and sometimes a third-party repair contractor, with different scopes and different rights to see commercial information. One shared link serves none of them correctly, and the usual workaround is a second folder, then a third, and then a reconciliation problem nobody owns.

sections.heading: Index by asset, not by delivery date
paragraphs: The highest-value design decision available is to make the equipment identifier the primary key of the portal. Reports hang off assets; jobs become a secondary view. The client navigates to V-1204 and sees its inspection history in date order, current status, next due date, open recommendations, and every report ever issued against it — including reports produced by other contractors, if the client chooses to load them alongside yours.

The identifier is not something you have to invent. API 510 clause 7.8.2(b) requires inspection reports to document the serial number or other identifier of the equipment inspected, alongside the date of the inspection, the date of the next scheduled inspection, the name of the person who performed it, a description of what was performed and the results. Those fields already have to exist. Making them structured data rather than text on page one is what turns a document into a queryable record.

The same five elements appear in OSHA's process safety management standard. 29 CFR 1910.119(j)(4)(iv) requires the employer to document each inspection and test performed on process equipment with the date, the name of the person who performed it, the serial number or other identifier of the equipment, a description of the inspection or test, and the results. Build the data model on those five fields and the portal satisfies the client's [mechanical integrity](/consulting/osha-psm-mechanical-integrity-ndt) retrieval need by construction rather than by luck.

sections.heading: Status is a field, not a phone call
paragraphs: Clients ask "where is my report" more often than they ask for the report itself, because the answer determines whether they can close a work order or release equipment back to service. A portal that exposes an explicit state — field work complete, data under reduction, technical review by Level III, issued for client comment, approved, superseded — answers that question every time without consuming a human on either side of the relationship.

There is a published expectation attached to this. API 510 clause 7.8.4 states that documented inspection results shall be approved by the responsible owner-operator inspector, engineer or qualified designee, and should be posted into the appropriate inspection data management system within ninety days of completion of the inspection or startup. The owner-operator carries that duty, and they cannot meet it if your report lands on day eighty-five with findings that need discussion.

Exposing your own state is uncomfortable and useful in equal measure. Firms that publish status discover the queue is almost never in the field — it sits in review. That is a resourcing conversation about [Level III review capacity](/consulting/asnt-level-iii-consulting-services), and it is far better had with data from your own status field than with an angry client on the phone quoting a date you promised three weeks ago.

sections.heading: Revision handling: the client must never open a superseded report by accident
paragraphs: Reports get revised. A transcription error is found, a client comment lands, a recommendation is reworded after an engineering assessment, a thickness reading is corrected. The dangerous failure mode is not the revision itself. It is the client who downloaded revision 0 in March, saved it to their own drive, and makes a [fitness-for-service](/consulting/fitness-for-service-api-579) decision from it in September without ever knowing revision 1 exists.

The portal has to make superseded status impossible to miss and current status one click away. That means a revision chain held on one record rather than separate files, a visible superseded marker on every earlier issue, a link from any superseded revision straight to the current one, and — where the client's own system pulled a copy — a notification to the specific contacts who accessed the earlier version.

Retention makes this a permanent requirement rather than a temporary one. API 653, Fifth Edition, November 2014 with Addendum 3, November 2023, clause 6.9.1 requires inspection reports along with inspector recommendations and documentation of disposition to be maintained by the owner/operator for the life of the tank. A revision chain that is legible in year one and ambiguous in year twelve has failed at exactly the moment it was built for.

sections.heading: Recommendations are objects, not paragraphs
paragraphs: The most valuable content in an inspection report is the recommendation, and it is the content a PDF handles worst. Buried in section seven of a forty-page document, a recommendation has no status, no owner, no due date and no closure record. The client's follow-up lives in a separate spreadsheet maintained by one person, and the link between that spreadsheet and your report is a human memory that leaves when they do.

API 510 clause 7.8.2(b) is explicit that the records should indicate the disposition of each inspection recommendation, including the reason why a recommendation was not implemented. That is a lifecycle, and lifecycles belong in a database rather than in prose. A portal carrying recommendations as tracked items — open, accepted, deferred with justification, closed, closed by repair — hands the client the exact artefact their auditor asks for, already assembled.

It also changes your commercial position. Open recommendations are the client's forward work list, and the contractor whose portal holds that list is present at the moment the next scope is defined. This is the quiet reason portals repay their cost, and it is the same reason [digital twin context](/digital-twins) beside a report shifts the conversation from document delivery to asset condition, where the next job actually comes from.

sections.heading: Access control across many contacts on one account
paragraphs: Client organisations are not single users. A workable permission model has three axes: who the person is, which assets or units they may see, and what they may do — view, download, comment, approve, or see commercial information such as rates and invoices. Collapsing that to one shared login guarantees either over-exposure or constant manual gatekeeping, and both are worse than the email traffic they replaced.

Two cases break naive designs. The first is the third party: an insurer's engineer, an authorised inspector, or a consultant retained by the client, who needs scoped read access for a defined period and no commercial visibility whatsoever. The second is the client's own repair contractor, who needs the inspection findings for the work they are quoting but has no business seeing the rest of the plant's records.

Both are solved by scoping access to asset groups with an expiry date, granted by the client's administrator rather than by your project manager. That puts the gatekeeping decision with the person who actually knows the answer, and it removes your firm from a judgement you should never be making — which of your client's people, and which of your client's other vendors, are entitled to see which of your client's records.

sections.heading: Who performed it, and were they qualified
paragraphs: The question arrives during audits, insurance reviews and disputes: who performed this examination, and were they certified in that method on that date. A portal showing a signature block answers half of it. API 510 clause 4.5.3 places the duty on the examiner's employer to maintain certification records of the examiners employed, including dates and results of personnel qualifications, and to make those records available to the inspector.

Meeting that from a filing cabinet takes a day of somebody's time. Meeting it from the same system that dispatched the technician takes a click, because the [certification record](/erp/ndt-personnel-certification-tracking) and the report are joined by the person and the date. Firms that can produce this on demand shorten audits materially, and audit friction is a real unbudgeted cost that nobody quotes for. It is also the strongest answer available when a report is challenged.

Exposing certification evidence through the portal is a choice rather than a requirement, and the firms that make it convert a compliance burden into a differentiator no competitor can match on a proposal. Where the client's own review process is the concern, the distinction between reviewing a report and re-running the examination is set out in [third-party review versus re-inspection](/report-validation/third-party-review-vs-re-inspection). The portal is where that review starts.

sections.heading: The 2am effect: what self-service does to your admin load
paragraphs: The commercial argument for a portal is usually made on client satisfaction. The larger effect lands on your own overhead. Every report request arriving by email consumes a coordinator's time twice — once to find the file, once to reply — and it arrives during your working hours regardless of when the client actually needed it. A client who retrieves the report themselves at 2am consumes none of it, and gets a better answer faster.

The volume is not trivial. Report requests, status enquiries, "is this the latest version", re-sends to a new contact, and "can you send everything for this unit" make up the bulk of an inspection coordinator's inbox. Structuring the portal around asset, status and revision removes the categories generating the most traffic, and that coordinator's time moves to work that is billable rather than work that is apologetic.

The retention argument closes it. Your client must hold these records for the service life of the equipment, and a portal keeping the current, approved, correctly indexed version available is doing part of their compliance job for them. Atlantis builds this on Odoo as part of the [inspection ERP](/erp) — affordable, accessible, fully customisable to your report formats and your clients' asset hierarchies. Ask for a demo against one unit of a real client's plant, or [request a quote](/contact).

faq.q: Should a portal replace emailing reports entirely?
faq.a: Keep the notification, drop the attachment. Email is the right channel for telling a named contact that a report has been issued or revised; it is the wrong channel for storage, because the attached copy diverges from the current revision the moment one is issued. Send a notification carrying a link into the record, and the version the client opens is always current.

faq.q: Who should be able to download the raw data files?
faq.a: Whoever the client's administrator says. Raw UT data files, phased array scan files, radiographs and thickness datasets are the client's records and belong in the portal alongside the report, scoped like any other artefact. The practical constraint is file size and format, not entitlement — publish them as downloadable attachments on the report record rather than holding them back until someone asks.

faq.q: What happens to portal access when a contract ends?
faq.a: The client keeps their records. Designing a portal so that access to already-delivered reports depends on an active contract creates a hostage relationship clients notice and remember, and it works against their own obligation to maintain permanent records. Expire third-party and repair-contractor access on schedule; leave the client's own contacts with continued read access to everything you delivered them.

faq.q: Does a portal help when a client wants a third-party report review?
faq.a: It removes the retrieval delay, which is most of the elapsed time in a review. A reviewer granted scoped access reads the current revision, the full revision history, the recommendation dispositions and the technique documentation without a single file transfer or a chase email. What such a review can and cannot conclude from that material is a separate question, covered across the report validation pages.

faq.q: Can the portal show asset context alongside the report?
faq.a: Yes, and it changes the conversation. A report attached to a 3D asset model carrying inspection history, corrosion rates and next-due dates moves the client from reading documents to assessing condition. Atlantis builds this on Odoo with an optional digital twin layer over the same asset records — affordable, accessible, fully customisable. Demo or quote on request.

title: UT Level I Practice Questions: 15 Worked Answers
description: Fifteen original UT Level I practice questions with worked answers, the physics or ASME code basis for each, and exactly where Level I authority stops.
h1: Ultrasonic Level I Practice Questions, Worked From the Physics Up
answer: Level I ultrasonic testing is set-up, calibration and recording to a written instruction — not interpretation. These fifteen original questions test what that scope actually requires: wavelength and velocity arithmetic, near field and dead zone, IIW block use, DAC construction, couplant control under ASME Section V Article 4, and the point where a Level I hands the indication to a Level II.
expansion:
Every number on this page was checked before it was written. Velocities come from published acoustic property tables; the calibration, couplant and temperature requirements come from ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4; the qualification structure comes from ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Where a value could not be confirmed, the requirement is stated without it.

That matters more at Level I than anywhere else, because a Level I is trained to execute a written instruction exactly and has no authority to correct it. A technician who memorises a wrong near-field constant will build a wrong set-up and record wrong data with complete confidence. The questions below are original, written on the published body of knowledge rather than copied from any examination, and each one carries the reasoning that makes the answer transferable to the next part you put a probe on.
source: Checked August 2026 against published ASME BPVC Section V, Article 4 text (T-432 temperature, T-433 couplant contaminant limits, Figure T-434.2.1 basic calibration block, T-463 calibration checks, T-471 scanning) and ASNT SNT-TC-1A (Level I scope wording, Table 6.3.1A training and experience hours, recommended grading), plus ISO 2400 for the IIW Type 1 (V1) block and published acoustic property tables for carbon steel and aluminium. These values have carried unchanged through recent Section V editions. Confirm every number against the edition your construction code invokes before applying it on a job.

table.caption: How a UT Level I qualification is built, and what each part actually tests

All three examinations taken together
